knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Smooth-Term Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive composites whose differentiable term may be nonconvex while the regularizer remains convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonconvex smooth-term composite on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(F(x)=f(x)+g(x)\), where \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable but need not be convex, and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. The objective is generally nonconvex and may be nonsmooth through \(g\). A composite stationary point is any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\) satisfying \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\). Every local minimizer satisfies this inclusion, but a stationary point need not be globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Here the smooth loss may be nonconvex while the regularizer is closed convex; local minimizers obey the composite stationarity inclusion, which is not globally sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) locally minimizes \(F\Rightarrow0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\), without a converse global-optimality guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Regularizer Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive composites with a smooth loss and a proper lower-semicontinuous nonconvex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonconvex-regularizer composite on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form \(F(x)=f(x)+r(x)\), where \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable and \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous but need not be convex. Using the limiting subdifferential, a stationary point satisfies \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial r(x)\). Every local minimizer at which the standard limiting-subdifferential sum rule applies satisfies this inclusion. Unlike the convex-regularizer case, the inclusion need not characterize global minimizers and \(\partial r(x)\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth term is combined with a proper closed nonconvex regularizer; limiting-subdifferential stationarity is necessary under the sum rule but does not ensure global optimality.
assumptions_latex: The limiting-subdifferential sum rule holds at the local minimizer considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) locally minimizes \(F\Rightarrow0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial r(x)\), subject to the stated sum rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Additive Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding a constrained smooth-plus-nonsmooth problem by an indicator-augmented objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\). With the indicator \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, the constrained problem \(\min_{x\in C}\{f(x)+g(x)\}\) is equivalent to \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{f(x)+g(x)+\delta_C(x)\}\). The two problems have identical infimal values and minimizers. If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \(C\) is convex, the extended objective is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provided the constrained objective is finite at some feasible point, adding the set indicator converts it into an unconstrained extended-real problem without changing its minimizers or infimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}(f(x)+g(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}(f(x)+g(x)+\delta_C(x))\), and the two infimal values are equal.

notation.meaning: effective domain where g is finite

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Additive Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional composite objectives over a fixed partition of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb{R}^n=E_1\times\cdots\times E_B\), write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_B)\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. A block-separable additive composite objective has the form \[F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{b=1}^{B}r_b(x_b),\] where each \(r_b:E_b\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. Its nonsmooth term \(R(x)=\sum_{b=1}^{B}r_b(x_b)\) contains no term depending jointly on two distinct blocks; extended values may encode blockwise constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth loss is augmented by a sum of nonsmooth terms, each depending on exactly one block of a coordinate partition.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{R}^n=E_1\times\cdots\times E_B\) is a fixed product decomposition.
\(f\) is differentiable and every \(r_b\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{b=1}^{B}r_b(x_b)\) is block-separable in its nonsmooth component.

notation.meaning: The component of x in block space E_b.
The extended-real regularizer or constraint term for block b.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicomponent Additive Composites
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite additive composites with component-specific linear feature maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. A multicomponent additive composite is an extended-real function \[F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j(L_jx),\] where \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable, each \(L_j:X\to Y_j\) is linear, and each \(r_j:Y_j\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. Unlike block separability, the maps \(L_j\) need not select disjoint coordinates, so several components may depend on the same variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a smooth function plus finitely many nonsmooth component functions applied to linear images that may reuse variables.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable; each \(L_j\) is linear and each \(r_j\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j\circ L_j\) is a multicomponent additive composite.

notation.meaning: Linear feature map for component j.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports this multicomponent linear-composite formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the multicomponent-additive leaf and its variables and domains are explicit, but no source with a specific locator supports the linear-image formulation or its distinction from block separability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive-cost models and their separable-dual form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum objective structure, componentwise algorithmic access, and the additive minimization representation of a separable problem's dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An additive-cost objective has the form \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x)\), where \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Its structure permits incremental methods that update \(x\) using one component \(f_i\) at a time and linearization methods that approximate the components individually. In particular, if \(q_i(\mu)=\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\{f_i(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{r}\mu_j g_{ij}(x_i)\}\), then the separable dual problem \(\max_{\mu\ge 0}\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_i(\mu)\) becomes the additive-cost minimization problem \(\min_{\mu\ge 0}\sum_{i=1}^{m}[-q_i(\mu)]\) after changing signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive-cost objective is a finite sum of component functions. This permits methods that use or approximate individual components rather than the whole objective. The dual objective of a separable problem is an important instance: after changing its sign, maximizing the sum of the component dual functions becomes minimizing the sum of their negatives over nonnegative multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x),\qquad \max_{\mu\ge0}\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_i(\mu)\equiv\min_{\mu\ge0}\sum_{i=1}^{m}[-q_i(\mu)].

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Block Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive regularization when coordinate blocks intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be nonempty coordinate groups, and let \(P_{G_j}x=x_{G_j}\). An overlapping block architecture has objective \[F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j(P_{G_j}x),\] with at least one pair \(j\ne k\) satisfying \(G_j\cap G_k\ne\varnothing\). Here \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and each \(r_j\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. A coordinate in an intersection contributes to every component whose group contains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several nonsmooth block terms act on intersecting coordinate groups, so a shared coordinate contributes to multiple regularizer components.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j(P_{G_j}x)\) has an overlapping block architecture.

children.title: Coupled Component Regularizers
children.top_down_role: Multicomponent models with regularizers linking otherwise distinct components.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Component Regularizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularizers containing genuine joint dependence across prescribed components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=E_1\times\cdots\times E_B\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_B)\). A proper lower-semicontinuous regularizer \(R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is coupled across the prescribed blocks if no functions \(r_b:E_b\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and constant \(c\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \[R(x)=c+\sum_{b=1}^{B}r_b(x_b)\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Thus an objective \(F(x)=f(x)+R(x)\) contains nonsmooth interactions or joint constraints that cannot be assigned independently to individual blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled regularizer cannot, even up to a constant, be decomposed into separate functions of the prescribed variable blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(X=E_1\times\cdots\times E_B\) is the prescribed block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is coupled exactly when \(R\ne c+\sum_{b=1}^{B}r_b\circ P_b\) for every admissible \(c\) and collection \((r_b)\).

notation.meaning: Canonical projection from X onto block E_b.

review_flags: The supplied sources do not identify a canonical definition of coupling relative to prescribed blocks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed nonseparability criterion is coherent relative to a prescribed product decomposition, but no cited source establishes that this is the intended canonical meaning of coupled component regularization. The admissible class of component functions in the conclusion also requires source-backed clarification.

children.title: Regularized Empirical Risk Model
children.top_down_role: Data-fit aggregation paired with structure-inducing regularization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Holdout and K-Fold Cross-Validation for Hyperparameter Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validation and cross-validated risks, hyperparameter selection, and final refitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\widehat\theta_\lambda(\mathcal D')\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\theta R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D')$. For disjoint training and validation sets, define $R_\lambda^{\mathrm{val}}=R_0(\widehat\theta_\lambda(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}}),\mathcal D_{\mathrm{valid}})$. For a partition $\mathcal D=\bigsqcup_{k=1}^K\mathcal D_k$, let $\mathcal D_{-k}=\mathcal D\setminus\mathcal D_k$ and define $R_\lambda^{\mathrm{cv}}=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K R_0(\widehat\theta_\lambda(\mathcal D_{-k}),\mathcal D_k)$. Select $\widehat\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\lambda R_\lambda^{\mathrm{cv}}$ and then refit $\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\theta R_{\widehat\lambda}(\theta,\mathcal D)$. If $K=N$ and each fold is a singleton, the procedure is leave-one-out cross-validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Holdout validation trains on one subset and evaluates unregularized loss on disjoint data. K-fold cross-validation averages held-out loss across folds, selects the hyperparameter minimizing that average, and refits the selected model using all observations. Singleton folds yield leave-one-out cross-validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_\lambda^{\mathrm{cv}}=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K R_0(\widehat\theta_\lambda(\mathcal D_{-k}),\mathcal D_k),\qquad \widehat\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\lambda R_\lambda^{\mathrm{cv}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized Empirical Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines complexity-penalized empirical risk and qualifies its penalized-likelihood interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given empirical risk $R(f,\mathcal D)$, a complexity functional $C$, and $\lambda\ge0$, the regularized empirical risk is $R_\lambda(f,\mathcal D)=R(f,\mathcal D)+\lambda C(f)$. For a parametric predictor, $R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D)=R(\theta,\mathcal D)+\lambda C(\theta)$. Under log loss with $C(\theta)=-\log p(\theta)$, $R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D)=-\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\log p(y_n\mid x_n,\theta)-\lambda\log p(\theta)$, whose minimizers are MAP estimators for the effective prior proportional to $p(\theta)^{N\lambda}$ whenever that prior is normalizable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized empirical risk adds a nonnegative-strength complexity penalty to empirical risk. With log loss and a negative-log-prior penalty, it has a MAP interpretation with prior weighting determined by the sample-size and regularization scaling.

p(\theta)^{N\lambda}\text{ is normalizable for the stated effective-prior interpretation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Risk Bound for Squared-Euclidean Regularized ERM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected population-risk guarantee for convex Lipschitz linear prediction with squared-Euclidean regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(\ell(y,\cdot)\) is convex and \(G\)-Lipschitz, predictions have the form \(x\mapsto\theta^\top\varphi(x)\) for \(\theta\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\|\varphi(x)\|_2\le R\) almost surely. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Training-Risk Selection Degeneracy and Structural Risk Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the zero-regularization degeneracy of selecting penalty strength by optimized training risk and contrasts it with population-risk-based selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D)=R(\theta,\mathcal D)+\lambda C(\theta)$, where $\lambda\ge0$ and $C(\theta)\ge0$. Then $\min_\theta R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D)\ge\min_\theta R_0(\theta,\mathcal D)$ for every $\lambda\ge0$, so $0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\ge0}\min_\theta R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D)$. Structural risk minimization instead selects model complexity using population risk or an estimate of it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a nonnegative penalty, the best achievable regularized training objective cannot improve on its value at zero regularization. Thus training-objective selection admits zero regularization as an optimum. Structural risk minimization instead uses population risk or an estimate of it to choose model complexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\ge0}\min_\theta R_\lambda(\theta,\mathcal D).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: BMRM Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cutting-plane bundle method for the regularized objective \(F=\lambda\Omega+R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\mathbf w_0\in\mathbb R^n\), at iteration \(t\geq1\) evaluate \(R(\mathbf w_{t-1})\) and choose \(R'(\mathbf w_{t-1})\in\partial R(\mathbf w_{t-1})\). Form \(R_t(\mathbf w)=\max_{0\leq i\leq t-1}\{R(\mathbf w_i)+\langle R'(\mathbf w_i),\mathbf w-\mathbf w_i\rangle\}\), define \(F_t(\mathbf w)=\lambda\Omega(\mathbf w)+R_t(\mathbf w)\), and set \(\mathbf w_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf w}F_t(\mathbf w)\). Terminate when \(F(\mathbf w_t)-F_t(\mathbf w_t)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: BMRM repeatedly adds a subgradient cutting plane for the empirical risk, minimizes the regularized piecewise-linear lower model, and stops when the true objective minus the model value at the new iterate is at most ε.
assumptions_latex: At every evaluated point, a subgradient \(R'(\mathbf w_i)\in\partial R(\mathbf w_i)\) is available.
Each displayed reduced-master problem admits a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\mathbf w_t)-F_t(\mathbf w_t)\leq\varepsilon\) at termination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: High-Probability Risk Bound for Norm-Penalized Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A norm-dependent population-risk bound whose geometry enters through the dual norm and its Rademacher parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^d\), with dual norm \(\Omega^*\), and suppose \(\mathcal R(\theta)=\mathbb E[\ell(y,\theta^\top\varphi(x))]\) is minimized at \(\theta_*\in\mathbb R^d\). Assume that \(\theta\mapsto\ell(y,\theta^\top\varphi(x))\) is convex and \(GR\)-Lipschitz on \(\{\theta:\Omega(\theta)\le2\Omega(\theta_*)\}\), and that \(\Omega^*(\varphi(x))\le R\) almost surely. Define \[\rho_\Omega=\sup_{\Omega^*(z_i)\le1,\ 1\le i\le n}\mathbb E_\varepsilon\!\left[\Omega^*\!\left(\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i z_i\right)\right],\] where \(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n\) are independent Rademacher variables. For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), set \[\lambda=\frac{4GR}{\sqrt n}\left(\rho_\Omega+\sqrt{\frac12\log\frac1\delta}\right).\] Then, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), every minimizer \(\widehat\theta_\lambda\) of \(\widehat{\mathcal R}(\theta)+\lambda\Omega(\theta)\) satisfies \[\mathcal R(\widehat\theta_\lambda)\le\mathcal R(\theta_*)+\Omega(\theta_*)\frac{8GR}{\sqrt n}\left(\rho_\Omega+\sqrt{\frac12\log\frac1\delta}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex loss that is Lipschitz on the specified norm ball and features bounded in the dual norm, the prescribed regularization parameter gives, with probability at least one minus delta, a norm- and Rademacher-geometry-dependent population-risk bound for every penalized empirical-risk minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\text{ is a norm on }\mathbb R^d\text{ with dual norm }\Omega^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\!\left(\mathcal R(\widehat\theta_\lambda)\le\mathcal R(\theta_*)+\Omega(\theta_*)\frac{8GR}{\sqrt n}\left(\rho_\Omega+\sqrt{\frac12\log\frac1\delta}\right)\ \text{for every minimizer }\widehat\theta_\lambda\right)\ge1-\delta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empirical Distribution, Empirical Risk, and ERM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-sample empirical representation of prediction risk and its minimization over a hypothesis class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dataset $\mathcal D=\{(x_n,y_n)\}_{n=1}^N$, the empirical distribution assigns mass $1/N$ to each observation. Hence the empirical risk of a predictor $f$ is $R(f,\mathcal D)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\ell(y_n,f(x_n))$, and empirical risk minimization selects $\widehat f_{\mathrm{ERM}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{f\in\mathcal H}R(f,\mathcal D)$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine sparsity constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines affine constraints on coordinatewise nonzero indicators and records the nonclosedness boundary for a lower cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\|\!\|x\|\!\|_0=(|x_1|_0,\ldots,|x_n|_0)^\top\), where \(|x_j|_0=1\) if \(x_j\neq0\) and \(|x_j|_0=0\) otherwise. Given \(A=[a_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^k\), an affine sparsity constraint is \(A\|\!\|x\|\!\|_0\le b\), equivalently \(\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}|x_j|_0\le b_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\). It includes cardinality bounds \(k_1\le\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|_0\le k_2\); the lower constraint \(\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|_0\ge k_1\) alone defines a nonclosed feasible set when \(1\le k_1\le n\), and negative coefficients in an affine sparsity inequality introduce lower-cardinality-type closure issues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine sparsity constraint is a system of affine inequalities in the indicators of which coordinates of x are nonzero. It can encode logical selection rules, budgets, and upper or lower cardinality bounds. A nontrivial lower cardinality constraint by itself has a nonclosed feasible set, while negative coefficients create analogous closure concerns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\|\!\|x\|\!\|_0\le b\iff \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}|x_j|_0\le b_i\ \forall i=1,\ldots,k;\quad \{x:\sum_{j=1}^n|x_j|_0\ge k_1\}\text{ is nonclosed for }1\le k_1\le n.

knowledge_statements.title: Group Sparsity Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-norm penalties over a partition of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{G}=\{G_1,\ldots,G_m\}\) be a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(w_g>0\), and choose \(q\in[1,\infty]\). The group sparsity penalty is \[R(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_q,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] It is a convex norm and is nonsmooth whenever an entire group vector \(x_g\) vanishes. For \(q=2\), this is the weighted group-lasso penalty and treats the coordinates within each group jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group sparsity penalty sums norms of disjoint coordinate groups, encouraging whole groups rather than isolated coordinates to vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_q\) is a convex group sparsity norm.

notation.meaning: Subvector of x indexed by group g.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Group GLM Lasso estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group-norm-regularized empirical risk estimator for generalized linear models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), a prescribed group family \(\mathcal G\), a GLM function \(\psi\), and regularization parameter \(\lambda_n\), the group GLM Lasso is any estimator
\[
\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\psi(\langle\theta,x_i\rangle)-y_i\langle\theta,x_i\rangle\right]+\lambda_n\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\|\theta_g\|_2\right\}.
\]
This family includes the least-squares group Lasso as a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The group GLM Lasso minimizes the empirical generalized-linear-model loss plus a regularization parameter times the sum of the Euclidean norms of predefined coefficient groups. It includes the least-squares group Lasso as a special case.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\theta\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\psi(\langle\theta,x_i\rangle)-y_i\langle\theta,x_i\rangle\right]+\lambda_n\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\|\theta_g\|_2\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: High-probability error bound for the group GLM Lasso
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Squared Euclidean estimation error under GLM regularity, grouped-design normalization, restricted strong convexity, prescribed tuning, and a group-support size condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\) i.i.d. samples come from a GLM satisfying \((G1')\) and \((G2)\), and suppose that
\[
\mathcal E_n(\Delta)\ge\kappa\|\Delta\|_2^2-c_1\left(\frac mn+\frac{\log|\mathcal G|}{n}\right)\|\Delta\|_{\mathcal G,2}^2
\quad\text{for all }\|\Delta\|_2\le1.
\]
Let \(\widehat\theta\) be a solution of the group GLM Lasso using
\[
\lambda_n=4BC\left(\sqrt{\frac mn}+\sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal G|}{n}}+\delta\right),\qquad \delta\in(0,1).
\]
If the true regression vector \(\theta^*\) has group support \(S_{\mathcal G}\) and
\[
|S_{\mathcal G}|\left(\lambda_n^2+\frac mn+\frac{\log|\mathcal G|}{n}\right)<\min\left\{\frac{4\kappa^2}{9},\frac{\kappa}{64c_1}\right\},
\]
then
\[
\|\widehat\theta-\theta^*\|_2^2\le\frac94\frac{|S_{\mathcal G}|\lambda_n^2}{\kappa^2}
\]
with probability at least \(1-2e^{-2n\delta^2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the group GLM Lasso with the prescribed regularization level, i.i.d. GLM data satisfying group normalization, condition (G2), and restricted strong convexity yield a high-probability squared Euclidean error bound. The result requires the group-support size times the combined tuning and statistical tolerance to be below the stated curvature thresholds.
assumptions_latex: \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\text{ are i.i.d. from a GLM satisfying }(G1')\text{ and }(G2)
\widehat\theta\text{ is a solution of the group GLM Lasso}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Group Lasso and Block-Sparsity Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularizers intended to select or eliminate predefined blocks of coefficients jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the parameter vector into predefined groups, \(w=[w_1,\ldots,w_G]\). A group-sparsity estimator minimizes \[\operatorname{NLL}(w)+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^G\|w_g\|_2,\qquad \lambda>0.\] With a least-squares negative log-likelihood, this is group lasso. The nonsquared group norms promote entire blocks \(w_g\) becoming zero. The variant \(\sum_g\|w_g\|_\infty\), where \(\|w_g\|_\infty=\max_{d\in g}|w_d|\), also promotes group sparsity. For a disjoint exhaustive partition, \(\sum_g\|w_g\|_2^2=\|w\|_2^2\), so squared group norms instead give an ordinary squared-L2 penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group lasso penalizes the sum of the Euclidean norms of predefined coefficient blocks, encouraging whole blocks to vanish. Infinity-norm block penalties are another group-sparsity variant. For disjoint exhaustive groups, summing squared block norms reduces to ordinary squared-L2 regularization.
assumptions_latex: \text{The squared-norm identity assumes that the groups form a disjoint exhaustive partition.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat w\in\operatorname*{argmin}_w\left\{\operatorname{NLL}(w)+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^G\|w_g\|_2\right\},\text{ a penalty designed to promote blockwise sparsity.}

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Group Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group penalties whose coordinate groups need not form a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{G}\) be a finite family of nonempty subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(g\cap h\ne\varnothing\) for some distinct \(g,h\in\mathcal{G}\). For weights \(w_g>0\) and \(q\in[1,\infty]\), the direct overlapping-group penalty is \[R(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_q.\] Every coordinate appearing in several groups is counted in each corresponding term. Thus the architecture is group-additive but not block-separable with respect to a coordinate partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularizer sums norms over intersecting coordinate groups, counting shared coordinates in every group that contains them.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{G}\) is a finite family of nonempty coordinate subsets with at least one overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}w_g\lVert x_g\rVert_q\) is a direct overlapping-group regularizer.

notation.meaning: Family of possibly intersecting coordinate groups.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adaptive group GLM Lasso squared-error bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-sample Euclidean estimation-error guarantee under the cited GLM and restricted-strong-convexity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(n\) i.i.d. samples from a GLM satisfying conditions \((\mathrm{G1}')\) and \((\mathrm{G2})\), suppose that the RSC condition (9.76) holds with curvature \(\kappa>0\), and that
\[
\left(\sqrt{|S_{\mathrm{elt}}|}+\omega\sqrt{|S_{\mathcal G}|}\right)^2\left(\lambda_n^2+\frac{\log d}{n}\right)<\min\left\{\frac{\kappa^2}{36},\frac{\kappa}{64c_1}\right\}.
\]
Then the adaptive group GLM Lasso estimate \(\widehat\theta\) satisfies
\[
\|\widehat\theta-\theta^*\|_2^2\leq \frac{36\lambda_n^2}{\kappa^2}\left(\sqrt{|S_{\mathrm{elt}}|}+\omega\sqrt{|S_{\mathcal G}|}\right)^2
\]
with probability at least \(1-3e^{-8n\delta^2}\).

GLM samples satisfying conditions (G1′) and (G2), if the cited restricted-strong-convexity condition holds with positive curvature and the stated smallness condition is satisfied, then the adaptive group GLM Lasso estimate obeys the stated squared Euclidean error bound with probability at least 1−3 exp(−8nδ²).

The RSC condition (9.76) holds with curvature \(\kappa>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Support Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ancestor-closed supports on a rooted coordinate hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a rooted tree or directed acyclic graph whose vertices index parameter blocks \((x_v)_{v\in V}\). A block support \[S(x)=\{v\in V:\lVert x_v\rVert_2>0\}\] satisfies the hierarchical support condition when, for every \(v\in S(x)\), every ancestor \(u\) of \(v\) also belongs to \(S(x)\). Equivalently, \(S(x)\) is ancestor-closed. The associated extended-real constraint is \(I_{\mathcal H}(x)=0\) when this condition holds and \(I_{\mathcal H}(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support is hierarchical when activating any block requires every ancestral block in the prescribed rooted hierarchy to be active.
assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a rooted tree or directed acyclic graph.
Each vertex \(v\in V\) indexes a parameter block \(x_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal H\) if and only if \(v\in S(x)\) implies \(\operatorname{Anc}(v)\subseteq S(x)\).

notation.meaning: Ancestors of vertex v, including or excluding v without affecting the condition.
Indicator of the hierarchically admissible parameter set.

review_flags: No supplied locator establishes the selected ancestor-closed convention for hierarchical support.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Ancestor closure is a coherent hierarchical-support convention and condition is an appropriate content kind, but no source establishes that this is the intended convention. children.title: Low-Rank Penalties
children.top_down_role: Matrix regularizers promoting low-dimensional latent structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value penalties used as soft surrogates for matrix rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1(X),\ldots,\sigma_r(X)\), where \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), a low-rank penalty has the spectral form \[R(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\rho(\sigma_i(X)),\qquad \rho(0)=0,\] with \(\rho:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]\). The choice \(\rho(t)=t\) gives the convex nuclear norm \(\lVert X\rVert_*=\sum_i\sigma_i(X)\); the choice \(\rho(t)=\mathbf{1}_{\{t>0\}}\) gives \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-rank penalties apply a scalar penalty to each singular value; nuclear norm and matrix rank are canonical soft and hard instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\rho(\sigma_i(X))\) penalizes the number or magnitude of nonzero singular values.

notation.meaning: The i-th singular value of X.

children.title: Spectral Regularizers
children.top_down_role: Matrix objectives determined by singular-value or eigenvalue profiles.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Regularizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally invariant matrix regularizers represented through singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\) and let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^r\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be invariant under coordinate permutations and sign changes. The associated spectral regularizer on \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is \[R(X)=\phi(\sigma(X)),\qquad \sigma(X)=(\sigma_1(X),\ldots,\sigma_r(X)).\] It is orthogonally invariant: \(R(UXV^{\mathsf T})=R(X)\) for all orthogonal \(U\) and \(V\). Conversely, every orthogonally invariant extended-real matrix function admits such a representation by an absolutely symmetric \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonally invariant matrix regularizer is exactly a symmetric function of the matrix singular values.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is an extended-real function invariant under signed coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\) is orthogonally invariant, and every orthogonally invariant \(R\) has this form.

notation.meaning: Vector of singular values of X.

children.title: Singular-Value Structure
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth geometry induced by multiplicities or thresholded singular values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\sigma(X))V^{\mathsf T}\), with \(\sigma_1(X)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_q(X)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: ordered singular-value vector of a matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real-matrix singular-value representation underlying spectral low-rank penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) admits a singular-value decomposition \(X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\sigma_1(X),\ldots,\sigma_q(X))V^{\mathsf T}\), where \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), the columns of \(U\) and \(V\) are orthonormal on the represented subspaces, and \(\sigma_1(X)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_q(X)\geq0\). Its rank is \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=|\{i:\sigma_i(X)>0\}|\), its nuclear norm is \(\|X\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^q\sigma_i(X)\), and its spectral norm is \(\|X\|_2=\sigma_1(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is characterized spectrally by ordered nonnegative singular values; rank counts the positive values, while nuclear and spectral norms aggregate them differently.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional singular-value representation and norm identities are standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the nontrivial claims.

children.title: Rank-Surrogate Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where spectral surrogates poorly represent rank structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|X\|_*\) is not a uniformly exact surrogate for \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\) without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete scaling obstruction to treating the nuclear norm as an unconditional rank surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any nonzero \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and scalar \(t>0\), one has \(\operatorname{rank}(tX)=\operatorname{rank}(X)\) but \(\|tX\|_*=t\|X\|_*\). Consequently, no constants \(0<a\leq b<\infty\) can satisfy \(a\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq\|X\|_*\leq b\operatorname{rank}(X)\) for every matrix \(X\). In particular, replacing rank by nuclear norm can change minimizers unless the feasible set or observation operator supplies normalization and recovery structure; exact recovery is therefore not guaranteed solely by convexity of the surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank is scale invariant whereas nuclear norm scales linearly, so nuclear-norm minimization cannot universally reproduce rank minimization without structural recovery assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Surrogate Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling obstruction is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the universal-surrogate and recovery-structure claims require an inspectable source.

children.title: Fused Regularization
children.top_down_role: Regularizers promoting equality across selected variable differences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\beta)=\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|D\beta\|_1\) is convex and nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized fused-lasso regularization with an arbitrary fixed difference operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times p}\) and weights \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\geq0\), the fused regularizer on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is \(R(\beta)=\lambda_1\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|+\lambda_2\sum_{k=1}^r|(D\beta)_k|\). The first term promotes zero coordinates, while the second promotes equality across coordinates compared by rows of \(D\). For the first-difference operator satisfying \((D\beta)_k=\beta_{k+1}-\beta_k\), zero differences partition the ordered coordinates into constant blocks. The function \(R\) is proper, finite, convex, and generally nondifferentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fused regularization combines coordinate sparsity with an l1 penalty on selected differences, encouraging coefficients to be both zero and equal in groups.
knowledge_statements.title: Fused Regularization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. Moreover, an arbitrary matrix D need not encode pairwise differences, so the claim that its rows promote coordinate equality requires D to be restricted to a difference or incidence operator.

children.title: Graph-Structured Regularization
children.top_down_role: Regularizers organized by edges or neighborhoods of a graph.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_G(\beta)=\sum_{e=(u,v)\in E}w_e|\beta_u-\beta_v|=\|W B\beta\|_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar graph total variation on a finite weighted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an arbitrary orientation of the edges of \(G=(V,E)\), let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|\times|V|}\) be its incidence matrix, and let \(W=\operatorname{Diag}((w_e)_{e\in E})\) with \(w_e\geq0\). Graph-structured regularization is defined by \(R_G(\beta)=\|WB\beta\|_1=\sum_{e=(u,v)\in E}w_e|\beta_u-\beta_v|\). It is independent of the chosen orientation, convex, and positively homogeneous. Moreover, \(R_G(\beta)=0\) exactly when \(\beta\) is constant on every connected component formed by positive-weight edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph regularization sums weighted absolute differences across edges, encouraging equal parameter values within well-connected graph regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Structured Regularization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted graph-total-variation definition and kernel characterization fit the leaf and are precise, but they have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Total-Variation Regularization
children.top_down_role: Variation penalties for spatial, temporal, or network-indexed signals.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}(u)=|Du|(\Omega)\), and \(u\in BV(\Omega)\) exactly when this value is finite.

notation.meaning: distributional derivative of the scalar function
space of functions of bounded variation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isotropic total variation for scalar functions on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in L^1(\Omega)\), its total variation is \[\operatorname{TV}(u)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u(x)\,\operatorname{div}\varphi(x)\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d),\ \|\varphi(x)\|_2\leq1\ \text{for all }x\right\}.\] The function belongs to \(BV(\Omega)\) when \(\operatorname{TV}(u)<\infty\), in which case \(\operatorname{TV}(u)=|Du|(\Omega)\). If \(u\) is continuously differentiable, then \(\operatorname{TV}(u)=\int_\Omega\|\nabla u(x)\|_2\,dx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total variation measures the distributional derivative's mass; finite total variation defines the bounded-variation class and favors piecewise-constant reconstructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Total-Variation Regularization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The BV definition is standard but uncited. The plain statement additionally says that TV favors piecewise-constant reconstructions, a modeling claim not expressed or qualified in the LaTeX statement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Total-Variation-Regularized Least Squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadrature-discretized TV regularization, including its convexity, nonsmoothness, and uniqueness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(\lambda>0\), and let \(L_1\) be a compatible discrete derivative operator. The discrete TV-regularized least-squares model is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda^2\|L_1x\|_1\right\}.\] Its objective is convex and can be nondifferentiable at points where components of \(L_1x\) vanish. If \(A\) has full column rank, the quadratic term is strictly convex and coercive, so the problem has a unique minimizer. Without an additional uniqueness condition, convexity alone does not imply uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete TV regularization minimizes squared residual error plus an L1 penalty on a discrete derivative. The objective is convex and may be nonsmooth. Full column rank of the data matrix is sufficient for a unique minimizer, while convexity alone is not.
assumptions_latex: L_1\text{ is a compatible linear discrete derivative operator}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_x\{\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda^2\|L_1x\|_1\}\text{ is convex and potentially nonsmooth; if }\operatorname{rank}(A)=n,\text{ it has a unique minimizer.}

children.title: Anisotropic versus Isotropic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alternative aggregation geometries for multidirectional variation.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) is a scalar array on a finite grid
\(D_j u\) denotes its difference in coordinate direction \(j\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)\leq\sqrt d\,\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of standard discrete scalar total-variation conventions on a finite grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each grid site \(i\), write \(D u_i=((D_1u)_i,\ldots,(D_du)_i)\). The anisotropic and isotropic penalties are \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)=\sum_i\sum_{j=1}^d|(D_ju)_i|\) and \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)=\sum_i(\sum_{j=1}^d|(D_ju)_i|^2)^{1/2}\), respectively. Applying \(\|z\|_2\leq\|z\|_1\leq\sqrt d\|z\|_2\) at every site gives \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\leq\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)\leq\sqrt d\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)\). The anisotropic penalty depends on coordinate axes, whereas the Euclidean isotropic penalty is invariant under orthogonal rotations of each local difference vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic TV sums directional magnitudes separately; isotropic TV groups them by Euclidean norm. They are equivalent up to a dimension-dependent factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic versus Isotropic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete norm comparison is standard but uncited. The sentence beginning with applying the pointwise norm inequality is proof-style text and should be removed from a sourced replacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isotropic and anisotropic two-dimensional total variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two standard aggregation geometries for horizontal and vertical finite differences on a rectangular image grid, including boundary-edge terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m,n\in\mathbb N\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the isotropic two-dimensional total variation is
\[
\operatorname{TV}_{I}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\sqrt{(x_{i,j}-x_{i,j+1})^2+(x_{i,j}-x_{i+1,j})^2}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|x_{m,j}-x_{m,j+1}|+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}|x_{i,n}-x_{i+1,n}|,
\]
and the \(\ell_1\)-based anisotropic total variation is
\[
\operatorname{TV}_{\ell_1}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigl(|x_{i,j}-x_{i,j+1}|+|x_{i,j}-x_{i+1,j}|\bigr)+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|x_{m,j}-x_{m,j+1}|+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}|x_{i,n}-x_{i+1,n}|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an m-by-n array, isotropic TV sums the Euclidean norm of the paired horizontal and vertical differences at each interior grid point, together with absolute differences on the unmatched bottom and right edges. Anisotropic TV sums the absolute values of all horizontal and vertical differences with the same boundary coverage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{TV}_{I}(x)\text{ and }\operatorname{TV}_{\ell_1}(x)\text{ are given by the displayed finite-difference formulas, including the bottom and right boundary terms.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb{R}^p=X_1\times\cdots\times X_s\) be a fixed block decomposition and let \(\lambda\geq0\). A regularized empirical objective has the form \(F(\beta)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i(\beta)+\lambda R(\beta)\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A prox-regular-outer composite at \(\bar x\) is a function \(f=h\circ c\), where \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is prox-regular at \(\bar z=c(\bar x)\) for some \(\bar v\in\partial h(\bar z)\). Concretely, locally compatible points \(z,z'\) and subgradients \(v\) near \((\bar z,\bar v)\) satisfy \(h(z')\geq h(z)+\langle v,z'-z\rangle-(r/2)\|z'-z\|^2\) for some \(r\geq0\). Prox-regularity of \(f\) itself requires additional compatibility between \(c\) and \(h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Composite Architectures

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(L\)-level nested composite architecture is a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n_0}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) of the form \(f(x)=h(c_L(c_{L-1}(\cdots c_1(x)\cdots)))\), where \(L\geq2\), each \(c_j:\mathbb{R}^{n_{j-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_j}\), and \(h:\mathbb{R}^{n_L}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). Defining \(y_0=x\) and \(y_j=c_j(y_{j-1})\) gives the auxiliary-variable representation \(f(x)=h(y_L)\) with \(y_j=c_j(y_{j-1})\) for \(j=1,\ldots,L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested composite passes an input through several dimension-compatible mappings before applying a terminal outer function; auxiliary variables expose each intermediate level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=h\circ c_L\circ\cdots\circ c_1\) is an \(L\)-level nested composite architecture.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Level Nonsmoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nested composites whose nonsmoothness occurs at multiple layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_0:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{d_1}\), let \(F_j:\mathbb{R}^{d_j}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{j+1}}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,L-1\), and let \(F_L:\mathbb{R}^{d_L}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). For \(z_0=\bar x\) and \(z_{j+1}=F_j(z_j)\), assume every composition is defined and each layer being tested for classical differentiability is finite-valued on a neighborhood of its input \(z_j\). The nested function \[f=F_L\circ F_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ F_0\] has multi-level nonsmoothness at \(\bar x\) if at least two maps \(F_j\) are not classically differentiable at their corresponding inputs \(z_j\). At those layers, the ordinary differentiable-chain-rule Jacobian product is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested composite has multi-level nonsmoothness at a point when at least two constituent maps are not classically differentiable at their corresponding intermediate inputs; consequently, the ordinary Jacobian chain rule is unavailable at those layers.
assumptions_latex: \(L\geq 1\), and all displayed compositions are defined at \(\bar x\).
Each layer being tested for classical differentiability is finite-valued on a neighborhood of its corresponding input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has at least two nondifferentiable constituent layers at \(\bar x\), so the ordinary Jacobian product chain rule cannot be applied through all layers.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Coupled Outer Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonseparable outer functions coupling coordinates of a vector-valued inner map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The outer map is dimension-coupled on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) if no functions \(h_i:\mathbb{R}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and constant \(a\) satisfy \(h(z)=a+\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(z_i)\) throughout \(D\). For example, \(h(z)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i\) couples the active coordinates, and \[\partial h(z)=\operatorname{conv}\{e_i:i\in\operatorname{argmax}_j z_j\}.\] Thus subgradients of \(h\circ c\) generally depend jointly on multiple components of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-coupled outer map is nonseparable across coordinates; its active subgradients and the resulting composite behavior depend jointly on several inner components.
assumptions_latex: The set \(D\) contains the inner-map values under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise scalar analysis is generally insufficient for \(h\circ c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Amenability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional convex-composite amenability and its basic qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is convex-composite amenable at \(\bar x\) when, on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), \(f=g\circ F\), where \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and the qualification \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}=\{0\}\] holds. Under these conditions the exact limiting-subdifferential chain rule is \[\partial f(\bar x)=\nabla F(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}\partial g(F(\bar x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Amenability combines a smooth inner map, a closed convex outer function, and a normal-cone qualification yielding an exact subdifferential chain rule.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(C^1\), and \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\nabla F(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}\partial g(F(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the effective domain of g.
Limiting subdifferential, coinciding with the convex subdifferential for g.

For \(f=g\circ F\), with \(F:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}^m\) continuously differentiable and \(g\) proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, qualification fails at \( ar x\) whenever there exists \(v
eq0\) such that \[v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F( ar x))\quad	ext{and}\quad 
abla F( ar x)^{\mathsf T}v=0.\] Such a nonzero abnormal multiplier is invisible after pullback. Without an alternative qualification, the equality \(\partial f( ar x)=

children.title: Degenerate Inner Mappings
children.top_down_role: Composite pathologies caused by locally degenerate inner maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Inner Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rank-degenerate inner map causing strict failure of the composite chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(F(x)=x^2\), let \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\), and set \(f=g\circ F\). Then \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so \(\partial f(0)=\mathbb{R}\). However, \(F'(0)=0\) and \(\partial g(F(0))=\mathbb{R}\), whence \[F'(0)\partial g(F(0))=\{0\}\subsetneq\mathbb{R}=\partial f(0).\] Thus degeneracy of the inner derivative can annihilate every outer multiplier and make the formal subdifferential pullback strictly too small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indicator outer function composed with the degenerate map x squared, the formal pullback is zero although the composite subdifferential is the whole line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'(0)\partial g(F(0))\subsetneq\partial(g\circ F)(0)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the singleton zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Domain Boundary Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification loss when the inner value lies on the relative boundary of the outer effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=g\circ F\), where \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(C^1\), and \(F(\bar x)\in\operatorname{dom}g\). If \(F(\bar x)\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\), then \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))=\operatorname{par}(\operatorname{dom}g)^{\perp},\] and the qualification holds exactly when \[\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)+\operatorname{par}(\operatorname{dom}g)=\mathbb{R}^m.\] At a relative-boundary point, additional normal directions may occur. Any nonzero \(v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}\) causes the standard composite qualification to fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-interior point the qualification is equivalent to transversality between the inner Jacobian range and the outer domain's parallel space. At a relative-boundary point, additional normal directions can enter the kernel of the transposed Jacobian and cause qualification failure.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(C^1\), and \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero \(v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}\) marks qualification failure.

notation.meaning: Parallel subspace of the affine hull of the effective domain of g.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-dimensional isotropic total variation denoising problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The isotropic TV term uses forward horizontal and vertical differences in the interior and one-dimensional differences along the last row and column.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integers m,n\ge2, data \mathbf d\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, and \lambda>0, define
\[
\operatorname{TV}_I(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\sqrt{(x_{i,j}-x_{i,j+1})^2+(x_{i,j}-x_{i+1,j})^2}
+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|x_{m,j}-x_{m,j+1}|+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}|x_{i,n}-x_{i+1,n}|.
\]
The associated denoising problem is
\[
\min_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}\left\{\frac12\|\mathbf x-\mathbf d\|_F^2+\lambda\operatorname{TV}_I(\mathbf x)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-dimensional isotropic total variation denoising minimizes squared Frobenius distance to the observed array plus lambda times an isotropic discrete total variation penalty, with separate horizontal and vertical differences on the terminal boundaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}\left\{\frac12\|\mathbf x-\mathbf d\|_F^2+\lambda\operatorname{TV}_I(\mathbf x)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke chain rule for a strictly differentiable inner map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space chain rule, including both stated equality regimes and inherited regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\to Y be a map between Banach spaces, strictly differentiable at x, and let g:Y\to\mathbb{R} be Lipschitz near F(x). Then f=g\circ F is Lipschitz near x and \[\partial f(x)\subset \partial g(F(x))\circ D_sF(x).\] Equality holds if either g or -g is regular at F(x); correspondingly, f or -f is regular at x. Equality also holds if F maps every neighborhood of x onto a set dense in a neighborhood of F(x), in particular if D_sF(x) is onto.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the inner Banach-space map is strictly differentiable and the outer function is locally Lipschitz, their composition is locally Lipschitz and its Clarke generalized gradient satisfies the chain-rule inclusion. The inclusion is an equality under the stated regularity condition, with regularity inherited by the corresponding composition, or when the inner map has the stated local dense-image property; surjectivity of its strict derivative is sufficient.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=g\circ F\text{ is Lipschitz near }x,\quad \partial f(x)\subset\partial g(F(x))\circ D_sF(x),\text{ with equality under either stated additional condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite regularized optimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted regularization and its intended fit-versus-structure tradeoff without assuming convexity, smoothness, or proximal tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an underlying objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), a regularizer \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and a weight \(\gamma\ge 0\), a regularized optimization problem has the composite form
\[
\min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^n}\;\phi_\gamma(w),\qquad \phi_\gamma(w):=f(w)+\gamma r(w).
\]
The term \(f\) measures the underlying fit or loss, while \(r\) favors prescribed structure such as sparsity, piecewise-constant images, low rank, or groupwise selection; varying \(\gamma\) controls their relative weighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularized optimization problem minimizes an underlying objective plus a nonnegatively weighted regularizer. The objective measures fit or loss, the regularizer favors desired structure, and the parameter gamma controls their relative weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^n}\phi_\gamma(w),\quad \phi_\gamma(w)=f(w)+\gamma r(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The proximal mapping of the ℓ1 norm is soft thresholding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form scalar and vector proximal formulas for a positive threshold parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda|\cdot|}(\theta)=\arg\min_z\left\{\lambda|z|+\frac12(z-\theta)^2\right\}=\operatorname{sign}(\theta)(|\theta|-\lambda)_+.
\]
Equivalently, the value is \(\theta-\lambda\) for \(\theta\geq\lambda\), zero for \(|\theta|\leq\lambda\), and \(\theta+\lambda\) for \(\theta\leq-\lambda\). Because the \(\ell_1\) norm is separable,
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_1}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(\boldsymbol\theta)\odot(|\boldsymbol\theta|-\lambda)_+.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal operator of the absolute value is soft thresholding: values within the threshold are set to zero, while larger magnitudes are reduced by the threshold. The proximal operator of the ℓ1 norm applies this rule coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\lVert\cdot\rVert_1}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(\boldsymbol\theta)\odot(|\boldsymbol\theta|-\lambda)_+

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection onto a Box
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise Euclidean projection onto finite or one-sided unbounded interval constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:l\le x\le u\}\), where \(l_k\le u_k\), \(l_k\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\), and \(u_k\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Then for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \((\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v))_k=\min\{u_k,\max\{l_k,v_k\}\}\). In particular, \(\Pi_{\mathbb R_+^n}(v)=v_+\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a possibly unbounded box clips each coordinate to its permitted interval. Projection onto the nonnegative orthant replaces each negative component by zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v))_k=\min\{u_k,\max\{l_k,v_k\}\},\qquad \Pi_{\mathbb R_+^n}(v)=v_+.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex variational representation of the squared ℓ1 norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes an optimizer in both the nonzero and zero-vector regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\ge 1\), let
\[
\Delta_n=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j=1\right\},
\]
and define \(\varphi(s,t)=s^2/t\) for \(t>0\), \(\varphi(0,0)=0\), and \(\varphi(s,t)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_n}\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi(x_j,\lambda_j)=\|x\|_1^2.
\]
An optimal solution is
\[
\lambda_j^*=\begin{cases}
|x_j|/\|x\|_1,&x\ne0,\\
1/n,&x=0,
\end{cases}
\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared ℓ1 norm is the minimum, over the probability simplex, of a sum of closed quadratic-over-linear coordinate terms. Normalized coordinate magnitudes are optimal for a nonzero vector, while the uniform simplex point is optimal at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_n}\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi(x_j,\lambda_j)=\|x\|_1^2,\qquad \lambda_j^*=\begin{cases}|x_j|/\|x\|_1,&x\ne0,\\1/n,&x=0.
\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Projection as a Quadratic Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-program representations of Euclidean projection and convex-quadratic proximal evaluation over a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ Cx\le d\}\ne\varnothing\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), the Euclidean projection \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)\) is the unique solution of \(\min_x \tfrac12\|x-v\|_2^2\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(Cx\le d\), which is a quadratic program. If \(q\) is convex quadratic, then \(\operatorname{prox}_{q+\delta_{\mathcal C}}(v)\) is obtained by adding \(q(x)\) to the same objective under the same constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty polyhedron is the unique solution of a squared-distance quadratic program. A convex quadratic restricted to the polyhedron has a proximal operator obtained by adding that quadratic to the projection objective.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad C\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}
q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex quadratic}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\,Cx\le d}\tfrac12\|x-v\|_2^2,\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{q+\delta_{\mathcal C}}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\,Cx\le d}\left(q(x)+\tfrac12\|x-v\|_2^2\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary point of a differentiable–convex composite objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stationarity through cancellation of the smooth gradient by a convex subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and let \(g:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}g\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). For \((P):\min_{x\in\mathbb{E}}f(x)+g(x)\), a point \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}g\) at which \(f\) is differentiable is stationary for \((P)\), equivalently for \(f+g\), when \(-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is stationary for a differentiable-plus-convex composite objective when the negative gradient of the differentiable term is a subgradient of the convex term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is stationary}\Longleftrightarrow-\nabla f(x^*)\in\partial g(x^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-norm subgradient and proximal-model step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences for the specified first-order approximation \(\widehat f\) of a locally Lipschitz function at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\), and let \(\widehat f\) be the specified approximation of \(f\) at \(x\). Define \(\widehat p=\arg\min_{g\in\partial f(x)}\tfrac12\|g\|^2\), and let \(\widehat d\) minimize \(\widehat f(x+d)+\tfrac12\|d\|^2\) over \(d\in\mathbb{R}^N\). Then \(\widehat d\) exists uniquely, \(-\widehat d=\widehat p\in\partial f(x)\), and \(\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,\widehat d\rangle=-\|\widehat p\|^2\). Moreover, \(\widehat f(x+\widehat d)=\widehat f(x)-\|\widehat p\|^2\) and \(\widehat f(x+t\widehat d)\le\widehat f(x)-t\|\widehat p\|^2\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Finally, \(\widehat d\ne0\) iff \(0\notin\partial f(x)\), and \(0\in\partial f(x)\) iff \(x\) is a global minimizer of \(\widehat f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the specified nonsmooth first-order model with unit quadratic regularization, the unique minimizing step is the negative minimum-norm subgradient. It satisfies exact support and model-decrease identities, is nonzero exactly at nonstationary points, and vanishes exactly when the base point globally minimizes the model.
assumptions_latex: \widehat f\text{ is the specified approximation of }f\text{ at }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\widehat d=\widehat p,\quad \max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,\widehat d\rangle=-\|\widehat p\|^2,\quad \widehat f(x+t\widehat d)\le\widehat f(x)-t\|\widehat p\|^2\ (t\in[0,1]),\quad \widehat d\ne0\iff0\notin\partial f(x),\quad 0\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\arg\min\widehat f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal mapping of sum-of-group-norm regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block soft thresholding for disjoint groups, together with the distinct linear-time evaluation claim for tree-structured overlapping groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda>0\). If \(\mathcal G\) is a partition of \([n]\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\lVert x_g\rVert_2\), then, for every \(g\in\mathcal G\), \[\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\bigr)_g=\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\lVert v_g\rVert_2}\right)_+v_g,\] with the value understood as \(0\) when \(v_g=0\). This is block soft thresholding. Separately, if \(\mathcal G\) is a tree-structured cover of \([n]\), meaning every pair of groups is disjoint or one contains the other, the corresponding proximal operator can be evaluated in linear time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a partition of the coordinates, the proximal mapping of the sum of group Euclidean norms applies block soft thresholding independently to each group. For an overlapping tree-structured cover whose groups are pairwise disjoint or nested, the proximal operator remains evaluable in linear time.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal G\text{ is a partition of }[n]\text{ for the blockwise formula}
\mathcal G\text{ is a cover of }[n]\text{ with every pair disjoint or nested for the linear-time claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\bigr)_g=\left(1-\lambda/\lVert v_g\rVert_2\right)_+v_g\quad(g\in\mathcal G),\qquad\text{and tree-structured covers permit linear-time proximal evaluation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lower and Upper Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set definition localized to a neighborhood of a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} and f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}. The function f is locally lower semicontinuous at \bar x if there exists \varepsilon>0 such that \{x\in\mathbb{B}(\bar x,\varepsilon)\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\} is closed for every \alpha\leq f(\bar x)+\varepsilon. Parallelly, f is locally upper semicontinuous at \bar x if, for some \varepsilon>0, \{x\in\mathbb{B}(\bar x,\varepsilon)\mid f(x)\geq\alpha\} is closed for every \alpha\geq f(\bar x)-\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where its value is finite, a function is locally lower semicontinuous when all sufficiently relevant sublevel sets restricted to some neighborhood are closed; local upper semicontinuity is defined analogously using superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall\alpha\leq f(\bar x)+\varepsilon:\ \{x\in\mathbb{B}(\bar x,\varepsilon)\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ is closed}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection onto an Affine Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Euclidean projection onto a consistent affine system, with full-row-rank and hyperplane specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\). Then for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=v-A^\dagger(Av-b)\). If \(m<n\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), then \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=v-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}(Av-b)\). In particular, if \(\mathcal C=\{x:a^Tx=b\}\) with \(a\ne0\), then \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=v+\frac{b-a^Tv}{\|a\|_2^2}a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty affine set has a pseudoinverse formula. For a full-row-rank system it uses the inverse Gram matrix, and for one nonzero linear equation it reduces to the hyperplane projection formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=v-A^\dagger(Av-b),\qquad \operatorname{rank}(A)=m\Rightarrow\Pi_{\mathcal C}(v)=v-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}(Av-b).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise stationarity for ℓ1 regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expands the ℓ1-subdifferential inclusion into sign-dependent coordinate conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)+\lambda\|x\|_1\), where \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\). If \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\), then \(x^*\) is stationary if and only if \(-\nabla f(x^*)\in\lambda\partial\|x^*\|_1\). Equivalently, for every \(i\), \(\partial_i f(x^*)=-\lambda\) when \(x_i^*>0\), \(\partial_i f(x^*)=\lambda\) when \(x_i^*<0\), and \(\partial_i f(x^*)\in[-\lambda,\lambda]\) when \(x_i^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity for an ℓ1-regularized differentiable objective is equivalent to a subgradient inclusion, which gives an exact coordinatewise condition according to whether each coordinate is positive, negative, or zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ stationary}\Longleftrightarrow-\nabla f(x^*)\in\lambda\partial\|x^*\|_1\Longleftrightarrow\partial_i f(x^*)\in\begin{cases}\{-\lambda\},&x_i^*>0,\\\{\lambda\},&x_i^*<0,\\[-\lambda,\lambda],&x_i^*=0\end{cases}\quad\forall i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Guarded Newton Evaluation of a Scalar Proximal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded Newton query selection within the scalar proximal localization procedure; no faster convergence guarantee is asserted by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and twice continuously differentiable on the relevant localization interval, let \(\lambda>0\), define \(\varphi(x)=f(x)+(x-v)^2/(2\lambda)\), and suppose \(x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\in[l,u]\). Choose \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), initialize \(x=(l+u)/2\), and define \[\alpha[l,u]=\left[\frac{l+u}{2}-\alpha\frac{u-l}{2},\frac{l+u}{2}+\alpha\frac{u-l}{2}\right].\] At each iteration set \[x\leftarrow\Pi_{\alpha[l,u]}\left(x-\frac{\varphi'(x)}{\varphi''(x)}\right).\] With \(g=\varphi'(x)\), return \(x\) if \(g=0\); if \(g>0\), set \([l,u]\leftarrow[l,u]\cap[x-\lambda g,x]\); and if \(g<0\), set \([l,u]\leftarrow[l,u]\cap[x,x-\lambda g]\). When \(\alpha=0\), the guarded interval is the singleton containing the midpoint, so the method reduces to midpoint localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method projects each Newton proposal for the scalar proximal objective onto a central portion of the current localization interval, then performs the usual derivative-sign interval update. Setting the guard parameter to zero recovers midpoint localization. Positive guard parameters allow Newton-informed queries but do not, from this extract alone, guarantee fewer iterations.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex and twice continuously differentiable on the relevant localization interval}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\leftarrow\Pi_{\alpha[l,u]}\left(x-\varphi'(x)/\varphi''(x)\right)\text{ is a safeguarded query for the localization update, and }\alpha=0\text{ recovers midpoint localization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions imposed on randomized proximal variants (6.103) and (6.104).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\), \(\omega_k\) is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and independent of \(\{x_k,z_{k-1},x_{k-1},\ldots,z_0,x_0\}\). There exists \(c\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, for every \(k\) and \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \[\max\{\|\widetilde\nabla f_i(z_k^i)\|,\|\widetilde\nabla h_i(z_k^i)\|\}\leq c,\] \[\max\{f_i(x_k)-f_i(z_k^i),h_i(x_k)-h_i(z_k^i)\}\leq c\|x_k-z_k^i\|.\] For iteration (6.103), \[z_k^i\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\left\{f_i(x)+\frac{\|x-x_k\|^2}{2\alpha_k}\right\},\] while for iteration (6.104) the minimization is over \(\mathbb R^n\).

Almost surely, the specified component subgradients are uniformly bounded and the one-sided component-value changes are bounded by the displacement. The hypothetical proximal point is constrained for (6.103) and unconstrained for (6.104).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient Localization of a Scalar Proximal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid localization procedure for an in-domain query; the extract's unconditional projection rule outside the domain is excluded because it does not hold for general convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(\lambda>0\), let \(v\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and define \(\varphi(x)=f(x)+(x-v)^2/(2\lambda)\). Starting with an interval \([l,u]\) containing \(x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(v)\), use \(x=v\) for the first query and subsequently \(x=(l+u)/2\). Choose \(h\in\partial f(x)\) and set \(g=h+(x-v)/\lambda\in\partial\varphi(x)\). If \(g=0\), return \(x=x^\star\). If \(g>0\), set \([l,u]\leftarrow[l,u]\cap[x-\lambda g,x]\); if \(g<0\), set \([l,u]\leftarrow[l,u]\cap[x,x-\lambda g]\). Each update retains \(x^\star\). After the first update, every midpoint update reduces the interval width by at least one half; thus, if the post-first-update width is \(2L\), after \(k\) further updates its width is at most \(2L\,2^{-k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an in-domain scalar query, a subgradient of the proximal objective determines an interval that still contains the proximal point. After the initial query, midpoint queries halve the interval width, while a zero subgradient identifies the proximal point exactly. The extract's claim that every outside-domain query projects to the closest domain endpoint is not valid for an arbitrary convex function.

h\in\partial f(x)\text{ is available at each queried point}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal decomposition of a convex multi-period portfolio model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-structure specialization showing how temporal and assetwise separability expose parallel proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, consider $\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_T}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(x_t-x_{t-1})$, where each $f_t$ and $g_t$ is closed, proper, and convex and $g_t(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n g_{t,i}(z_i)$. For $X=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_T]$, define $f(X)=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)$ and $g(X)=\sum_{t=1}^T g_t(x_t-x_{t-1})$. For $\lambda>0$, $\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}$ separates into $T$ independent periodwise problems, whereas $\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}$ separates into $n$ independent assetwise sequence problems. Each assetwise problem has nearest-neighbor temporal coupling; a method exploiting this specific structure can solve it in $O(T)$ operations. Extended values of $f_t$ and $g_t$ encode constraints on holdings and trades, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex multi-period portfolio model splits into stage costs and transaction costs. Assetwise separability of transaction costs makes the stage-cost proximal operator separate by period and the transaction-cost proximal operator separate by asset. Each assetwise subproblem has nearest-neighbor coupling in time and can be solved in linear time by a method exploiting that specific structure. Extended function values can impose constraints on holdings and trades.
assumptions_latex: x_0\in\mathbb R^n\text{ is given, and }x_t\in\mathbb R^n\text{ for }t=1,\ldots,T.
f_t\text{ and }g_t\text{ are closed, proper, and convex for every }t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\text{ separates over the }T\text{ periods, while }\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}\text{ separates over the }n\text{ assets into nearest-neighbor temporal problems that a structure-exploiting method can solve in }O(T)\text{ operations each.}

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Proximal Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise decomposition of proximal mappings for separable convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) have the separable form \(g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x_i)\), where each \(g_i:\mathbb{R}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every \(\lambda>0\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the proximal minimization separates, and \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_1}(x_1),\ldots,\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_n}(x_n)\bigr).\] Hence evaluating the full proximal map reduces exactly to \(n\) independent scalar proximal problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map of a coordinate-separable closed convex function is obtained by independently applying each scalar proximal map.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x))_i=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_i}(x_i)\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Unique minimizer of g plus the scaled squared Euclidean distance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise proximal representation is correct and fits the separable proximal-model leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partition-separable functions and componentwise proximal mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines separability over a partition, records the associated blockwise proximal decomposition, and states the corresponding two-partition composite model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P=\{c_1,\ldots,c_N\}\) be a partition of \([n]\). A function \(f\) is \(\mathcal P\)-separable if \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_{c_i})\), where each \(f_i\) depends only on the subvector indexed by its scope \(c_i\). When the component proximal mappings are well-defined, \((\operatorname{prox}_f(v))_{c_i}=\operatorname{prox}_{f_i}(v_{c_i})\) for every \(i\), so the blocks can be evaluated independently. If closed proper convex functions \(f\) and \(g\) are respectively separable over partitions \(\mathcal P=\{c_i\}_{i=1}^N\) and \(\mathcal Q=\{d_j\}_{j=1}^M\), then \(f(x)+g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_{c_i})+\sum_{j=1}^M g_j(x_{d_j})\). Full separability is the special case in which every block is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is separable over a partition when it is a sum of terms that each depend on one variable block. Its proximal mapping then decomposes into independent block proximal mappings when those mappings are well-defined. Two functions separable over different partitions produce a composite objective containing both families of block terms. Singleton blocks give full separability.
assumptions_latex: \text{The component proximal mappings are well-defined for the proximal-decomposition claim}
\text{For the composite model, }f,g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ are closed, proper, convex, and respectively }\mathcal P\text{- and }\mathcal Q\text{-separable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\operatorname{prox}_f(v))_{c_i}=\operatorname{prox}_{f_i}(v_{c_i})\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\qquad f(x)+g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_{c_i})+\sum_{j=1}^M g_j(x_{d_j}).
