knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Proximal Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value representation of proximal maps for convex spectral functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\) on real matrices, where \(\phi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and absolutely symmetric, and \(\sigma(X)\) is the singular-value vector. If \(X=U\operatorname{Diag}(s)V^{\mathsf T}\) is a singular value decomposition, then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(X)=U\operatorname{Diag}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\phi}(s))V^{\mathsf T}.\] The expression is independent of the chosen singular vectors, including when singular values are repeated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex spectral function, the matrix proximal map preserves singular vectors and applies the corresponding vector proximal map to singular values.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and absolutely symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed singular-value proximal representation holds.

notation.meaning: Vector of singular values of X.
Rectangular diagonal matrix with diagonal s.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value proximal representation is standard under the stated absolute-symmetry and convexity hypotheses and fits the leaf, but it requires a theorem-level source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Reducible Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal evaluations reducible to Euclidean projections onto closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For its indicator \(\delta_C\) and support function \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{z\in C}\langle u,z\rangle\), proximal evaluation reduces to projection: \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\delta_C}(x)=\Pi_C(x),\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\sigma_C}(x)=x-\lambda\Pi_C(x/\lambda),\] for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda>0\). The second identity is Moreau decomposition applied to the conjugate pair \(\sigma_C\) and \(\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicators and support functions of closed convex sets have proximal maps computable directly from Euclidean projection onto the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both displayed proximal maps reduce to evaluating \(\Pi_C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both projection identities are correct for a nonempty closed convex set and fit the projection-reducible leaf, but no source supports the Moreau-decomposition claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Proximal Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal points characterized implicitly by monotone optimality inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda>0\), a vector \(z\) is the proximal point of \(x\) if and only if \[0\in\partial g(z)+\lambda^{-1}(z-x),\] equivalently, \(x\in z+\lambda\partial g(z)\). The strongly convex proximal objective makes this solution unique, so \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}=(I+\lambda\partial g)^{-1}.\] This inclusion supplies an implicit interface when no closed-form proximal formula is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit proximal model represents the proximal point as the unique solution of a subgradient inclusion, equivalently as a resolvent value.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x)\iff x\in z+\lambda\partial g(z)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimality inclusion and resolvent representation are correct and fit the implicit proximal-model leaf, but the record lacks an authoritative source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Piece-Partition Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-smooth functions specified by a finite explicit partition of their domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be covered by finitely many sets \(D_1,\ldots,D_r\), and let each \(f_i\) be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(D_i\). An explicit piece-partition model is the function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \[f(x)=f_i(x)\quad\text{whenever }x\in D_i,\] subject to \(f_i(x)=f_j(x)\) on every overlap \(D_i\cap D_j\). Its nonsmooth locus is contained in the union of piece boundaries and overlap sets where active gradients differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit piece-partition model assigns a smooth formula to each member of a finite domain cover, with agreement on overlaps ensuring a well-defined function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is well-defined and piecewise \(C^1\) on \(D\).

notation.meaning: Smooth formula assigned to the i-th piece.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition broadly fits the leaf, but no source establishes that the stated unrestricted finite cover is sufficient for the intended notion of piecewise-C1 structure or supports the claimed nonsmooth-locus characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous functions locally selecting among finitely many smooth component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_r:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is a selection function of \(\{f_1,\ldots,f_r\}\) if \[f(x)\in\{f_1(x),\ldots,f_r(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Its active selection set is \[I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}:f(x)=f_i(x)\}.\] Switching among active indices can produce nondifferentiability even though every component function is smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selection-function model continuously chooses at every point one value from a finite family of smooth component functions; switching between active components can create nonsmoothness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\in\{f_i(x):1\leq i\leq r\}\) for every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Indices whose component value equals the selected value at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Surface Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional piecewise-smooth models whose active formula changes across smooth switching surfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:U\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(h_1,\ldots,h_q:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(\sigma:U\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\) be constant on every connected component of \(U\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^q\{x:h_j(x)=0\}\). A switching-surface model is the selection \(f(x)=f_{\sigma(x)}(x)\), with values on the switching set specified by a selection rule. It is continuous at \(\bar x\) only if all pieces selected along sequences converging to \(\bar x\) have the same limiting value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth equations divide the domain into regions carrying smooth formulas. At a switching surface, consistency of adjacent limiting values determines continuity.
assumptions_latex: The pieces \(f_i\) and switching functions \(h_j\) are continuously differentiable.
The selection index is regionwise constant off the switching surfaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=f_{\sigma(x)}(x)\) is piecewise smooth, with possible nonsmoothness or discontinuity on \(\bigcup_j\{h_j=0\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the switching-surface leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied. Source support is also needed for the stated continuity criterion and the treatment of values on the switching set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and uniqueness for a strongly convex finite-max subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the minimizer of the threshold-parametrized finite maximum over a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and suppose \(f_i\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu,L}^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\) for \(i=0,1,\ldots,m\), with \(\mu>0\). For any \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), define
\[
f(t;x)=\max\{f_0(x)-t,f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x)\},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Then
\[
\min_{x\in Q}f(t;x)
\]
admits a unique minimizer, denoted by \(x^*(t)\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each real threshold t, the maximum of the shifted objective component and the constraint components has exactly one minimizer over Q when every component belongs to the stated smooth strongly convex class and Q is nonempty, closed, and convex.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,x^*(t)\in Q\quad\text{such that}\quad f(t;x^*(t))=\min_{x\in Q}f(t;x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Danskin-type formula for a smooth parameterized maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional differentiation of a compactly parameterized maximum with a continuous partial gradient, including sublinearity in the direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be open, \(Y\) compact, and \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) continuous. Suppose \(\nabla_x f(x,y)\) exists and is continuous on \(X\times Y\). Define \(\varphi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)\) and \(R(x)=\{y\in Y:f(x,y)=\varphi(x)\}\). Then, for every \(x\in X\) and direction \(g\), \[\varphi'(x;g)=\max_{y\in R(x)}\langle\nabla_x f(x,y),g\rangle.\] Moreover, \(g\mapsto\varphi'(x;g)\) is sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a compactly parameterized family is jointly continuous and has a continuous partial gradient in the decision variable, then its maximum is directionally differentiable in every direction. The derivative is the maximum active partial-gradient pairing and is a sublinear function of the direction.
assumptions_latex: \nabla_x f\text{ exists and is continuous on }X\times Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in X\ \forall g,\quad \varphi'(x;g)=\max_{y\in R(x)}\langle\nabla_x f(x,y),g\rangle,\quad\text{and }g\mapsto\varphi'(x;g)\text{ is sublinear.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower- and Upper-\(\mathcal C^k\) Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local compact-index representations of real-valued functions on open subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and \(f:O\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^k\) on \(O\) if every \(\bar x\in O\) has a neighborhood \(V\) on which \(f(x)=\max_{t\in T}f_t(x)\), where \(T\) is compact, each \(f_t\in\mathcal C^k(V)\), and \(f_t(x)\) together with all partial derivatives through order \(k\) depends jointly continuously on \((t,x)\in T\times V\). Upper-\(\mathcal C^k\) is defined by replacing the maximum with a minimum, equivalently \(f\) is upper-\(\mathcal C^k\) iff \(-f\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^k\). Finite maxima of \(\mathcal C^k\) functions and every \(\mathcal C^k\) function are lower-\(\mathcal C^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is lower-C-k when it is locally the maximum of a compact, jointly continuously parameterized family of C-k functions, including joint continuity of derivatives through order k. Upper-C-k uses minima, equivalently negation. Finite smooth maxima and ordinary C-k functions are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^k\iff \text{it admits the stated local compact-index maximum representation; }f\text{ is upper-}\mathcal C^k\iff -f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional-stationarity equivalence for the minimax ratio and residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: B-differentiable stationarity equivalence at the ratio value attained by the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be componentwise positive in a neighborhood of $\bar x\in X$, and suppose $F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ are B-differentiable at $\bar x$. Define $\bar\theta:=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}F_i(\bar x)/G_i(\bar x)$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferentials of Smooth and Convex Finite Maxima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact active-index formulas for finite maxima of functions differentiable at the reference point and of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For i=1,\ldots,m, let f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable at x and let g_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex. Define
\[
f(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(y),\qquad g(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}g_i(y),
\]
and
\[
I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\},\qquad J(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=g(x)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\},
\qquad
\partial_c g(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in J(x)}\partial_c g_i(x)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite maximum of functions continuously differentiable at x is the convex hull of the active gradients. The convex subdifferential of a finite maximum of convex functions is the convex hull of the active component subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: f(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(y),\quad g(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}g_i(y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\},\qquad \partial_c g(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in J(x)}\partial_c g_i(x)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise sufficient separation condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines uniform almost-sure separation between active and inactive pieces for each of two max representations near a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\bar x\in X\), the pointwise sufficient separation condition holds at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\delta>0\), \(c>0\), and a probability-one set \(\Xi_{\bar x}^{ss}\) such that, for every \(\xi\in\Xi_{\bar x}^{ss}\) and \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb B(\bar x;\delta)}\left[\max_{j\in\mathcal A_i(x;\xi)}\psi_{ij}(x;\xi)-\max_{j\notin\mathcal A_i(x;\xi)}\psi_{ij}(x;\xi)\right]\ge c.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference point satisfies pointwise sufficient separation if, almost surely, the maximum over the active pieces exceeds the maximum over the inactive pieces by a uniform positive margin throughout a neighborhood, for each of the two piece families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative of a maximum function with a parameter-dependent constraint set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded statement for the value function denoted by \(\varphi\) in the omitted formula (6.20); notation is retained from the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a\) be Hausdorff continuous, suppose its support function \(a(x,\ell)\) is u.w.u.d. at \((x_0,\ell)\) for every \(\ell\in\mathcal B\), and let \(f\) be jointly convex in all variables. Then the value function \(\varphi\) is directionally differentiable at \(x_0\), with
\[
\varphi'(x_0;g)=\max_{y\in R_a(x_0)}\max_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)\in\xi_y}\bigl[(\ell_1,g)+a'(x_0,\ell_2;g)\bigr],
\]
where
\[
R_a(x)=\left\{y:\varphi(x)=\max_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)\in\partial f(x,y)}\max_{z\in a(x)}\bigl[(\ell_2,z-y)+f(x,y)\bigr]\right\},
\]
and
\[
\xi_y=\left\{(\ell_1,\ell_2)\in\partial f(x,y):\varphi(x)=\max_{z\in a(x)}\bigl[(\ell_2,z-y)+f(x,y)\bigr]\right\}.
\]
If \(f\) is nonaffine on every closed interval joining \((x_0,z)\) and \((x_0,y)\) with \(z\in R_a(x_0)\) and \(y\notin R(x_0)\), where \(R(x)=\{y:\varphi(x)=f(x,y)\}\), then \(R_a(x_0)\) may be replaced by \(R(x_0)\) in the derivative formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the set-valued mapping is Hausdorff continuous, its support function has the stated uniform weak upper directional derivative, and the integrand is jointly convex, then the associated parameter-dependent maximum value function is directionally differentiable. Its derivative is the maximum, over active points and active subgradients, of the sum of the parameter-subgradient pairing and the support-function derivative. Under the stated strict nonaffinity condition, the enlarged active set may be replaced by the ordinary maximizer set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linearized improvement-function bundle subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint handling for a nonsmooth problem with finitely many inequality constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraint functions \(g_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), define \(g(x):=\max_{1\le i\le p}g_i(x)\) and, at \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(H(x;y):=\max\{f(x)-f(y),g(x)\}\). If every f_i is convex, then f'(x;d)=\max\{\langle g_i,d\rangle:i\in I(x),\ g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\} for every d and \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite pointwise maximum, only active component functions contribute to its directional derivative and subdifferential. Active gradients give the smooth formulas, while active subgradients give the convex formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized minimax fractional program and parameterized residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a vector-ratio minimax problem and its scalar Dinkelbach-type residual model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, define $F(x)/G(x):=(F_1(x)/G_1(x),\ldots,F_m(x)/G_m(x))$. Its associated single-parameter model is the maximum of the componentwise differences between the numerator and the parameter-scaled denominator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative of a compactly parameterized maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-envelope rule preserving the source's u.w.u.d. hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be open, \(Y\) compact, and \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) jointly continuous. Define \(\varphi(z)=\max_{y\in Y}f(z,y)\) and \(R(x)=\{y\in Y:f(x,y)=\varphi(x)\}\). Fix \(x\in X\) and a direction \(g\). If \(f\) is u.w.u.d. at \((x,y)\) in direction \(g\) for every \(y\in R(x)\), then \[\varphi'(x;g)=\max_{y\in R(x)}f'(x,y;g).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a jointly continuous function maximized over a compact parameter set, the stated u.w.u.d. condition at every active maximizer ensures directional differentiability of the maximum; its derivative is the largest active component derivative.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is u.w.u.d. at }(x,y)\text{ in direction }g\quad\forall y\in R(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi'(x;g)\text{ exists and }\varphi'(x;g)=\max_{y\in R(x)}f'(x,y;g).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), be continuously differentiable. A finite min-type model is \[f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x),\qquad x\in U.\] Its active-minimizer set is \(I_-(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). The function \(f\) is continuous and locally Lipschitz on \(U\), and, for every \(x\in U\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), is directionally differentiable with \[f'(x;d)=\min_{i\in I_-(x)}\langle\nabla f_i(x),d\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite min-type model selects the smallest of finitely many continuously differentiable pieces. It is locally Lipschitz, and its active gradients determine its directional derivative.

children.title: Lower-Envelope Models

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Envelope Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower envelopes represented as pointwise infima over an indexed function family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(Y\) be an index set, and let \(F:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The lower envelope of the family \(\{F(\cdot,y):y\in Y\}\) is \[v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y).\] When the infimum is attained, the active-minimizer set is \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\), and \(v(x)=F(x,y)\) for every \(y\in S(x)\). For finite \(Y\) and finite continuous component functions, \(v\) is continuous and the infimum is attained everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower envelope is the pointwise infimum of an indexed family; attained minimizers identify the pieces supporting its value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\), with \(v(x)=F(x,y)\) whenever \(y\in S(x)\).

notation.meaning: set of indices attaining the infimum

children.title: Active-Minimizer Tie Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiple components attain the lower envelope.

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(\bar x\) is in a tie regime exactly when \(|I_-(\bar x)|\ge 2\); equality of all active gradients implies differentiability at \(\bar x\), whereas two unequal active gradients imply nondifferentiability there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tie points at which two or more component functions attain a finite lower envelope.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(\bar x\in U\), and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\). For \(f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\), define \(I_-(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). The point \(\bar x\) lies in an active-minimizer tie regime precisely when \[|I_-(\bar x)|\ge 2.\] For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f'(\bar x;d)=\min_{i\in I_-(\bar x)}\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),d\rangle.\] The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\) if all active gradients coincide, and it is not differentiable there if two active gradients differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-minimizer tie occurs when at least two pieces attain the minimum. Coincident active gradients yield differentiability, while unequal active gradients force nondifferentiability.

children.title: Envelope Discontinuity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Lower-envelope settings with unstable or discontinuous value behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Discontinuity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanisms permitting a lower envelope to lose continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite lower envelope \(v(x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) of continuous real-valued functions is continuous; hence active-piece switching alone cannot create discontinuity in this setting. Discontinuity may occur when finiteness, continuity of the pieces, or a fixed index family is removed. For example, with \(f_k(x)=kx\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), \[v(x)=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}}kx=\begin{cases}x,&x\ge0,\\-\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}\] Thus an infinite family can produce an extended-real lower envelope that is discontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite minima of continuous pieces remain continuous. Infinite families, discontinuous pieces, or changing feasible indices can break continuity.
assumptions_latex: For the continuity guarantee, the family is finite and every component is continuous.
For the counterexample, extended-real envelope values are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite continuous case excludes discontinuity, whereas \(v(x)=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}}kx\) is discontinuous at \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the stated example is mathematically plausible when the positive-integer convention for the natural numbers and extended-real continuity are used. No source with a specific locator is supplied for either the boundary claim or the example, so source review is required.

children.title: Median Models
children.top_down_role: Models based on central order-statistic selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Median Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise median selection from an odd finite family of scalar component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=2r+1\) and let \(f_1,ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\). For each \(x\in X\), write the ordered component values as \(f_{(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le f_{(m)}(x)\), counting multiplicities. The median model is \[M(x)=f_{(r+1)}(x).\] Equivalently, \[M(x)=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\\|S|=r+1}}\ \max_{i\in S}f_i(x).\] If all component functions are continuous, then \(M\) is continuous; if they are locally Lipschitz, then \(M\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an odd number of scalar pieces, the median model selects the middle ordered value and inherits continuity or local Lipschitzness from its pieces.

notation.meaning: j-th smallest component value at x
half the number of nonmedian observations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The median formula and min-max representation are standard, but the LaTeX contains the malformed text "f_1,ldots,f_m". In addition, continuity and local Lipschitzness are asserted although X is only a set, with no topology or metric specified. No supporting source with a locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Median of a Finite Ordered Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued median convention for finitely many distinct ordered real numbers, including the even-cardinality interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_n\) and \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\). A number \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) is a median of \(A\) if \[\#\{i:a_i\le\beta\}\ge\frac n2\quad\text{and}\quad\#\{i:a_i\ge\beta\}\ge\frac n2.\] Thus the set of medians is \[\operatorname{median}(A)=\begin{cases}\{a_{(n+1)/2}\},&n\text{ odd},\\[a_{n/2},a_{n/2+1}],&n\text{ even}.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A median has at least half the observations on each side. With an odd number of distinct ordered observations it is the middle observation; with an even number, every point between the two middle observations is a median.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{median}(A)=\begin{cases}\{a_{(n+1)/2}\},&n\text{ odd},\\[a_{n/2},a_{n/2+1}],&n\text{ even}\end{cases}

children.title: Trimmed Models
children.top_down_role: Models excluding selected extreme ordered components.

knowledge_statements.title: Trimmed Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sums or averages after deleting prescribed lower and upper order statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and write \(f_{(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le f_{(m)}(x)\). For integers \(\ell,u\ge0\) satisfying \(\ell+u<m\), the \((\ell,u)\)-trimmed sum and mean are \[T_{\ell,u}(x)=\sum_{j=\ell+1}^{m-u}f_{(j)}(x),\qquad \bar T_{\ell,u}(x)=\frac{T_{\ell,u}(x)}{m-\ell-u}.\] They discard the \(\ell\) smallest and \(u\) largest component values. Continuity, respectively local Lipschitz continuity, of every \(f_i\) implies the same regularity for both trimmed models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trimmed model removes fixed numbers of the smallest and largest component values, then sums or averages those remaining.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\ell,u}(x)=\sum_{j=\ell+1}^{m-u}f_{(j)}(x)\) and \(\bar T_{\ell,u}(x)=T_{\ell,u}(x)/(m-\ell-u)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trimmed-sum and trimmed-mean formulas fit the leaf, but continuity and local Lipschitzness are not meaningful until a topology or metric on X is specified. The record also has no source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Top-k Order Models
children.top_down_role: Models retaining a prescribed number of largest ordered components.

knowledge_statements.title: Top-k Order Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum or average of the largest k values in a finite scalar family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and write their values in nonincreasing order as \(f_{[1]}(x)\ge\cdots\ge f_{[m]}(x)\). For \(1\le k\le m\), the top-\(k\) sum is \[S_k(x)=\sum_{j=1}^k f_{[j]}(x)=\max_{\substack{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\\|I|=k}}\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x).\] The top-\(k\) average is \(A_k(x)=S_k(x)/k\). If each \(f_i\) is continuous, respectively locally Lipschitz, then so are \(S_k\) and \(A_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A top-k model sums or averages the k largest component values and equals a maximum over all k-element index subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k(x)=\sum_{j=1}^k f_{[j]}(x)=\max_{|I|=k}\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The top-k subset representation is mathematically standard and the representation content kind is suitable, but the regularity claims require a topological or metric domain rather than an unspecified set X. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Tie-Dependent Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Order-statistic regimes where ties alter selected component sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Dependent Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-statistic thresholds where membership in a selected rank set is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\in\mathbb{R}\) and write \(z_{[1]}\ge\cdots\ge z_{[m]}\). A top-\(k\) selection has a boundary tie when \(z_{[k]}=z_{[k+1]}\) for \(1\le k<m\). Then the index subset attaining \(\max_{|I|=k}\sum_{i\in I}z_i\) need not be unique, although the selected sum is unique. Any rule returning a particular maximizing subset can therefore change discontinuously under arbitrarily small perturbations, while the top-\(k\) value remains continuous as a function of \(z\). The analogous ambiguity occurs for median or trimmed selections when equal values straddle a retained-rank boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ties across a rank cutoff make the selected indices nonunique. The order-statistic value stays continuous, but a particular index selection may jump.
assumptions_latex: A selection rule returns one maximizing index subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(z_{[k]}=z_{[k+1]}\), the maximizing subset may be nonunique and a single-valued subset selector may be discontinuous.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary-tie condition and nonuniqueness of maximizing subsets are correct, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. However, discontinuity of a subset-valued selector requires an explicit topology or metric on the selector codomain, and no source with an inspectable locator supports the claim.

children.title: Piecewise Affine-Quadratic Model Family
children.top_down_role: Piecewise polynomial models separated by convexity and domain partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finitely partitioned piecewise-affine mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is piecewise affine if there exist finitely many closed polyhedral sets \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) covering \(\mathbb{R}^n\), matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and vectors \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(F(x)=A_i x+b_i\) whenever \(x\in P_i\). The affine formulas must agree at every point belonging to overlapping pieces, so that \(F\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is piecewise affine when a finite polyhedral cover exists on whose pieces the mapping has mutually consistent affine formulas.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) are closed polyhedral sets with \(\bigcup_{i=1}^N P_i=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=A_i x+b_i\) for every \(x\in P_i\) and every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued finite-dimensional piecewise linear-quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is piecewise linear-quadratic if its domain is the union of finitely many polyhedral sets \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) and, for each \(i\), there are a symmetric matrix \(Q_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), a vector \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and a scalar \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\) for every \(x\in P_i\). Formulas agree wherever pieces overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real function is piecewise linear-quadratic when its domain has a finite polyhedral cover and a consistent quadratic-affine formula on each piece.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^N P_i\) for finitely many polyhedral sets \(P_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_{P_i}\) is quadratic-affine for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Piecewise-Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued piecewise-quadratic models whose assembled function is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-valued function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is a nonconvex piecewise-quadratic model if there exist finitely many polyhedral sets \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) covering \(\mathbb{R}^n\), symmetric matrices \(Q_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and scalars \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\) for every \(x\in P_i\), with consistent formulas on overlaps, and such that the assembled function is not convex. Equivalently, there exist \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t\in(0,1)\) for which \[f(tx+(1-t)y)>tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued piecewise-quadratic model is nonconvex when its consistent quadratic formulas assemble into a function that violates the convexity inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has consistent quadratic-affine formulas on a finite polyhedral cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \exists t\in(0,1): f(tx+(1-t)y)>tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand-Differentiable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand differentiability at a point in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there in every direction and its directional derivative \(F'(\bar x;\cdot)\) gives a first-order approximation uniformly along perturbations: \[F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-F'(\bar x;h)=o(\lVert h\rVert)\quad\text{as }h\to0.\] The map \(h\mapsto F'(\bar x;h)\) is positively homogeneous but need not be linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability means that the directional derivative exists in every direction and approximates the mapping with an error negligible relative to the perturbation norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)=F(\bar x)+F'(\bar x;h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: directional derivative of F at the base point
remainder divided by the perturbation norm tends to zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand and Strong Bouligand Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines pointwise, strong, and neighborhood Bouligand differentiability for finite-dimensional vector-valued maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), where \(\mathcal O\) is open, and let \(x\in\mathcal O\). The map \(\Phi\) is Bouligand-differentiable (B-differentiable) at \(x\) if it is Lipschitz continuous in a neighborhood of \(x\) and directionally differentiable at \(x\). Its directional derivative \(\Phi'(x;d)\) is then called its B-derivative along \(d\). Define \(e(y)=\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)-\Phi'(x;y-x)\). The B-derivative is strong, and \(\Phi\) is strongly B-differentiable at \(x\), if \[\lim_{\substack{y^1\ne y^2\\(y^1,y^2)\to(x,x)}}\frac{e(y^1)-e(y^2)}{\|y^1-y^2\|}=0.\] The map is B-differentiable near \(x\) if it is B-differentiable at every point of some neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is B-differentiable at a point when it is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable there; the directional derivative is its B-derivative. It is strongly B-differentiable when the difference of its remainders at any two distinct nearby points is little-o of the distance between them. It is B-differentiable near the point when it has the pointwise property throughout some neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ is B-differentiable at }x\iff \Phi\text{ is Lipschitz continuous in a neighborhood of }x\text{ and directionally differentiable at }x;\quad \Phi\text{ is strongly B-differentiable at }x\iff \lim_{\substack{y^1\ne y^2\\(y^1,y^2)\to(x,x)}}\frac{e(y^1)-e(y^2)}{\|y^1-y^2\|}=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Approximation by the B-Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the first-order remainder property implied by Bouligand differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(x\in\mathcal O\), and let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m\) be B-differentiable at \(x\). Then \[\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\y\ne x}}\frac{\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)-\Phi'(x;y-x)}{\|y-x\|}=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a map is B-differentiable at a point, its B-derivative gives a first-order approximation whose remainder divided by the displacement norm converges to zero as the displaced point approaches the base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\substack{y\to x\\y\ne x}}\frac{\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)-\Phi'(x;y-x)}{\|y-x\|}=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chain Rule for Bouligand-Differentiable Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the B-derivative chain rule and sufficient conditions for preservation of a strong B-derivative under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathcal O'\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be open. Let \(\bar x\in\mathcal O\), let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m\) be B-differentiable at \(\bar x\), and let \(\Psi:\mathcal O'\to\mathbb R^\ell\) be B-differentiable at \(\Phi(\bar x)\in\mathcal O'\). Suppose that \(\Phi\) maps a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) into \(\mathcal O'\). Then \(H=\Psi\circ\Phi\) is B-differentiable at \(\bar x\), and \[H'(\bar x;d)=\Psi'\bigl(\Phi(\bar x);\Phi'(\bar x;d)\bigr)\qquad\forall d\in\mathbb R^n.\] If, additionally, \(\Psi\) is strongly F-differentiable at \(\Phi(\bar x)\) and \(\Phi\) has a strong B-derivative at \(\bar x\), then \(H\) has a strong B-derivative at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composition of suitably composable B-differentiable maps is B-differentiable, with the outer B-derivative evaluated in the direction supplied by the inner B-derivative. If the outer map is strongly F-differentiable and the inner map has a strong B-derivative, then the composition has a strong B-derivative.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ and }\mathcal O'\subseteq\mathbb R^m\text{ are open}
\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is B-differentiable at }\bar x
\Psi:\mathcal O'\to\mathbb R^\ell\text{ is B-differentiable at }\Phi(\bar x)
\Phi\text{ maps a neighborhood of }\bar x\text{ into }\mathcal O'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H=\Psi\circ\Phi\text{ is B-differentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }H'(\bar x;d)=\Psi'(\Phi(\bar x);\Phi'(\bar x;d))\ \forall d\in\mathbb R^n;\quad [\Psi\text{ is strongly F-differentiable at }\Phi(\bar x)\land\Phi\text{ has a strong B-derivative at }\bar x]\Rightarrow H\text{ has a strong B-derivative at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-Jacobian semismoothness for locally Lipschitz mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally Lipschitz mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\) and, for every sequence \(h_k\to0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h_k)\), \[F(\bar x+h_k)-F(\bar x)-V_kh_k=o(\lVert h_k\rVert).\] Here \(\partial_C F(x)\) is the Clarke generalized Jacobian, the convex hull of limiting Jacobians at differentiability points approaching \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping is semismooth when every nearby Clarke generalized Jacobian yields a first-order model with a little-o residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise semismoothness implies semismoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inheritance of ordinary and strong semismoothness under finite continuous selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), where \(\mathcal O\) is open, and let \(\bar x\in\mathcal O\). If \(G\) is piecewise semismooth near \(\bar x\), then \(G\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\). If \(G\) is piecewise strongly semismooth near \(\bar x\), then \(G\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional map that is piecewise semismooth near a point is semismooth there. The corresponding implication holds for strong semismoothness.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is piecewise semismooth or piecewise strongly semismooth near }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is respectively semismooth or strongly semismooth at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous-selection definition for ordinary and strong piecewise semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(G\) is piecewise semismooth near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}G\) if, in a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), it is a continuous selection of finitely many semismooth maps. It is piecewise strongly semismooth near \(\bar x\) if the finitely many selection maps are strongly semismooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is piecewise semismooth near a point when it continuously selects among finitely many semismooth maps locally. Requiring all selection maps to be strongly semismooth defines piecewise strong semismoothness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is piecewise semismooth, respectively piecewise strongly semismooth, near }\bar x\text{ under the stated selection condition.}

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Semismooth Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-residual strengthening of semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally Lipschitz mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and there exist \(c>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for every \(x\in U\) and every \(V\in\partial_C F(x)\), \[\lVert F(x)-F(\bar x)-V(x-\bar x)\rVert\le c\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2.\] Thus every nearby generalized Jacobian supplies a uniformly second-order-accurate local model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness requires every nearby Clarke generalized Jacobian model to have a residual bounded quadratically in the displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh=O(\lVert h\rVert^2)\) uniformly for \(V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise affine maps are strongly semismooth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global class inclusion together with the local directional-derivative identity supporting it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every piecewise affine map \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is strongly semismooth. More precisely, for every \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), there exists a neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[G'(\bar x;x-\bar x)=G'(x;x-\bar x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathcal N.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every piecewise affine map between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces is strongly semismooth. Near any base point, the relevant directional derivatives based at the base point and at the nearby point coincide.
assumptions_latex: G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is piecewise affine}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is strongly semismooth, and locally }G'(\bar x;x-\bar x)=G'(x;x-\bar x).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonregular Switching Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimum-type switch showing failure of Clarke regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x)=\min\{x,-x\}=-|x|\). This continuous piecewise-affine switching model has directional derivative \(f'(0;d)=-|d|\). Its Clarke generalized directional derivative is \(f^{\circ}(0;d)=|d|\). Hence \(f'(0;d)\ne f^{\circ}(0;d)\) whenever \(d\ne0\), so \(f\) is not Clarke regular at the switching point \(0\), although each selected piece is smooth and \(f\) is Bouligand differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of two affine pieces, minus absolute value, is Bouligand differentiable but not Clarke regular at its switching point.
assumptions_latex: Clarke regularity requires \(f'(0;d)=f^{\circ}(0;d)\) for every direction \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;d)=-|d|\ne |d|=f^{\circ}(0;d)\) for every \(d\ne0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct computation gives the two directional derivatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and derivative calculations are mathematically correct and fit the nonregular-switching container, but no inspectable citation supports the stated Clarke-regularity convention.

children.title: Piecewise-Smooth Oracle Model
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces distinguished by active-piece information, multiple activity, and hidden switching.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Active-Piece Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order oracle for a max model at points with a unique active piece.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le N} f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable, define \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). A single-active-piece oracle is queried only at points satisfying \(I(x)=\{i_x\}\) and returns \(\mathcal O_1(x)=(f(x),i_x,\nabla f_{i_x}(x))\). At such a point, \(f\) is differentiable and the returned gradient equals \(\nabla f(x)\). The interface is unspecified at ties unless an additional selection rule is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a uniquely active point of a finite smooth maximum, this oracle returns the value, active index, and the ordinary gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le N}f_i(x)\) with each \(f_i\) continuously differentiable.
\(I(x)\) is a singleton at every admissible query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_1(x)=(f(x),i_x,\nabla f(x))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unique activity makes a finite smooth maximum locally equal to its active piece

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unique-active-piece calculus is standard, but the specifically named oracle interface is a constructed definition with no source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Multi-Active-Piece Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces exposing several simultaneously active pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Active-Piece Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order oracle exposing all active pieces of a finite smooth maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le N}f_i(x)\) with continuously differentiable pieces, a multi-active-piece oracle returns \[\mathcal O_M(x)=\bigl(f(x),I(x),\{(f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x)):i\in I(x)\}\bigr),\qquad I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}.\] The response includes every tied maximizer. Consequently it determines the directional derivative \(f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla f_i(x)^{\mathsf T}d\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), without requiring a unique active index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-active oracle returns every tied active piece and its gradient, thereby determining the directional derivative of a finite smooth maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla f_i(x)^{\mathsf T}d\) is determined by \(\mathcal O_M(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directional derivative formula for a finite maximum of smooth functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-maximum directional-derivative formula is standard and the definition fits the terminal container, but the multi-active oracle interface has no cited source.

children.title: Tie-Aware Oracle Responses
children.top_down_role: Oracle outputs that retain information about tied piece values.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Aware Oracle Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable response certificate for tied finite smooth maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_i f_i(x)\), a reported tuple \((v,J,\{g_i\}_{i\in J})\) is a valid tie-aware first-order response at \(x\) when \(v=f_i(x)\) and \(g_i=\nabla f_i(x)\) for every \(i\in J\), while \(f_j(x)<v\) for every \(j\notin J\). These finitely checkable relations certify \(J=I(x)\), \(v=f(x)\), and \[\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{g_i:i\in J\},\qquad f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in J}g_i^{\mathsf T}d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Piece values and gradients certify a tie-aware response when all reported pieces attain the maximum and every omitted piece lies strictly below it.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le N}f_i(x)\) with continuously differentiable pieces.
All piece values and reported gradients are exactly evaluable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J=I(x)\), \(v=f(x)\), and \(\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{g_i:i\in J\}\).

notation.meaning: reported gradient of active piece i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite maximum calculus yields the displayed generalized gradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated finite checks correctly identify the complete active set, and the generalized-gradient formulas are standard for a finite smooth maximum. The certificate interpretation and interface nevertheless lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Hidden Multiplicity Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by oracle responses concealing multiple active pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Multiplicity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A hidden tie defeats an interface that reports only one selected active gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an interface that, at a query point, reports a function value and the gradient of one selected active piece even when several pieces are active. At \(x=0\), compare the smooth model \(f(x)=x\) with the switching model \(g(x)=\max\{x,-x\}=|x|\). By selecting the piece \(x\) for \(g\), the interface returns the identical response \((0,1)\) for both models. Nevertheless, in direction \(d=-1\), one has \(f'(0;d)=-1\) and \(g'(0;d)=1\). Thus a value and one selected active gradient do not reveal hidden active-piece multiplicity and cannot determine the directional model at a tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth linear function and absolute value can produce the same value and selected-gradient response at zero while having different directional derivatives, so the response hides the tie.
assumptions_latex: The interface reports only a function value and one selected active-piece gradient.
For \(g(x)=\max\{x,-x\}\), the interface may select the piece \(x\) at \(0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct directional-derivative computation establishes the indistinguishability failure

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Switching Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle interface for a finite piecewise-smooth maximum with an undisclosed active branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)\), where \(I\) is finite and every \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable. Define the active set by \(I(x)=\{i\in I:\phi_i(x)=f(x)\}\). A hidden-switching oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal O\) such that, for every query \(x\), it selects some \(i_x\in I(x)\) and returns \(\mathcal O(x)=(f(x),\nabla\phi_{i_x}(x))\), while neither revealing \(i_x\) nor returning the other active gradients. Its output may therefore vary between repeated queries at a tie point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns the value and one active-piece gradient, but hides the selected piece and all other active gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O(x)\in\{(f(x),\nabla\phi_i(x)):i\in I(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: set of pieces active at the query point
active index selected but not disclosed by the oracle

review_flags: Exact hidden-oracle convention lacks a supplied supporting locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hidden-switching convention has no cited evidence. In addition, a deterministic mapping cannot vary between repeated queries at the same point; that behavior requires a set-valued, randomized, or stateful oracle specification. A source is needed to determine the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Piece Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite partially separable objectives whose components independently select smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A component-piece decomposition of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a representation \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m} f_j(U_jx),\qquad f_j(z)=\max_{k\in K_j}\phi_{jk}(z),\] where each \(K_j\) is finite, \(U_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{d_j}\) is linear, and every \(\phi_{jk}:\mathbb R^{d_j}\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable. knowledge_statements.title: Chained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-neighbor partially separable functions on an ordered variable chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i}\), a chained model is a function of the form \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\psi_i(x_i,x_{i+1}),\] where each link function \(\psi_i:\mathbb R^{d_i+d_{i+1}}\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz. Each interior block \(x_i\) occurs only in links \(\psi_{i-1}\) and \(\psi_i\), while the endpoint blocks occur in one link each.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chained model sums locally Lipschitz terms coupling consecutive variable blocks only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\psi_i\circ P_i\), where \(P_i x=(x_i,x_{i+1})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Chained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chained objectives whose individual links select from finitely many smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A piecewise-chained model is a chained function \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\max_{k\in K_i}\phi_{ik}(x_i,x_{i+1}),\] where every \(K_i\) is finite and every link piece \(\phi_{ik}:\mathbb R^{d_i+d_{i+1}}\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable. At \(x\), link \(i\) has active set \(K_i(x)=\{k\in K_i:\phi_{ik}(x_i,x_{i+1})=\max_{r\in K_i}\phi_{ir}(x_i,x_{i+1})\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Coupling Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence representation of nearest-neighbor coupling in a path-structured objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_N\) be the path with vertices \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and edges \(E=\{(i,i+1):1\le i<N\}\). A chain-coupled objective admits the representation \[f(x)=\sum_{(i,i+1)\in E}\psi_i(P_i x),\qquad P_i x=(x_i,x_{i+1}).\] Consequently, the block-term incidence matrix \(B\), defined by \(B_{ji}=1\) when term \(j\) depends on block \(x_i\), has consecutive ones in every row and at most two nonzero entries in every column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chain coupling corresponds to a path graph: each term uses two consecutive blocks, and each block meets at most two terms.
assumptions_latex: Each link term depends only on \((x_i,x_{i+1})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{ji}=1\) exactly when \(i\in\{j,j+1\}\), so every column of \(B\) has at most two ones.

knowledge_statements.title: Switching Along Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local piece changes and generalized gradients in finite max-type chain links.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a piecewise-chained model, select \(k_i\in K_i(x)\) independently at every link. The corresponding selected-piece gradient is \[g(x;k_1,\ldots,k_{N-1})=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}P_i^{\mathsf T}\nabla\phi_{ik_i}(P_i x).\] A link can switch only where at least two of its pieces tie. Moreover, because finite maxima of smooth functions are Clarke regular, the Clarke subdifferential satisfies \[\partial_C f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}P_i^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla\phi_{ik}(P_i x):k\in K_i(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each link switches at a local tie; generalized gradients combine convex hulls of active link gradients along the chain.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\phi_{ik}\) is continuously differentiable near \(P_i x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)=\sum_i P_i^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla\phi_{ik}(P_i x):k\in K_i(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: active piece indices at link i
Clarke subdifferential of f at x
projection onto consecutive blocks i and i+1

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Partial Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial separability allowing different component functions to share variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is overlapping partially separable if \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}f_j(U_jx)\] for linear variable-selection maps \(U_j\), and there exist distinct \(j,\ell\) whose selected coordinate sets overlap. If \(S_j\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is the support selected by \(U_j\), the overlap degree is \(\omega=\max_{r}|\{j:r\in S_j\}|\); genuine overlap means \(\omega\ge2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Weakly Convex Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation preserves a uniform almost-sure weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space and let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\Omega\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be jointly measurable. Suppose that for almost every \(\xi\), the function \(x\mapsto F(x,\xi)+(\rho/2)\|x\|^2\) is proper and convex, and that \(F(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\). Then \[f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\] is \(\rho\)-weakly convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable expectation of sample functions sharing one weak-convexity modulus retains that modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\cdot,\xi)+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is proper and convex almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2=\mathbb E[F(\cdot,\xi)+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2]\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Weak-Convexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convexity restricted to a specified convex neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. The function \(f\) is locally \(\rho\)-weakly convex on \(U\) if \[x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\] is convex on \(U\). It is locally weakly convex at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if there exist an open convex neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a finite \(\rho\ge0\) for which this condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local weak convexity means that adding a quadratic makes the function convex on some convex neighborhood of the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex on \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Global Weak-Convexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single quadratic convexification modulus valid throughout the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is globally \(\rho\)-weakly convex, for \(\rho\ge0\), if \[x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\] is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)+\frac{\rho}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global weak convexity uses one finite quadratic modulus valid for every pair of points in the function's domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Dependent Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local weak-convexity modulus on an open convex neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex. Define
\[
\rho_f(U):=\inf\{\rho\geq 0: x\mapsto f(x)+(\rho/2)\|x\|^2\text{ is convex on }U\},
\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The function is weakly convex near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) precisely when \(\rho_f(U)<+\infty\) for some such neighborhood \(U\ni\bar x\). If \(U_1\subset U_2\), then \(\rho_f(U_1)\leq\rho_f(U_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The neighborhood-dependent modulus is the infimum of the quadratic curvature corrections that make the function convex on the chosen open convex neighborhood. The function is locally weakly convex at a point exactly when this modulus is finite on some such neighborhood of that point, and shrinking the neighborhood cannot increase the modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally weakly convex at \(\bar x\) iff \(\rho_f(U)<+\infty\) for some \(U\ni\bar x\), and \(U_1\subset U_2\Rightarrow\rho_f(U_1)\leq\rho_f(U_2)\).

notation.meaning: Least weak-convexity modulus valid on U.

knowledge_statements.title: Globalization Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local weak convexity need not admit one global modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-x^4\). On every bounded interval \((-R,R)\), the function \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\rho_R/2)x^2\) is convex whenever \(\rho_R\geq12R^2\), because its second derivative is \(\rho_R-12x^2\). Hence \(f\) is locally weakly convex everywhere. No finite \(\rho\) makes \(f(x)+(\rho/2)x^2\) convex on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), since \(\rho-12x^2<0\) for sufficiently large \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function minus x to the fourth is weakly convex on every bounded interval, but its required modulus grows without bound, preventing globalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally weakly convex everywhere but is not globally \(\rho\)-weakly convex for any finite \(\rho\).

notation.meaning: Weak-convexity modulus used on the interval of radius R.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise prox-regularity relative to a limiting subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) if \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\) and there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\geq0\) such that
\[
f(x')\geq f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\|x'-x\|^2
\]
whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(\|x'-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\), \(|f(x)-f(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\), and \(v\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(\|v-\bar v\|<\varepsilon\). Here \(\partial f\) is the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a reference point and subgradient, every nearby limiting subgradient supports the function up to a uniform local quadratic error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed uniform local quadratic support inequality defines prox-regularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of f at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation resembles the standard pointwise definition, but prox-regularity conventions and the limiting-subdifferential convention require an authoritative exact locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set prox-regularity expressed through nearby normal vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\in C\) for \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\geq0\) such that
\[
\langle v,x'-x\rangle\leq\frac r2\|x'-x\|^2
\]
for all \(x,x'\in C\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and all \(v\in N_C(x)\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar v)\). Equivalently, the indicator function \(\delta_C\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), under the limiting-normal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed set is prox-regular when nearby normal vectors satisfy a uniform quadratic support inequality; equivalently, its indicator is a prox-regular function.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) and \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal inequality, equivalently prox-regularity of \(\delta_C\), defines prox-regularity of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to C at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal inequality and indicator-function equivalence are plausible, but their exact quantifiers and limiting-normal convention require a supporting source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prox-regularity of a closed set at a point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local normal-cone inequality and its exterior-ball interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closed set \(S\) is prox-regular at \(\bar{x}\in S\) if there exists \(\rho>0\) such that all distinct \(x,x'\in S\) sufficiently near \(\bar{x}\) and all sufficiently small \(v\in N_S(x)\) satisfy \[\langle v,x'-x\rangle<\rho\|x'-x\|^2.\] Geometrically, the ball centered at \(x+v/(2\rho)\), with \(x\) on its boundary, has interior disjoint from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed set is prox-regular at a point if nearby distinct set points and sufficiently small normal vectors satisfy a uniform quadratic support inequality. The associated externally tangent balls have interiors disjoint from the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\rho>0:\ \langle v,x'-x\rangle<\rho\|x'-x\|^2\quad\text{for all distinct nearby }x,x'\in S\text{ and sufficiently small }v\in N_S(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Prox-Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One prox-regularity modulus valid over a prescribed normal bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed, let \(S\subset C\), and let \(R>0\). The set \(C\) is uniformly \(r\)-prox-regular on \(S\) for normals of length at most \(R\) if some neighborhood \(U\supset S\) satisfies
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq\frac r2\|y-x\|^2
\]
for every \(x,y\in C\cap U\) and every \(v\in N_C(x)\) with \(\|v\|\leq R\). Uniformity means that the same neighborhood and finite modulus \(r\) work for all admissible base points and normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform prox-regularity requires one neighborhood and one quadratic modulus to control all bounded normal vectors over the prescribed subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A common neighborhood \(U\) and modulus \(r<+\infty\) satisfy the displayed normal inequality for every admissible \(x\), \(y\), and \(v\).

notation.meaning: Subset on which uniformity is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Uniform prox-regularity has several radius, normal-scaling, and neighborhood conventions. An exact source is needed to validate this particular bounded-normal formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersecting branches destroy quadratic normal support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{R}^2.
\]
At \(\bar x=(0,0)\), the vector \(\bar v=(0,1)\) belongs to \(N_C(\bar x)\). Taking \(x=\bar x\), \(v=\bar v\), and \(x'=(0,t)\in C\) with \(t>0\), the prox-regularity inequality would require \(t\leq(r/2)t^2\). This fails for every finite \(r\) when \(t>0\) is sufficiently small. Thus \(C\) is not prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of the coordinate axes is not prox-regular at their crossing: a branch-aligned displacement violates every finite quadratic normal bound.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the union of the two coordinate axes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite local modulus \(r\) satisfies the prox-regularity inequality at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone at the crossing point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossing-axes calculation is mathematically plausible under the limiting-normal convention, but it lacks evidence. After sourcing, failure_boundary should be considered instead of counterexample to match the exact terminal container.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-C2 Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local lower-C representation by smooth maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-valued function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is lower-\(C^2\) near \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), a compact index space \(T\), and functions \(\phi_t:U\to\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{t\in T}\phi_t(x)\qquad(x\in U),
\]
where every \(\phi_t\) is twice continuously differentiable in \(x\), and \((t,x)\mapsto\phi_t(x)\), \((t,x)\mapsto\nabla_x\phi_t(x)\), and \((t,x)\mapsto\nabla_x^2\phi_t(x)\) are jointly continuous on \(T\times U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-C2 function is locally the maximum of a compact, jointly C2-continuous family of smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{t\in T}\phi_t(x)\) locally, with joint continuity through second derivatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Amenable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-convex composition with the basic normal qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is strongly amenable at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if, on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\),
\[
f(x)=g(F(x)),
\]
where \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(C^2\), \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, and
\[
N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.
\]
The last condition is the basic constraint qualification for this representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly amenable function is locally a convex lower-semicontinuous function composed with a C2 mapping satisfying a normal-cone qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
\(F\) is \(C^2\) and \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local composition and normal qualification define strong amenability at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the convex domain of g.
Adjoint derivative of F at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Amenability Implies Prox-Regularity and Subdifferential Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local regularity consequences of strong amenability, including persistence along the relative domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be strongly amenable at $\bar x$. Then $f$ is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at $\bar x$. Moreover, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $\bar x$ such that these properties hold at every $x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function strongly amenable at x-bar is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous there, and both properties persist at every domain point sufficiently near x-bar.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni\bar x\ \forall x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f:\ f\text{ is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality conditions for MPECs with strongly amenable potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amenability removes the additional lower-regularity and graph-closedness assumptions from the composite-potential GVI theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\bar x,\bar y)$ be a local solution of the finite-dimensional MPEC, with $\Omega$ locally closed near $\bar x$, $f$ continuous near $(\bar x,\bar y)$, and $\phi=\psi\circ g$ strongly amenable there. If additionally $\varphi$ is locally Lipschitz near $(\bar x,\bar y)$, its lower-subdifferential inclusion also holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Amenability Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate inner mappings invalidate the amenable chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=\delta_{(-\infty,0]}\), let \(F(x)=x^2\), and set \(f=g\circ F=\delta_{\{0\}}\). At \(\bar x=0\), one has \(F'(0)=0\) and
\[
N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(0))=N_{(-\infty,0]}(0)=[0,+\infty),
\]
so the qualification intersection is nontrivial. Correspondingly,
\[
F'(0)^*\partial g(F(0))=\{0\}\quad\text{but}\quad\partial f(0)=\mathbb{R}.
\]
Thus the subdifferential chain-rule equality associated with this smooth-convex representation fails when the qualification is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indicator composed with the squaring map, degeneracy violates the qualification and makes the formal subgradient chain rule strictly underestimate the true subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The qualification fails and \(F'(0)^*\partial g(F(0))\neq\partial(g\circ F)(0)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the set S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calculations are consistent, but the precise subdifferential chain-rule equality being shown to fail and its conventions require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Proximal Subgradient Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine subgradient model with quadratic proximal stabilization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex, choose \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(v\in\partial f(x)\), and \(\lambda>0\). The proximal subgradient model is
\[
M_{x,v,\lambda}(y)=f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2.
\]
Convexity gives \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\). The model is strongly convex and has the unique minimizer
\[
y^+=x-\lambda v.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, an affine subgradient minorant plus a proximal quadratic has the explicit unique minimizer x minus lambda times the subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine term globally minorizes \(f\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_y M_{x,v,\lambda}(y)=\{x-\lambda v\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Proximal Subgradient Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic subgradient lower model for weakly convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, and take \(v\in\partial f(x)\). Then
\[
f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\frac\rho2\|y-x\|^2.
\]
For \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), with the convention \(1/0=+\infty\), the stabilized model
\[
M_{x,v,\lambda}(y)=f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\frac12(\lambda^{-1}-\rho)\|y-x\|^2
\]
is strongly convex and has the unique minimizer \(y^+=x-\lambda v/(1-\lambda\rho)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convexity replaces the affine minorant by a downward quadratic model; sufficient proximal curvature restores strong convexity and yields an explicit minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed stabilized model is strongly convex with minimizer \(x-\lambda v/(1-\lambda\rho)\).

notation.meaning: Proximal parameter satisfying the curvature threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Proximal Subgradient Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic subgradient model supplied by prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), with local constants \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\geq0\). For admissible \((x,v)\) near \((\bar x,\bar v)\), define the local proximal subgradient model
\[
M_{x,v,\lambda}(y)=f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\frac12(\lambda^{-1}-r)\|y-x\|^2,
\]
where \(0<\lambda<1/r\), interpreting \(1/0=+\infty\). On the neighborhood where prox-regularity holds, its unregularized part underestimates \(f(y)\), while the displayed model is strongly convex and has unconstrained minimizer \(x-\lambda v/(1-\lambda r)\); validity requires this trial point to remain in that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity supplies a local downward-quadratic subgradient model; stronger proximal curvature gives an explicit trial point whose validity remains neighborhood-dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) with modulus \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local stabilized model has minimizer \(x-\lambda v/(1-\lambda r)\), provided the modeled point remains within the prox-regularity neighborhood.

notation.meaning: Locally valid stabilized proximal subgradient model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic model is plausible, but prox-regularity only supplies a locally quantified support inequality. A source is needed to validate the precise admissibility restrictions, locality claim, and named model.

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Linear Local Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-composite prox-linear model with optional convex regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=h(c(x))+r(x)\), where \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper closed convex, \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable, and \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper closed convex. At a point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), the prox-linear local model is \[m_x(y)=h\bigl(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(y-x)\bigr)+r(y).\] Given \(t>0\), a prox-linear trial point is any minimizer of \[m_x(y)+\frac{1}{2t}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.\] The model is exact at its center: \(m_x(x)=F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the smooth inner map, retain the convex outer and regularizer exactly, and optionally add a quadratic proximal term to select a trial point.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(r\) are proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_x(y)=h(c(x)+\nabla c(x)(y-x))+r(y)\) and \(m_x(x)=F(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The prox-linear representation is mathematically precise and fits the container, but no inspectable source or standard-field rationale is supplied.
