knowledge_statements.title: Convex Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity under partial minimization in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). If \(F\) is jointly convex, then \(v\) is convex in the extended-valued sense: for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[v(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\leq tv(x_1)+(1-t)v(x_2).\] Partial minimization does not by itself guarantee lower semicontinuity, attainment, or differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partially minimizing a jointly convex function preserves convexity, but the resulting marginal function need not be lower semicontinuous, attained, or differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The marginal function \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is convex, although it need not be differentiable or closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Lower-Solution Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete bilevel response ambiguity caused by two lower minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the lower problem \(\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}}(y^2-1)^2\), whose solution mapping is \(M(x)=\{-1,1\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). With \(H(x,y)=xy\), the responses \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) yield \(x\) and \(-x\), respectively, so lower optimality does not determine a single response value. Under the optimistic convention, \[\varphi(x)=\min_{y\in M(x)}xy=\min\{x,-x\}=-|x|,\] whereas the pessimistic value is \(|x|\). Both values are nondifferentiable at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally optimal lower responses produce different upper objectives; optimistic and pessimistic conventions yield minus absolute value and absolute value, both nonsmooth at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lower-solution nonuniqueness makes response substitution ambiguous and produces the optimistic value \(-|x|\), which is nondifferentiable at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Scenario Worst-Case Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite adversarial scenario maximum and simplex representation for real-valued scenario losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for every \(i\in I\). The finite-scenario worst-case objective is \[F(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x)=\max_{p\in\Delta_N}\sum_{i=1}^N p_i f_i(x),\qquad \Delta_N=\{p\in\mathbb{R}_+^N:\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}p=1\}.\] Its active scenario set is \(I(x)=\{i\in I:f_i(x)=F(x)\}\), which is nonempty. If all \(f_i\) are differentiable, ties between active scenarios with unequal gradients can make \(F\) nondifferentiable. If all \(f_i\) are convex, then \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-scenario worst-case model is the maximum of real-valued scenario losses, equivalently the maximum expected loss over the probability simplex; active-scenario ties can create nonsmoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(I=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) is a nonempty finite scenario set.
Each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a real-valued scenario loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case loss is \(F(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), equivalently the simplex maximum, and active scenarios attain this value.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic worst-case value induced by a prescribed uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(U\neq\varnothing\) be an uncertainty set, and let \(\ell:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a loss function. The uncertainty-set value model is
\[V(x):=\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u),\qquad x\in X.\]
Thus the robust optimization problem \(\inf_{x\in X}V(x)\) is equivalent to \(\inf\{t:(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R,\ \ell(x,u)\le t\ \text{for every }u\in U\}\). Even when every function \(\ell(\cdot,u)\) is smooth, the supremum can be nonsmooth where multiple uncertainty realizations attain the worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust value is the largest loss over the uncertainty set; minimizing it is equivalent to imposing one epigraph inequality for every uncertainty realization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u)\)

notation.meaning: loss at decision x and realization u

knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\) be a measurable space, let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty collection of probability measures on \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). For a measurable loss \(\ell:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) whose expectation is well defined for every \(P\in\mathcal P\), the distributionally robust value is
\[V(x):=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)].\]
The associated model minimizes \(V\) over \(X\). Nonsmoothness may arise when the maximizing distribution changes or several distributions attain the supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributionally robust model minimizes the largest expected loss among all probability laws in a prescribed ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and has a well-defined expectation for every \(x\in X\) and \(P\in\mathcal P\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic–Pessimistic Probability-Ambiguity Value Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample value model combining favorable and adverse probability reweightings of sample losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_s(x)=\varphi(m(x,\xi^s);z_s)\), let \(w_{\mathrm o},w_{\mathrm p}>0\), let \(\Delta_{\mathrm o},\Delta_{\mathrm p}\) be closed convex sets of discrete probability vectors, and let \(c_{\mathrm o},c_{\mathrm p}\) be nonnegative cost functions. Define
\[
v_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{pr}}(x)=w_{\mathrm o}\min_{p^{\mathrm o}\in\Delta_{\mathrm o}}\left\{(p^{\mathrm o})^Ty(x)+c_{\mathrm o}(p^{\mathrm o})\right\}+w_{\mathrm p}\max_{p^{\mathrm p}\in\Delta_{\mathrm p}}\left\{(p^{\mathrm p})^Ty(x)-c_{\mathrm p}(p^{\mathrm p})\right\}.
\]
The optimistic and pessimistic probability optimizations are separable. If both ambiguity sets are the singleton containing the uniform empirical probability vector and both costs vanish there, this value reduces to the empirical average loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value combines an optimistic minimum and a pessimistic maximum over probability reweightings of the sample losses. These two inner optimizations separate. Restricting both ambiguity sets to the uniform empirical distribution and using zero costs recovers empirical risk minimization.
assumptions_latex: \Delta_{\mathrm o},\Delta_{\mathrm p}\subseteq\{p\in\mathbb R_+^N:\mathbf 1^Tp=1\}\text{ are closed and convex}

knowledge_statements.title: Interdiction Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential attack followed by an optimizing defender response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be the feasible interdiction set and let \(Y(a)\neq\varnothing\) be the defender's feasible response set after attack \(a\in A\). Given an attacker payoff \(L(a,y)\), define the defender-response value
\[q(a):=\inf_{y\in Y(a)}L(a,y).\]
A max-min interdiction model is
\[\sup_{a\in A}q(a)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{y\in Y(a)}L(a,y).\]
The value function \(q\) may be nonsmooth when the optimal defender response changes, and it may be discontinuous when the response mapping \(Y\) lacks suitable stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attacker selects an interdiction action, after which the defender optimally responds; the attacker maximizes the resulting response value.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Response Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value model generated by an adversary's optimal response correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(U(x)\neq\varnothing\) be the adversary's feasible-response set, and let \(L:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be the modeled loss. The adversarial response correspondence and induced value function are
\[R(x):=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u\in U(x)}L(x,u),\qquad V(x):=\sup_{u\in U(x)}L(x,u).\]
Whenever the maximum is attained, every \(u\in R(x)\) satisfies \(V(x)=L(x,u)\). Changes in the active response set \(R(x)\) are a primary source of nonsmoothness of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adversary chooses a feasible response maximizing loss; the optimized response value can become nonsmooth when the active response changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: White-box targeted and untargeted attack formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained input-space loss maximization with known model parameters, including gradient-sign and projected-gradient attacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given known model parameters $\theta$ and a permitted set $\Delta(\mathbf x)$, choose $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{adv}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathbf x'\in\Delta(\mathbf x)}\mathcal L(\mathbf x',y;\theta)$. For an untargeted attack one may take $\mathcal L=-\log p(y\mid\mathbf x')$; for a targeted attack toward $y'\ne y$, one may take $\mathcal L=\log p(y'\mid\mathbf x')$. A common constraint is $\Delta(\mathbf x)=\{\mathbf x':\|\mathbf x'-\mathbf x\|_p<\epsilon\}$. A gradient-sign step for a targeted attack has the form $\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf x_t+\epsilon\,\operatorname{sign}(\nabla_{\mathbf x}\log p(y'\mid\mathbf x,\theta)|_{\mathbf x_t})$, with projected-gradient variants restoring feasibility after successive steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With full knowledge of the model, an attacker maximizes an input-space loss over a set of allowed perturbations. Untargeted attacks suppress the true label, targeted attacks promote a chosen wrong label, and gradient-sign or projected-gradient iterations approximately solve the constrained problem.
assumptions_latex: y'\ne y\text{ in the targeted case}
\Delta(\mathbf x)=\{\mathbf x':\|\mathbf x'-\mathbf x\|_p<\epsilon\}\text{ in the bounded-perturbation model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf x_{\mathrm{adv}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathbf x'\in\Delta(\mathbf x)}\mathcal L(\mathbf x',y;\theta).

knowledge_statements.title: Attacker-Defender Value Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stackelberg value with an attacker moving before a minimizing defender.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be the attack set, let \(D(a)\neq\varnothing\) be the defender's feasible set after \(a\in A\), and let \(L(a,d)\) denote the attacker's payoff. The defender value and attacker-defender value are
\[q(a):=\inf_{d\in D(a)}L(a,d),\qquad V:=\sup_{a\in A}q(a).\]
If both extrema are attained, a pair \((a^*,d^*)\) realizes this sequential value when \(d^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in D(a^*)}L(a^*,d)\) and \(a^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}q(a)\). This sequential value need not equal the reversed min-max value.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected integrand as a deterministic stochastic-programming objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(h:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be measurable in its second argument. At every \(x\in X\) for which the expectation is well defined, the expectation function is
\[F(x):=\mathbb E_P[h(x,\xi)]=\int_{\Xi}h(x,z)\,P(dz).\]
An expectation-function model minimizes \(F\) over \(X\), possibly with additional deterministic constraints. Nonsmoothness of \(F\) can be inherited from \(h(\cdot,z)\), even when integration averages over the random outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation-function model optimizes the probability-weighted average of a measurable random integrand over the decision set.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and its expectation is well defined on the stated domain

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Average Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample empirical approximation of an expectation-function objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) and an integrand \(h:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the sample-average approximation of \(F(x)=\mathbb E[h(x,\xi)]\) is
\[F_N(x):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}h(x,\xi^j),\qquad x\in X.\]
The sample-average model is \(\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)\), together with any sampled or deterministic constraints specified by the underlying stochastic program. For a fixed sample, \(F_N\) is a finite-sum nonsmooth objective whenever one or more sampled functions \(h(\cdot,\xi^j)\) are nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample-average model replaces an expectation by the arithmetic mean of losses evaluated at finitely many sampled outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x,\xi^j)\) is defined for every \(x\in X\) and \(j=1,\ldots,N\)

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Recourse Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected optimal second-stage value induced by a first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the first-stage feasible set. For outcome \(\xi\), let \(Y(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\) be the feasible recourse set and let \(q(x,y,\xi)\) be the second-stage cost. Define
\[Q(x,\xi):=\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(x,y,\xi),\qquad F(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)].\]
The two-stage recourse model is \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\), provided the expectation is well defined. The value \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) can be nonsmooth when the optimal recourse solution or active constraints change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-stage decision incurs immediate cost plus the expected optimal cost of adapting through a feasible second-stage response.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\) is measurable in \(\xi\) and has a well-defined expectation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=c(x)+\mathbb E[\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(x,y,\xi)]\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essentially Bounded Random Vector or Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general probability-theoretic definition, together with the stated moment consequence for random vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random vector or matrix \(\mathcal Z\) is essentially bounded if there exists \(B>0\) such that
\[\mathbb P\!\left(\|\mathcal Z\|\le B\right)=1.\]
For an essentially bounded \(\mathcal Z\), define
\[\|\mathcal Z\|_\infty:=\inf\left\{B>0:\mathbb P\!\left(\|\mathcal Z\|\le B\right)=1\right\}.\]
An essentially bounded random vector has finite mean and variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random vector or matrix is essentially bounded when its norm has a finite almost-sure bound. Its infinity norm is the infimum of such bounds. An essentially bounded random vector has finite mean and variance.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Z\text{ is a random vector or random matrix}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal Z\text{ essentially bounded}\implies \|\mathcal Z\|_\infty<\infty;\qquad \mathcal Z\text{ a random vector}\implies \mathbb E\|\mathcal Z\|<\infty\text{ and }\mathbb E\|\mathcal Z\|^2<\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Stage Stochastic Program with Quadratic Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a linearly biparameterized two-stage stochastic program with positive-semidefinite quadratic recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_1}\) be compact and convex and let \(\varphi\) be convex. The two-stage stochastic program is
\[\min_{x\in X}\ \zeta(x):=\varphi(x)+\mathbb E_{\widetilde\xi}[\psi(x,\widetilde\xi)],\]
where
\[\psi(x,\xi):=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^{n_2}}\left\{[f(\xi)+G(\xi)x]^\top y+\tfrac12y^\top Qy\;:\;A(\xi)x+Dy\ge b(\xi)\right\}.\]
The mappings \(f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{n_2}\), \(G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}\), \(A:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^{\ell\times n_1}\), and \(b:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^\ell\) are continuous; \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite; and \(D\in\mathbb R^{\ell\times n_2}\) is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-stage stochastic program with quadratic recourse minimizes a convex first-stage objective plus the expected value of a second-stage convex quadratic program. Its random linear and constraint data depend continuously on the random parameter, while the quadratic matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite and the recourse matrix D is deterministic.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_1}\text{ is compact and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\left\{\varphi(x)+\mathbb E_{\widetilde\xi}[\psi(x,\widetilde\xi)]\right\},\qquad \psi(x,\xi)=\min_y\left\{[f(\xi)+G(\xi)x]^\top y+\tfrac12y^\top Qy:A(\xi)x+Dy\ge b(\xi)\right\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Chance-Constraint Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability threshold imposed on simultaneous satisfaction of random inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(\xi\) be a random element with law \(P\), let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^m\) be measurable in \(\xi\), and choose \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). A decision \(x\in X\) satisfies the joint chance constraint exactly when
\[P\!\left(g_i(x,\xi)\le 0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m\right)\ge 1-\alpha.\]
Equivalently, its violation probability obeys \(P(\max_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x,\xi)>0)\le\alpha\). The resulting feasible set may be nonconvex or nonsmooth because probabilities of threshold events change across their boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chance constraint permits random inequality violations only with probability at most the prescribed risk tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\ \forall i)\ge1-\alpha\)

knowledge_statements.title: Bilevel Value-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimistic bilevel problem expressed through the lower-level optimal-value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the upper-level set, let \(Y(x)\neq\varnothing\) be the lower-level feasible set, and let \(f\) and \(F\) be the lower- and upper-level objectives. Define the lower value and solution mapping by
\[\varphi(x):=\inf_{z\in Y(x)}f(x,z),\qquad S(x):=\{y\in Y(x):f(x,y)=\varphi(x)\}.\]
The optimistic bilevel model is equivalently
\[\inf\{F(x,y):x\in X,\ y\in Y(x),\ f(x,y)-\varphi(x)\le0\}.\]
Because feasibility already gives \(f(x,y)\ge\varphi(x)\), the final inequality enforces lower-level optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilevel model replaces the follower's optimal-response requirement by equality between its objective and the lower-level value function.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi(x)\) is finite wherever the value-function constraint is imposed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in S(x)\iff y\in Y(x)\ \text{and}\ f(x,y)-\varphi(x)\le0\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary condition for the local minimizer of the specified linear bilevel problem; the multiplier system permits an abnormal objective multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $(x^0,y^0)$ is a local minimizer of problem (3.7), then there exist $\lambda^0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a nonzero vector $(\kappa_0,\kappa,\eta^1,\eta^2,\gamma^1,\gamma^2,\xi)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^l\times\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m$ such that
\[
\kappa_0d^1-A^{1\top}\eta^1+\gamma^2=0,
\quad
\kappa_0d^2+A^{3\top}\kappa-\xi-\binom{-A^{2\top}\eta^1}{\eta^2}=0,
\quad
A^1\eta^2+\gamma^1=0,
\]
\[
(a-A^1x^0-A^2y^{20})_i\eta_i^1=0,
\quad \lambda_i^0\gamma_i^1=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,p),
\]
\[
(A^{1\top}\lambda^0+y^{10})_i\eta_i^2=0,
\quad x_i^0\gamma_i^2=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),
\]
\[
\eta_i^1\gamma_i^1\ge0\quad\text{whenever }(a-A^1x^0-A^2y^{20})_i=\lambda_i^0=0,
\]
\[
\eta_i^2\gamma_i^2\ge0\quad\text{whenever }(A^{1\top}\lambda^0+y^{10})_i=x_i^0=0,
\]
and $\xi\ge0$, $y_i^0\xi_i=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$, $\lambda^0\ge0$, and $\kappa_0\ge0$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic and Pessimistic Bilevel Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Favorable and adverse selection among lower-level optimal responses, including the possible nonexistence of pessimistic optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Psi(x)\) be the lower-level solution mapping. A pessimistic optimal solution need not exist in general.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantee conditional on the vertex-enrichment algorithm generating an infinite sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the algorithm generates an infinite sequence \(\{(x^t,y^t)\}_{t=1}^{\infty}\), the set \(\{(x,y):G(x)\leq0,\ g(x,y)\leq0,\ x\in X\}\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\forall\widetilde x\in X\;\exists\widetilde y\) such that \(g(\widetilde x,\widetilde y)<0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph representation of a smooth primal-stationarity constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent inverse-image formulation of the stationarity-constrained single-level problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume f and every g_i are continuously differentiable, define Q(x,y):=N_{Y(x)}(y), \[\xi(x,y):=(G(x),x,y,-\nabla_y f(x,y)),\qquad \Omega:=\mathbb{R}_{-}^{q}\times\operatorname{gph}Q.\] Then \[\min_{x,y}\{F(x,y):G(x)\le0,\;-\nabla_y f(x,y)\in Q(x,y)\}=\min_{x,y}\{F(x,y):\xi(x,y)\in\Omega\}=\min_{x,y}\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in\xi^{-1}(\Omega)\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier necessary conditions for a Lipschitzian optimistic bilevel program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary conditions under partial calmness, inner semicontinuity, and separate lower- and upper-level regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\bar x,\bar y)$ be a local solution of the optimistic bilevel program in value-function form (7.8.2). Assume that $\varphi,\psi,f_i$ are locally Lipschitz around $(\bar x,\bar y)$, each $g_j$ is locally Lipschitz around $\bar x$, the lower-level solution map $S$ is inner semicontinuous at $(\bar x,\bar y)$, the lower- and upper-level regularity conditions hold, and problem (7.8.2) is partially calm there with constant $\kappa>0$. Then there exist multipliers $\lambda_i,\mu_j,v_i\geq0$ and $u\in\operatorname{co}\partial\vartheta(\bar x)$ such that $$\lambda_i f_i(\bar x,\bar y)=0,\qquad v_i f_i(\bar x,\bar y)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,r),$$ $$\mu_jg_j(\bar x)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,s),$$ $$ (u,0)\in\operatorname{co}\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r v_i\operatorname{co}\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y),$$ and $$ (u,0)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\kappa^{-1}\partial\psi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j\bigl(\partial g_j(\bar x),0\bigr).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local Lipschitz continuity, inner semicontinuity of the lower-level solution map, level-specific regularity, and partial calmness, a local optimistic bilevel solution admits nonnegative complementary multipliers and a convexified lower-value-function subgradient satisfying two coupled nonsmooth stationarity inclusions.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a local solution of the optimistic bilevel program in form (7.8.2)}
\varphi,\psi,f_i\text{ are locally Lipschitz around }(\bar x,\bar y)
g_j\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x
S\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y)
\text{problem (7.8.2) is partially calm at }(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ with }\kappa>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda_i,\mu_j,v_i\geq0,\ \exists u\in\operatorname{co}\partial\vartheta(\bar x)\text{ satisfying the stated complementarity conditions and both stationarity inclusions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex lower-level stationarity reformulation and feasible-set closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal stationarity representation of an optimistic bilevel problem and a sufficient closedness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let T=\mathbb{R}^m, X=\mathbb{R}^n, let y\mapsto f(x,y) be convex, and let Y be convex-valued. The bilevel problem is represented by \[\min\{F(x,y):G(x)\le 0,\;0\in\partial_y f(x,y)+N_{Y(x)}(y)\}.\] If (x,y)\mapsto\partial_y f(x,y) is upper semicontinuous, every G_i is continuous, X is closed, and Q(x,y):=N_{Y(x)}(y) is closed, then the feasible set of this reformulation is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With Euclidean upper- and lower-level spaces, convex lower-level objective in y, and convex-valued lower feasible-set mapping, lower-level optimality is represented by a subdifferential-plus-normal-cone inclusion. If the subdifferential mapping is upper semicontinuous, the upper constraints are continuous, X is closed, and the parametric normal-cone mapping is closed, then the reformulated feasible set is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{feas}\!\left\{(x,y):G(x)\le0,\;0\in\partial_y f(x,y)+N_{Y(x)}(y)\right\}\text{ is closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Optimal Solutions and the Lower Envelope of the Pessimistic Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's bilevel notation: response map \(\Psi\), upper objective \(F\), feasible upper-level set \(Y\), and pessimistic value function \(\varphi_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\mathcal S:=\left\{(x,y):y\in Y,\ x\in\Psi(y),\ F(x,y)\leq\inf_z\varphi_p(z)\right\}.
\]
The elements of \(\mathcal S\) are called lower optimal solutions. The defining upper bound need not be attained when \(\varphi_p\) fails to be lower semicontinuous. Its lower envelope is
\[
\varphi_p^0(y):=\liminf_{z\to y}\varphi_p(z).
\]
The function \(\varphi_p^0\) is lower semicontinuous on its domain and satisfies \(\varphi_p^0(y)=\varphi_p(y)\) at every point where \(\varphi_p\) is lower semicontinuous. If an optimistic solution exists, then \(\mathcal S\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower optimal solutions are bilevel-feasible response pairs whose upper objective is no greater than the infimum of the pessimistic value function. This bound may fail to be attained if that value function is not lower semicontinuous. Its liminf envelope is lower semicontinuous and agrees with the original function at its lower-semicontinuity points. Existence of an optimistic solution implies that the lower-optimal solution set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(y\in Y\) and \(x\in\Psi(y)\) describe bilevel-feasible response pairs.
\(F\) and \(\varphi_p\) denote the upper objective and pessimistic value function of the referenced bilevel formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi_p^0\text{ is lower semicontinuous on its domain},\quad \varphi_p^0(y)=\varphi_p(y)\text{ wherever }\varphi_p\text{ is lower semicontinuous},\quad \text{and optimistic solvability implies }\mathcal S\neq\varnothing.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique continuous regularized follower response and minimum-norm limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise selection and parameter continuity of convex Tikhonov-regularized follower solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Y is compact and convex, F is continuous on X\times Y, \lambda_n\to+\infty, and F(x,\cdot) is convex on Y for every x\in X. Then, for every x\in X and n\in\mathbb N, \[\{\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x)\}=\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}\left(F(x,y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda_n}\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}\right).\] Moreover, \bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x)\to\widehat\varphi(x), where \[\{\widehat\varphi(x)\}=\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in M(x)}\|y\|_Y.\] For each fixed n and every x_k\to x, \[\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x_k)\to\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x),\qquad F(x_k,\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x_k))\to F(x,\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each convex regularized follower problem has a unique response. As regularization vanishes, that response converges to the minimum-norm unregularized follower solution; for each fixed regularization level, both the response and its objective value vary continuously with the leader parameter.
assumptions_latex: F(x,\cdot)\text{ is convex on }Y\ \forall x\in X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}\left(F(x,y)+\frac{\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}}{2\lambda_n}\right)=\{\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x)\},\quad \bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x)\to\widehat\varphi(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in M(x)}\|y\|_Y,\quad x_k\to x\Rightarrow \bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x_k)\to\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pessimistic Linear Bilevel Programming Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the linear pessimistic model and its independent special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and define \(\Psi(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\ge0}\{w^\top y:By\le b-Ax\}\). A pessimistic linear bilevel programming problem has the form
\[
\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in\Psi(x)} c^\top x+d^\top y,
\]
where \(c,x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(d,w,y\in\mathbb R^m\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). If \(A=0\), the follower feasible region is independent of \(x\), and the model is an independent pessimistic linear bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pessimistic linear bilevel problem minimizes the leader's linear objective under the worst follower-optimal response of a parameterized linear lower-level problem. If A is zero, the follower feasible region is independent of the leader variable.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n},\quad B\in\mathbb R^{p\times m},\quad b\in\mathbb R^p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in\Psi(x)}(c^\top x+d^\top y),\qquad A=0\Rightarrow\text{independent follower feasible region}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary Multiplier Conditions for the Value-Function Program $(VP)_1$
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessary conditions at a local solution of the formulation denoted $(VP)_1$ in the extraction context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $(\bar x,\bar y)$ is a local optimal solution of $(VP)_1$, then there exist $\delta\geq0$ and $\bar v,\alpha\in\mathbb R^r$ such that
\[
0=\nabla_xF(\bar x,\bar y)+C^T(\alpha-\delta\bar v),
\]
\[
0=\nabla_yF(\bar x,\bar y)+D^T(\alpha-\delta\bar v),
\]
and
\[
0\leq\alpha\perp-\bigl(C\bar x+D\bar y-q\bigr)\geq0,
\qquad
0\leq\bar v\perp-\bigl(C\bar x+D\bar y-q\bigr)\geq0.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Procedure for Computing a Weak Optimistic Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative procedure based on optimistic response sets, induced upper-level minimizers, and the sets L_o(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x^0\in X$, set $k:=0$. At iteration $k$, compute $\widehat\Psi_o(x^k)$ and $\bar\varphi_o(x^k)$, and set $M(x^k):=\{y\in\widehat\Psi_o(x^k):F(x^k,y)=\bar\varphi_o(x^k)\}$. If there exists $y^k\in M(x^k)$ such that $x^k\notin L_o(y^k)$, choose $x^{k+1}\in L_o(y^k)$ and repeat; otherwise stop and return $x^k\in\operatorname{locmin}\{\bar\varphi_o(x):x\in X\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a feasible upper-level point. At each iteration, form the optimistic response points attaining the induced upper-level value. If one of them yields a set L_o containing an improving replacement for the current point, move to any such replacement; otherwise stop. The returned point is a local minimizer of the optimistic value function over X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^k\in\operatorname{locmin}\{\bar\varphi_o(x):x\in X\}\quad\text{upon termination}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity of a Bilevel Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local transfer of upper semicontinuity from the lower objective and feasible mapping to the lower-level value function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Stability Under Local Uniform Moment Integrability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity and persistence results for risk, value, and complete local minimizing-set mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), \(P=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^s\), and that \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal M_s^p\) is locally uniformly \(\|\cdot\|^p\)-integrating. Then \(\mathcal Q_{\mathcal R}|_{\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal M}\) is real-valued and weakly continuous, and \(\varphi_{\mathbb R^n}|_{\mathcal M}\) is weakly upper semicontinuous. If additionally \(\mu_0\in\mathcal M\) and \(\phi_V(\mu_0)\) is a CLM set of \(P_{\mu_0}\) with respect to an open bounded proper subset \(V\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\), then \(\varphi_V|_{\mathcal M}\) is weakly continuous at \(\mu_0\); \(\phi_V|_{\mathcal M}\) is weakly upper semicontinuous at \(\mu_0\) in Berge's sense; and there is a weakly open neighborhood \(\mathcal U\) of \(\mu_0\) such that \(\phi_V(\mu)\) is a CLM set of \(P_\mu\) with respect to \(V\) for every \(\mu\in\mathcal U\cap\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform p-moment integrability makes the risk functional weakly continuous and the global value function weakly upper semicontinuous. Around a parameter possessing a complete local minimizing set in an open bounded proper localization set, the localized value is continuous, the localized solution mapping is upper semicontinuous, and the complete-local-minimizer property persists under nearby weak perturbations.
assumptions_latex: V\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\text{ is open and bounded}
\phi_V(\mu_0)\text{ is a CLM set of }P_{\mu_0}\text{ with respect to }V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncooperative Pessimistic Linear Bilevel Multi-Follower Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The followers share no decision variables, objective functions, or constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,M\), define
\[
\Psi_i(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y_i\ge0}\{w_i^\top y_i:A_ix+B_iy_i\le b_i\}.
\]
An uncooperative pessimistic linear bilevel multi-follower problem, with no variables, objectives, or constraints shared among followers, is
\[
\min_{x\in X}\left[c^\top x+\sum_{i=1}^M\max_{y_i\in\Psi_i(x)}d_i^\top y_i\right].
\]
Here \(x,c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(y_i,d_i,w_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\), \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times n}\), \(B_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times m_i}\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each follower independently solves its own parameterized linear problem, with no shared follower variables, objectives, or constraints; the leader minimizes its objective plus the sum of worst follower-optimal contributions.
assumptions_latex: A_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times n},\quad B_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times m_i},\quad b_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i}
\text{Followers share no decision variables, objective functions, or constraint functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\left[c^\top x+\sum_{i=1}^M\max_{y_i\in\Psi_i(x)}d_i^\top y_i\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized multiplier necessary condition under generalized Slater
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-qualified necessary condition for a local minimizer of the specified linear bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $(x^0,y^0)$ is a local minimizer of problem (3.7) and the generalized Slater condition holds for problem (3.17), then there exist $\lambda^0\in\mathbb R^p$, $\kappa\in\mathbb R^l$, $\eta^1,\gamma^1\in\mathbb R^p$, $\eta^2,\gamma^2\in\mathbb R^n$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^m$ such that
\[
d^1-A^{1\top}\eta^1+\gamma^2=0,
\quad
d^2+A^{3\top}\kappa-\xi-\binom{-A^{2\top}\eta^1}{\eta^2}=0,
\quad
A^1\eta^2+\gamma^1=0,
\]
\[
(a-A^1x^0-A^2y^{20})_i\eta_i^1=0,
\quad \lambda_i^0\gamma_i^1=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,p),
\]
\[
(A^{1\top}\lambda^0+y^{10})_i\eta_i^2=0,
\quad x_i^0\gamma_i^2=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),
\]
\[
\eta_i^1\gamma_i^1\ge0\quad\text{whenever }(a-A^1x^0-A^2y^{20})_i=\lambda_i^0=0,
\]
\[
\eta_i^2\gamma_i^2\ge0\quad\text{whenever }(A^{1\top}\lambda^0+y^{10})_i=x_i^0=0,
\]
and $\xi\ge0$, $y_i^0\xi_i=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$, and $\lambda^0\ge0$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Growth Sufficient Condition for Strict Bilevel Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strong first-order growth condition for a bilevel problem with a strongly stable convex lower-level response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(x^0,y^0)$ be feasible for the bilevel problem with a convex lower-level problem satisfying MFCQ, SSOC, and CRCQ at $(x^0,y^0)$. Define
\[
v_1:=\min_{r}\ \nabla_xF(x^0,y^0)^\top x'(y^0;r)+\nabla_yF(x^0,y^0)^\top r
\]
subject to
\[
\nabla G_i(y^0)^\top r\leq0\quad\forall i\text{ with }G_i(y^0)=0,
\qquad \|r\|=1.
\]
If $v_1>0$, then $(x^0,y^0)$ is a strict local solution. More precisely, for every $c\in(0,v_1)$ there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
F(x(y),y)\geq F(x^0,y^0)+c\|y-y^0\|
\]
whenever $\|y-y^0\|\leq\varepsilon$ and $G(y)\leq0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the reduced upper-level objective has a uniformly positive directional derivative over every unit upper-level linearized feasible direction, then the feasible bilevel point is a strict local solution with local linear growth of any rate below the directional minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall c\in(0,v_1)\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall y:\ [\|y-y^0\|\leq\varepsilon\land G(y)\leq0]\Rightarrow F(x(y),y)\geq F(x^0,y^0)+c\|y-y^0\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Monotonicity-Based Upper-Approximation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The procedure uses the componentwise order. Its upper-bound interpretation requires componentwise nondecreasing behavior of the value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\varphi\) is nondecreasing with respect to the componentwise order on \([d_l,d_u]\). Choose \(r\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\varphi(x)\le r\) for every \(x\in[d_l,d_u]\), and initialize \(\xi(x):=r\) on that domain. Select points \(d^1,\ldots,d^p\) at which \(\varphi\) is defined, evaluate \(\varphi(d^i)\), and set \(\xi_i(x):=\varphi(d^i)\) whenever \(x\leqq d^i\). For \(i=1,\ldots,p\), update \(\xi(x):=\min\{\xi_i(x),\xi(x)\}\) when \(x\leqq d^i\), leaving \(\xi(x)\) unchanged otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a constant upper bound. For every sampled parameter vector, use its value as an upper bound for componentwise smaller vectors and tighten the approximation by taking the minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\text{ is nondecreasing with respect to the componentwise order.}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi(x)\leftarrow\begin{cases}\min\{\varphi(d^i),\xi(x)\},&x\leqq d^i,\\\xi(x),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad i=1,\ldots,p.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-Value Reformulation of a Bilevel Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-level value-function reformulation and its nonsmooth constraint-qualification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi(x)=\min\{f(x,z):g(x,z)\le0\}\) be the lower-level optimal value. The optimistic bilevel graph problem is equivalently represented by \(\min\{F(x,y):G(x)\le0,\ x\in X,\ g(x,y)\le0,\ f(x,y)\le\varphi(x)\}\). The resulting problem is generally nonsmooth because \(\varphi\) need not be differentiable even under restrictive assumptions, and the nonsmooth Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification fails at every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-level optimal response can be imposed by lower feasibility together with an objective value no larger than the lower optimal-value function. This formulation is equivalent, but it is generally nonsmooth and violates nonsmooth MFCQ at every feasible point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz regularity and subdifferential estimate under quasi-normality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the value function of a nonconvex lower-level program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume restricted inf-compactness holds around \( ar x\) and \(( ar x, ar y)\) is quasi-normal for every \( ar y\in S( ar x)\). Then \(V\) is Lipschitz continuous around \( ar x\) and \(\partial V( ar x)\subseteq\widetilde W( ar x)\), where \(\widetilde W( ar x)= igcup_{ ar y\in S( ar x)}\{
abla_x f( ar x, ar y)+
abla_x g( ar x, ar y)^T\lambda^g+
abla_x h( ar x, ar y)^T\lambda^h:(\lambda^g,\lambda^h)\in\mathcal M( ar x, ar y)\}\), and \(\mathcal M( ar x, ar y)\) is the set of multipliers satisfying lower-level stationarity, \(\lambda^g\ge0\), and the stated quasi-normal sequence conditions. If additionally \(\widetilde W( ar x)=\{\zeta\}\), then \(V\) is strictly differentiable at \( ar x\) and \(
abla V( ar x)=\zeta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted inf-compactness and quasi-normality at every lower-level solution imply local Lipschitz continuity and a quasi-normal-multiplier upper estimate for the value-function subdifferential. A singleton estimate implies strict differentiability with that vector as gradient.
assumptions_latex: \forall\bar y\in S(\bar x),\ (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is quasi-normal}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x,\quad\partial V(\bar x)\subseteq\widetilde W(\bar x);\quad\widetilde W(\bar x)=\{\zeta\}\Rightarrow V\text{ is strictly differentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }\nabla V(\bar x)=\zeta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-level and upper-level regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized MFCQ-type regularity definitions for active lower- and upper-level constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $$I(\bar x,\bar y):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}:f_i(\bar x,\bar y)=0\}.$$ A point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ is lower-level regular if, whenever active-constraint subgradients $(u_i,v_i)\in\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y)$ and coefficients $\lambda_i\geq0$ satisfy $$\sum_{i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)}\lambda_i v_i=0,$$ one has $\lambda_i=0$ for every $i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)$. For an upper-level feasible point $\bar x$, let $$J(\bar x):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,s\}:g_j(\bar x)=0\}.$$ The point is upper-level regular if $$0\in\sum_{j\in J(\bar x)}\mu_j\partial g_j(\bar x),\quad \mu_j\geq0,$$ implies $\mu_j=0$ for every $j\in J(\bar x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-level regularity excludes nonzero nonnegative dependence among the lower-variable components of selected active lower-level subgradients. Upper-level regularity excludes nonzero nonnegative active multipliers whose weighted upper-level subdifferentials contain zero.
assumptions_latex: (u_i,v_i)\in\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ for }i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)}\lambda_i v_i=0\Rightarrow\lambda_i=0\ \forall i\in I(\bar x,\bar y),\qquad 0\in\sum_{j\in J(\bar x)}\mu_j\partial g_j(\bar x)\Rightarrow\mu_j=0\ \forall j\in J(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and lower-boundedness assumptions for a quadratic bilevel program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The compactness condition is stated pointwise for a fixed projected upper-level point, while the lower-level objective bound is uniform over all projected points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed $x\in\Pr(Z):=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:\exists y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Z\}$, assume that $Y_*(x)$ is nonempty and compact. Assume that $U:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n:Ax+By\le b,\ A_1x+B_1y\le b_1\}$ is nonempty and that $\exists F_->-\infty$ such that $F(x,y)\ge F_-$ for every $(x,y)\in U$. Also assume $\inf_{x\in\Pr(Z)}\inf_{y\in Y(x)}\left\{\tfrac12\langle y,D_1y\rangle+\langle d_1,y\rangle+\langle x,Qy\rangle\right\}>-\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the fixed projected upper-level point under consideration, the lower-level solution set is nonempty and compact. The joint constraint set is nonempty, the upper-level objective is bounded below on it, and the lower-level quadratic objective is uniformly bounded below over all projected upper-level points and their feasible lower-level sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y_*(x)\ne\varnothing\text{ and is compact},\quad \exists F_->-\infty\ \forall(x,y)\in U:\ F(x,y)\ge F_-,\quad \inf_{x\in\Pr(Z)}\inf_{y\in Y(x)}\left(\tfrac12\langle y,D_1y\rangle+\langle d_1,y\rangle+\langle x,Qy\rangle\right)>-\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lp regularity of the stochastic bilevel value mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrability and Lipschitz regularity of the random value mapping induced by the uncertainty vector Z.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\) and \(\mu_Z\in\mathcal M_s^p\) for some \(p\in[1,\infty)\). Then the mapping \(F:P_Z\to L^0(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), defined by \(F(x):=f(x,Z(\cdot))\), takes values in \(L^p(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) and is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the \(L^p\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the deterministic value function has nonempty domain and the distribution of Z has a finite p-th moment, then each random value F(x) lies in Lp and the mapping F is Lipschitz in the Lp norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(P_Z)\subseteq L^p(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\quad\text{and}\quad F\text{ is Lipschitz continuous with respect to }\|\cdot\|_{L^p}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonempty domain and attainment for a bilevel linear value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of nonempty domain and global lower-level attainment over the feasible parameter polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Regularization by Constraint Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner-regularization guarantees for two constraint-relaxed reaction-map families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(Y\) is convex and compact and \(F\) is continuous on \(X\times Y\). Define \((C_5)\) by \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall x\in X\ \exists y\in Y:\quad \max_{1\le i\le k}g_i(x,y)<\varepsilon.\] If \((C_1)-(C_3)\) and \((C_5)\) hold, then \(\widetilde{\mathfrak G}=\{\widetilde G^\varepsilon:\varepsilon>0\}\) is an inner regularization. If, in addition, \((H_1)\) holds, then \(\mathfrak G=\{G^\varepsilon:\varepsilon>0\}\) is an inner regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When Y is convex and compact, F is continuous, conditions C1–C3 hold, and every positive constraint tolerance admits a point satisfying all constraints below that tolerance, the family tilde-G is an inner regularization. With the additional assumption H1, G is also an inner regularization.
assumptions_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0,\ \forall x\in X,\ \exists y\in Y:\ \max_{1\le i\le k}g_i(x,y)<\varepsilon.
\text{For the conclusion concerning }\mathfrak G,\ (H_1)\text{ also holds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[(C_1)-(C_3),(C_5)\Rightarrow\widetilde{\mathfrak G}\text{ is an inner regularization}\bigr]\ \land\ \bigl[(C_1)-(C_3),(C_5),(H_1)\Rightarrow\mathfrak G\text{ is an inner regularization}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Linearized-Value Procedure for an Optimistic Bilevel Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration for the referenced standard optimistic bilevel problem using a proximal subproblem and a refreshed lower-level solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \((x^0,y^0,v^0)\in X\times Y\times Y\) with \(y^0=v^0\in S(x^0)\), and let \(\tau>0\). For \(k\ge 0\), compute
\[
(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\left\{F(x,y)+\frac{\tau}{2}\|(x,y)-(x^k,y^k)\|^2:\ f(x,y)\le f(x^k,v^k)+\nabla_1 f(x^k,v^k)^T(x-x^k)+\varepsilon\right\},
\]
and then choose \(v^{k+1}\in S(x^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from x0, y0, and v0 with y0=v0 a lower-level solution at x0, and choose a positive proximal parameter. At each iteration, minimize the upper-level objective plus a quadratic proximal term over X×Y subject to the stated epsilon-relaxed first-variable linearization of the lower-level value condition. Then select a new lower-level solution at the updated x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k\ge 0,\ (x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\left\{F(x,y)+\frac{\tau}{2}\|(x,y)-(x^k,y^k)\|^2:\ f(x,y)\le f(x^k,v^k)+\nabla_1f(x^k,v^k)^T(x-x^k)+\varepsilon\right\},\quad v^{k+1}\in S(x^{k+1}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand stationarity at accumulation points of modified descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit-point guarantee for the referenced modified descent algorithm with a fixed sufficiently small approximate-active-set parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the referenced bilevel programming problem whose lower-level problem is a convex parametric optimization problem. Suppose assumptions \((C)\), \((ULR)\), \((FRR)\), \((MFCQ)\), \((CRCQ)\), and \((SSOC)\) hold for every \((x,y)\) such that \(x\in\Psi(y)\) and \(G(y)\le 0\). Fix a sufficiently small \(\kappa>0\), and let \(\{(y^k,\lambda^k,\mu^k,d^k,r^k,s^k,t^k,\gamma^k,\eta^k,K^k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\) be computed by the modified descent algorithm. If \(y^0\) is an accumulation point of \(\{y^k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\), then \((x(y^0),y^0)\) is a Bouligand-stationary point of the bilevel programming problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity of the parametric lower level, the six stated assumptions, and a fixed sufficiently small active-set parameter, any accumulation point of the upper-level iterates generated by the modified descent algorithm induces a Bouligand-stationary bilevel point.
assumptions_latex: \text{The lower-level problem is a convex parametric optimization problem.}
\{(y^k,\lambda^k,\mu^k,d^k,r^k,s^k,t^k,\gamma^k,\eta^k,K^k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\text{ is computed by the modified descent algorithm.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Preservation of Lower-Level Constraint-Gradient Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stability assumption preserving linear independence of selected active inequality gradients and all equality gradients at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every sequence $y^k\to y^0$ and every fixed index set $K$ satisfying
\[
K\subseteq I(x(y^k),y^k)\quad\text{for all }k,
\]
if, for every $k$, the family
\[
\{\nabla_x g_i(x(y^k),y^k):i\in K\}\cup
\{\nabla_x h_j(x(y^k),y^k):\text{all }j\}
\]
is linearly independent, then
\[
\{\nabla_x g_i(x(y^0),y^0):i\in K\}\cup
\{\nabla_x h_j(x(y^0),y^0):\text{all }j\}
\]
is linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along every parameter sequence approaching the reference parameter, any fixed selection of active lower-level inequality gradients that remains linearly independent together with all equality gradients must remain linearly independent at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional-convexificator necessary condition for an optimistic bilevel local solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized stationarity and support contact under the seven stated regularity, continuity, convexity, and boundedness hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) be a local solution of the bilevel problem. Assume: (1) \(F\) has a bounded convexificator at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), upper semicontinuous there, and \(0\notin\operatorname{conv}\partial^*F(\bar x,\cdot)(\bar y)\); (2) for every \(z^*\in Z^*_{\Psi(\bar x)}:=\{z^*:\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\bar x)>-\infty\}\) with \(\|z^*\|\le1\), the scalarization \(\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,x):=\min_{z\in\Psi(x)}z^\top z^*\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), continuous at \(\bar x\) in the directions of a common nonzero set \(\bar D_x\), and satisfies \((A_0)\); (3) these scalarizations admit bounded directional convexificators on \(U(\bar x)\cap(\{\bar x\}+\bar D_x)\), where \(\bar D_x=\bigcap_{z^*\in Z^*_{\Psi(\bar x)}}D_{\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\cdot)}(\bar x)\ne\{0\}\); (4) every nearby \(\Psi(x)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(\Psi\) has the cl-property for the convexificator and directional convexificator; (5) \(G\equiv0\), \(T=\mathbb R^m\), \(X=\mathbb R^n\), and \(\{(x,y):y\in\Psi(x),F(x,y)\le c\}\) is nonempty and bounded for some finite \(c\); (6) \(\rho(y,\Psi(x))\) is locally convex in \(x\) along all its continuity directions at \(\bar x\); and (7) \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(\rho(y_k,\Psi(x_k))\to0\), and \(z_k^*\to z^*\) imply \(\mathcal C_\Psi(z_k^*,x_k)\to\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\bar x)\). Then there exist \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) and \(z^*\in Z^*_{\Psi(\bar x)}\), \(\|z^*\|=1\), such that \[0\in\operatorname{conv}\partial^*F(\bar x,\bar y)+\alpha\operatorname{conv}\left\{\big(\partial^*_{\bar D_x}\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\cdot)(\bar x)+N_{\bar D_x}(0)\big)\times\{-z^*\}\right\},\qquad \mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\bar x)=\langle z^*,\bar y\rangle,\] with \(\bar D_x\) convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the seven stated hypotheses, every local optimistic bilevel solution admits a unit scalarization direction and a scalar multiplier satisfying a directional-convexificator stationarity inclusion and a support-contact equality; the common continuity-direction set is convex and closed.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a local bilevel solution}
\partial^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is bounded and upper semicontinuous, and }0\notin\operatorname{conv}\partial^*F(\bar x,\cdot)(\bar y)
\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\cdot)\text{ satisfies the stated lower-semicontinuity, directional-continuity, }(A_0)\text{, and bounded directional-convexificator hypotheses}
\Psi(x)\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex nearby and has the cl-property}
G\equiv0,\ T=\mathbb R^m,\ X=\mathbb R^n,\text{ and the stated nonempty bounded level set exists}
\rho(y,\Psi(x))\text{ is locally convex in }x\text{ along all continuity directions at }\bar x
(x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y),\ \rho(y_k,\Psi(x_k))\to0,\ z_k^*\to z^*\Longrightarrow\mathcal C_\Psi(z_k^*,x_k)\to\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\bar x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\alpha\in\mathbb R\ \exists z^*\in Z^*_{\Psi(\bar x)},\ \|z^*\|=1:\ 0\in\operatorname{conv}\partial^*F(\bar x,\bar y)+\alpha\operatorname{conv}\{(\partial^*_{\bar D_x}\mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\cdot)(\bar x)+N_{\bar D_x}(0))\times\{-z^*\}\},\ \mathcal C_\Psi(z^*,\bar x)=\langle z^*,\bar y\rangle,\ \bar D_x\text{ is convex and closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible descent algorithm for Clarke-stationary bilevel solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for the referenced bilevel problem using feasible directions and an Armijo-type decrease test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(y^0\) with \(G(y^0)\le 0\), choose \(\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\), and set \(k=0\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(r^k,s^k\) such that \(\mathcal F'(y^k;r^k)\le s^k\), \(\nabla_yG_i(y^k)r^k\le-\overline G_i(y^k)+s^k\) for \(i=1,\ldots,l\), and \(s^k<0\). Choose \(t^k\) satisfying \(\mathcal F(y^k+t^kr^k)\le\mathcal F(y^k)+\varepsilon t^ks^k\) and \(G(y^k+t^kr^k)\le0\); set \(y^{k+1}=y^k+t^kr^k\), compute \(x^k\in\Psi(y^k)\), and repeat until the stopping criterion holds. The stated output is a Clarke-stationary solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an upper-level feasible point, repeatedly compute a strict descent direction satisfying the linearized constraint inequalities, select a feasible Armijo step, update the upper variable, and evaluate a lower-level solution. The stated output is a Clarke-stationary bilevel solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns a Clarke-stationary solution of the bilevel problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard Bilevel Reformulation for Common Risk Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-scenario reformulation using risk-specific auxiliary variables and, for probability or quantile risks, a sufficiently large big-M constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), \(\mathcal R\in\{\mathbb E,\mathrm{EE}_\eta^1,\mathrm{SD}_\rho^1,\mathrm{EP}_\eta,\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha,\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha,\mathcal R_{\max}\}\), and that the polyhedron \(X\subseteq P_Z\); if \(\mathcal R\in\{\mathrm{EP}_\eta,\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha\}\), also assume that \(X\) is bounded. For every admissible risk parameter \(\beta\), there exists \(M>0\) such that \[\min_{x\in X}\mathcal R[F(x)]\] is equivalent to a standard bilevel program whose lower-level solution mapping is \[\Psi_{\mathcal R}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_w\left\{\sum_{k\in I}d^\top y_k\ \middle|\ Ay_k\le Tx+Z_k,\ b_k(x,w)\ge0\ \forall k\in I\right\}.\] For \(\mathcal R\ne\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha\), the upper level minimizes the corresponding risk-specific expression \(a(x,w)\), with an additional infimum over \(\eta\) for \(\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha\); for \(\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha\), it minimizes \(c^\top x+\inf_\eta\{\eta\mid \min_{w\in\Psi_{\mathcal R}(x)}a(x,w)\ge\alpha\}\). The auxiliary variables and constraints are risk-specific, with binary big-\(M\) variables for \(\mathrm{EP}_\eta\) and \(\mathrm{VaR}_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each listed risk measure, a finite-scenario bilevel stochastic linear problem over a polyhedron has an equivalent ordinary bilevel formulation using a common lower-level scenario program and risk-specific upper-level auxiliaries. Probability and value-at-risk cases additionally require bounded X and a sufficiently large big-M constant; CVaR and VaR retain an outer threshold variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M>0:\ \min_{x\in X}\mathcal R[F(x)]\text{ is equivalent to the stated standard bilevel formulation based on }\Psi_{\mathcal R}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The named conditions are retained symbolically because their definitions are outside the supplied extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(X\) is compact and \(Y\) is convex and compact. Suppose \(F_n\to F\) and \(g_{i,n}\to g_i\) continuously on \(X\times Y\), conditions \((C_1)-(C_4)\), \((C_{3,n})\), \((C_{4,n})\), \((H_1)\), and \((H_{2,n})\) hold for every \(n\), and \((H_{3,n})\) holds: for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) and every \((x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)\), \(L(x,y)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}L_n(x_n,y_n)\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\operatorname{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\mathcal S_n^\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal S^\varepsilon\) and \(\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n^\varepsilon=s^\varepsilon\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{Limsup}_{\varepsilon\to0}(\operatorname{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\mathcal S_n^\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness, convexity, continuous convergence of the problem data, the stated structural conditions, and a liminf condition on the payoffs, fixed-regularization solution outer limits lie in the limiting regularized solution set and the values converge; subsequently letting the regularization vanish yields only solutions of the original problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity conditions for a partially calm optimistic bilevel program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilevel-specific necessary conditions for a value-function reformulation without upper-level constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) be a local optimal solution of the equivalent value-function formulation of an optimistic bilevel program without upper-level constraints. Suppose that \(\varphi,\psi,f_i\) are locally Lipschitz around \((\bar x,\bar y)\), the lower-level solution map \(S\) is inner semicontinuous there, the stated lower-level regularity condition holds, the reformulated problem is partially calm there with constant \(\kappa>0\), and \(\widehat\partial\vartheta(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\). Then there exist \(u\in\widehat\partial\vartheta(\bar x)\) and multipliers \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) and \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\), satisfying the stated sign and complementary-slackness conditions, such that
\[(u,0)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r v_i\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y),\]
and
\[(u,0)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\kappa^{-1}\partial\psi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local Lipschitzness, inner semicontinuity of the lower-level solution map, lower-level regularity, partial calmness, and a nonempty Fréchet subdifferential of the value function, a local optimistic bilevel solution satisfies two generalized stationarity inclusions with multipliers obeying the stated sign and complementary-slackness conditions.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a local optimal solution of the equivalent optimistic bilevel formulation without upper-level constraints}
\varphi,\psi,f_i\text{ are locally Lipschitz around }(\bar x,\bar y)
S\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y)
\text{the reformulated problem is partially calm at }(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ with constant }\kappa>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists u\in\widehat\partial\vartheta(\bar x),\ \exists(v_i)_{i=1}^r,\ \exists(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^r\text{ satisfying the stated sign and complementary-slackness conditions}:\ (u,0)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r v_i\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y),\quad (u,0)\in\partial\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)+\kappa^{-1}\partial\psi(\bar x,\bar y)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\partial f_i(\bar x,\bar y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bilevel value-function and solution-map representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents lower-level optimality by an optimal-value function and solution-set mapping. Multiple lower-level optima leave the follower-response interpretation unspecified unless an optimistic, pessimistic, or other selection convention is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the lower-level problem \(\min_{y\in Y}\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le 0\}\), define \(\varphi(x):=\min_{y\in Y}\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le0\}\) and \(\Psi(x):=\{y\in Y:g(x,y)\le0,\ f(x,y)\le\varphi(x)\}\). Then \(\operatorname{gph}\Psi:=\{(x,y):y\in\Psi(x)\}\) encodes lower-level optimality, and the bilevel model may be written as \(\min_{x,y}\{F(x,y):G(x)\le0,\ x\in X,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\}\). If \(\Psi(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every upper-level-feasible \(x\), the lower-level minimum is attained and the displayed objects are well defined. If \(\Psi(x)\) contains multiple points, the hierarchical interpretation requires a convention specifying the follower's response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-level optimal value and optimizer set define a set-valued response map. Requiring the upper- and lower-level decisions to lie in its graph enforces lower-level optimality in the bilevel model. Nonemptiness of the optimizer set at every upper-level-feasible point ensures attainment. When several lower-level optimizers exist, the model's hierarchical meaning depends on the chosen follower-response convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\iff y\in\arg\min_{z\in Y}\{f(x,z):g(x,z)\le0\};\quad |\Psi(x)|>1\text{ leaves the follower-response convention unspecified.}

Then \((\mathrm{BPP})\) possesses an optimal solution if either (i) \(f\) is weakly sequentially upper semicontinuous and \(\Gamma\) is weakly-weakly inner semicontinuous on \(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\times\mathcal Z\), or (ii) \(\mathcal X\) is finite-dimensional, \(f\) is upper semicontinuous, and \(\Gamma\) is inner semicontinuous on \(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\times\mathcal Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standing weak compactness and lower-semicontinuity assumptions, the bilevel program attains an optimum in either the weak sequential continuity regime or the stated finite-dimensional ordinary continuity regime.

\(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\) is nonempty and weakly sequentially compact.
\(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\subset\operatorname{dom}\Gamma\) and \((X_{\mathrm{ad}}\times\mathcal Z)\cap\operatorname{gph}\Gamma\) is weakly sequentially compact.

Either \(f\) is weakly sequentially upper semicontinuous and \(\Gamma\) is weakly-weakly inner semicontinuous on \(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\times\mathcal Z\), or \(\dim\mathcal X<\infty\), \(f\) is upper semicontinuous, and \(\Gamma\) is inner semicontinuous there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subdifferential estimate for a bilevel value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz regularity and a multiplier-based upper estimate of the Clarke subdifferential at a reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the parametric lower-level problem with \(T=\mathbb R^m\). Suppose \(f,g_i\in C^1(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), the set \(\{(x,y):g(x,y)\leq 0\}\) is nonempty and compact, and MFCQ holds at \((\bar x,y)\) for every \(y\in Y(\bar x)\). Then \(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz continuous at \(\bar x\), and \[\partial^{Cl}\varphi(\bar x)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{y\in\Psi(\bar x)}\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar x,y)}\nabla_xL(\bar x,y,\lambda).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under continuous differentiability, compact nonempty joint feasibility, and MFCQ at every lower-level feasible point for the reference parameter, the value function is locally Lipschitz there. Its Clarke subdifferential is contained in the convex hull of the upper-variable Lagrangian gradients taken over lower-level solutions and their multiplier sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-level reaction set, inducible region, and permissible decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility for a linear bilevel program through the parameterized lower-level solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $R$ be the polyhedron defined by the upper-level constraints, let $S$ be the polyhedron defined by the lower-level constraints, and set $T=R\cap S$. For each $x\in\mathbb R^{n_1}$, define
\[
S(x)=\{y\in\mathbb R^{n_2}:(x,y)\in S\}
=\{y\ge0:B_2y\le b_2-A_2x\}
\]
and the lower-level rational-reaction set
\[
M(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in S(x)}d_2y.
\]
The inducible region is
\[
\mathrm{IR}=\{(x,y)\in T:y\in M(x)\}.
\]
A pair $(x,y)$ is bilevel feasible exactly when it belongs to $\mathrm{IR}$, and $x$ is permissible exactly when there exists $y\in\mathbb R^{n_2}$ such that $(x,y)\in\mathrm{IR}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed upper-level decision, the lower-level feasible set is the corresponding slice of the lower-level polyhedron, and the rational-reaction set consists of its optimal lower-level solutions. The inducible region contains the jointly feasible pairs whose lower-level component is a rational reaction. Its points are precisely the bilevel-feasible solutions, and an upper-level decision is permissible when it occurs in at least one such pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y)\text{ is bilevel feasible}\iff (x,y)\in\mathrm{IR},\qquad x\text{ is permissible}\iff \exists y\in\mathbb R^{n_2}:(x,y)\in\mathrm{IR}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of local nonoptimality in an optimistic linear bilevel program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if test using the optimistic value and a common lower-level basis-stability region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\bar x,\bar y)$ be feasible for the optimistic linear bilevel problem, with $\bar x\in\Psi_L(\bar y)$, $A^3\bar y=b$, and $\bar y\ge0$. Then $(\bar x,\bar y)$ is not a local optimistic solution if and only if either
\[
\langle d^1,\bar x\rangle>\varphi_o(\bar y),
\]
or there exist $\widetilde y$ and $\mathbf B\in\mathcal M(\bar y)$ such that
\[
A^3\widetilde y=b,\quad \widetilde y\ge0,\quad \bar y,\widetilde y\in\mathcal R(\mathbf B),
\]
and
\[
\left\langle d_B^1,\mathbf B^{-1}A^2(\widetilde y^2-\bar y^2)\right\rangle<\left\langle d^2,\bar y-\widetilde y\right\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible optimistic bilevel point fails local optimality exactly when its follower choice is not optimistic at the current parameter, or a feasible parameter in a common optimal-basis stability region satisfies the stated strict improvement inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is not locally optimistic-optimal}\iff \langle d^1,\bar x\rangle>\varphi_o(\bar y)\ \lor\ \exists(\widetilde y,\mathbf B)\text{ satisfying the displayed basis-region improvement conditions}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic Linear Bilevel Formulation and Value-Function Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of optimistic follower selection and its conditional value-function representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the follower solution mapping \(\Psi_L(y)\), the optimistic bilevel problem is
\[
\min_{x,y}\left\{\langle d^1,x\rangle+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0,\ x\in\Psi_L(y)\right\}.
\]
An optimal solution of this problem is an optimistic optimal solution. If this problem has an optimal solution, it can equivalently be written as
\[
\min_y\left\{\varphi_o(y)+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0\right\},
\qquad
\varphi_o(y):=\min_{x\in\Psi_L(y)}\langle d^1,x\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the optimistic convention, the follower selects from its solution set a response best for the leader. An optimum of the resulting joint problem is an optimistic optimum; when such an optimum exists, the problem has the stated minimum-value-function formulation.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the stated equivalence, the optimistic problem has an optimal solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x,y}\{\langle d^1,x\rangle+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0,\ x\in\Psi_L(y)\}\equiv\min_y\{\varphi_o(y)+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Optimality Transfer for the Optimistic Value Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States both directions of local-optimality transfer, retaining inner semicontinuity as a hypothesis only for the converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Psi_o(x):=\{y\in\Psi(x):F(x,y)\le\varphi_o(x)\}\). If \(\bar x\) is a local optimal solution of the optimistic reduced problem and \(\bar y\in\Psi(\bar x)\), then \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a local optimal solution of the associated bilevel problem. Conversely, if \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a local optimal solution of the associated bilevel problem and \(x\mapsto\Psi_o(x)\) is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), then \(\bar x\) is a local optimal solution of the optimistic reduced problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local solution of the optimistic reduced problem lifts with any lower-level solution to a local solution of the associated bilevel problem. The converse requires inner semicontinuity of the optimistic solution mapping at the candidate pair.
assumptions_latex: \bar y\in\Psi(\bar x)\text{ for the forward implication}
x\mapsto\Psi_o(x)\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ for the converse}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ locally solves the reduced problem}\Rightarrow(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ locally solves the bilevel problem};\quad (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ locally solves the bilevel problem and ISC holds}\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ locally solves the reduced problem}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: cl-property of a set-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential closedness of convexificators of lower-support scalarizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For H:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m, define \(\mathcal C_H(z^*,x):=\min_{z\in H(x)}z^\top z^*\). The mapping H has the cl-property if, whenever \(x_k^*\to x^*\), \(z_k^*\to z^*\), and \(x_k\to x\), \[x_k^*\in\partial^*\mathcal C_H(z_k^*,\cdot)(x_k)\quad\forall k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^*\in\partial^*\mathcal C_H(z^*,\cdot)(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping has the cl-property when limits of convexificator elements of its lower-support scalarizations remain convexificator elements at the limiting direction and base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k^*\to x^*,\ z_k^*\to z^*,\ x_k\to x,\ x_k^*\in\partial^*\mathcal C_H(z_k^*,\cdot)(x_k)\ \forall k\Longrightarrow x^*\in\partial^*\mathcal C_H(z^*,\cdot)(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eventual Lower Bound for the Algorithmic Parameter Along Convergent Subsequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A componentwise estimate along any subsequence converging to an accumulation point of the bilevel ℓp algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Assumptions A1–A3 hold. Let \((\mathbf w^*,\boldsymbol\lambda^*)\) be an arbitrary accumulation point of \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k)\}\), and let \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k)\}_{k\in K}\) be an arbitrary subsequence converging to it. Then there exists \(\gamma>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(k\in K\) and every \(i\in I(\mathbf w^*)\), \(\mu_{k-1}\geq\gamma|w_i^k|^{1/(2-p)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along any subsequence converging to an accumulation point, the algorithmic parameter μ at the preceding iteration eventually dominates a positive constant times each indexed component magnitude raised to 1/(2−p).
assumptions_latex: \((\mathbf w^*,\boldsymbol\lambda^*)\) is an arbitrary accumulation point of \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\gamma>0\;\exists k_0\;\forall k\in K\text{ with }k\geq k_0\;\forall i\in I(\mathbf w^*):\ \mu_{k-1}\geq\gamma|w_i^k|^{\frac{1}{2-p}}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Monotonicity-Based Upper-Approximation Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The procedure constructs an upper approximation on a bounded scalar interval. Its upper-bound interpretation requires the section's nondecreasing-value-function condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\varphi\) is nondecreasing on \([d_l,d_u]\). Choose \(r\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\varphi(x)\le r\) for every \(x\in[d_l,d_u]\), and initialize \(\xi(x):=r\). Choose \(d^1,\ldots,d^p\in[d_l,d_u]\) with \(d^p\le d^{p-1}\le\cdots\le d^1\), evaluate \(\varphi(d^i)\), and set \(\xi_i(x):=\varphi(d^i)\) for \(x\le d^i\). For \(i=1,\ldots,p\), update \(\xi(x):=\min\{\xi_i(x),\xi(x)\}\) when \(x\le d^i\), leaving \(\xi(x)\) unchanged otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a constant upper bound. At each ordered sample, use the sampled value as an upper bound for smaller parameters and tighten the approximation by taking the minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi(x)\leftarrow\begin{cases}\min\{\varphi(d^i),\xi(x)\},&x\le d^i,\\\xi(x),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad i=1,\ldots,p.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial calmness of the value-function reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: At a local solution \((\bar x,\bar y)\) of \((VP)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) be a local solution of \((VP)\). The problem is partially calm there if there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(\mu>0\) such that, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb B_\delta\) and every \((x,y)\in\mathbb B_\delta(\bar x,\bar y)\) feasible for \((VP_\alpha)\), with \(f(x,y)-V(x)+\alpha=0\), \(g(x,y)\le0\), \(h(x,y)=0\), \(G(x,y)\le0\), and \(H(x,y)=0\), one has \(F(x,y)-F(\bar x,\bar y)+\mu\|\alpha\|\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial calmness means that no nearby feasible perturbation of the value-function equality can improve the upper-level objective by more than a fixed multiple of the perturbation norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundedness, Positivity, and Nondegeneracy Assumptions for the Bilevel ℓp Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assumptions imposed on the sequence generated by the proposed bilevel hyperparameter algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k,\boldsymbol\zeta^k,\boldsymbol\eta^k)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^r\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^r\) be generated by the proposed algorithm. Assume (A1) \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\lambda_1^k>0\); (A2) \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k,\boldsymbol\zeta^k,\boldsymbol\eta^k)\}\) is bounded; and (A3), if \(p=1\), every accumulation point \((\mathbf w^*,\boldsymbol\lambda^*)\) of \(\{(\mathbf w^k,\boldsymbol\lambda^k)\}\) satisfies \(\lambda_1^*\neq\left|\frac{\partial G(\mathbf w^*,\overline{\boldsymbol\lambda}^{*})}{\partial w_i}\right|\) for every \(i\in I(\mathbf w^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first hyperparameter stays asymptotically bounded away from zero, the full generated sequence is bounded, and, when p=1, every accumulation point satisfies the stated nondegeneracy inequality for all indices in I(w*).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified descent algorithm targeting Bouligand stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier- and active-set-sampling descent method with threshold reduction and feasible geometric backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(y^0\) with \(G(y^0)\le0\), choose \(\varepsilon'>0\), sufficiently small \(\kappa>0\), \(\varepsilon,\varrho\in(0,1)\), and \(w<0\). At iteration \(k\), sample \((\lambda^k,\mu^k)\in E\Lambda(x(y^k),y^k)\) and \(K^k\in\mathcal I(\lambda^k)\), solve problem (6.3) for \((d^k,r^k,\gamma^k,\eta^k,s^k)\), and accept a sample when \(s^k<w\). After exhausting samples, replace \(w\) by \(w/2\); when \(|w|<\varepsilon'\), use sets \(K^k\subseteq I_\kappa(x(y^k),y^k)\) satisfying (C2) and choose multipliers minimizing \(\|\nabla_xL(x(y^k),y^k,\lambda,\mu)\|^2\) subject to \(\lambda_j=0\) for \(j\notin K^k\). For an accepted direction, take the largest \(t^k\in\{\varrho,\varrho^2,\ldots\}\) satisfying \(\mathcal F(y^k+t^kr^k)\le\mathcal F(y^k)+\varepsilon t^ks^k\) and \(G(y^k+t^kr^k)\le0\). If \(t^k<\varepsilon'\), discard the current \(K^k\) and resample; otherwise set \(y^{k+1}=y^k+t^kr^k\). In the fallback sampling phase, stop if all sets are exhausted and repeated threshold reduction gives \(|w|<\varepsilon'\). The stated output is a Bouligand-stationary solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method samples eligible lower-level multipliers and active-index sets, solves a direction subproblem, progressively relaxes a negative descent threshold, switches to approximate-active-set multiplier minimization near the threshold, and applies feasible geometric backtracking. Failed small steps cause the active set to be discarded. The stated output is a Bouligand-stationary solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The modified algorithm returns a Bouligand-stationary solution of the bilevel problem.}
