knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Pessimistic Bilevel Programming Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the general pessimistic formulation and the independent-follower-feasible-set case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), let \(X'=\{x:G(x)\le0\}\) and
\[
\Psi(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le0\}.
\]
A general pessimistic bilevel problem is
\[
\min_{x\in X'}\max_{y\in\Psi(x)}F(x,y).
\]
If \(g(x,y)=g(y)\), so that the follower feasible set does not depend on \(x\), the problem is called independent pessimistic bilevel programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The leader minimizes its worst objective value over all optimal follower responses. The problem is independent when the follower feasible set does not depend on the leader variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X'}\max_{y\in\Psi(x)}F(x,y),\qquad g(x,y)=g(y)\Rightarrow\text{independent pessimistic bilevel problem}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz continuity of a bilevel value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stability consequence for a parameter-dependent marginal value. Because \(\vartheta\) is defined on the parameter space, its local Lipschitz conclusion is around \(\bar x\), correcting the dimensionally inconsistent source wording around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be lower semicontinuous, let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) have closed graph, and define \(\vartheta(x):=\inf\{\varphi(x,y)\mid y\in F(x)\}\) and \(M(x):=\{y\in F(x)\mid\varphi(x,y)=\vartheta(x)\}\). Suppose \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}M\), \(M\) is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), \(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz around \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and \(F\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then \(\vartheta\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the standing marginal-function assumptions hold, the argminimum mapping is inner semicontinuous, the cost is locally Lipschitz, and the constraint mapping is Lipschitz-like at a minimizing parameter-response pair, then the optimal value function is locally Lipschitz near the parameter.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y)
\varphi\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }(\bar x,\bar y)
F\text{ is Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \vartheta\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic and Pessimistic Bilevel Value-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines optimistic and pessimistic bilevel models through the solution map of a parameterized lower-level optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi,\psi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\), \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). For each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(S(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}\{\varphi(x,y)\mid y\in F(x)\}\). The optimistic bilevel model minimizes \(\mu(x):=\inf\{\psi(x,y)\mid y\in S(x)\}\) over \(x\in\Omega\), whereas the pessimistic bilevel model minimizes \(\eta(x):=\sup\{\psi(x,y)\mid y\in S(x)\}\) over \(x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each parameter x, the lower-level solution map contains the feasible lower-level minimizers. The optimistic model minimizes over the upper-level feasible set the infimum of the upper-level cost among those solutions, while the pessimistic model minimizes the corresponding supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\Omega}\mu(x),\quad \mu(x):=\inf_{y\in S(x)}\psi(x,y),\qquad \min_{x\in\Omega}\eta(x),\quad \eta(x):=\sup_{y\in S(x)}\psi(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pessimistic Linear Bilevel Formulation and Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of worst-case follower selection through a pessimistic value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the follower solution mapping \(\Psi_L(y)\), define
\[
\varphi_p(y):=\max_{x\in\Psi_L(y)}\langle d^1,x\rangle.
\]
The pessimistic bilevel problem is
\[
\min_y\left\{\varphi_p(y)+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0\right\}.
\]
An optimal solution of this problem is called a pessimistic optimal solution of the bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the pessimistic convention, the leader minimizes against the follower response that is worst for the leader. An optimum of the resulting worst-response value-function problem is a pessimistic bilevel optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y^*\in\operatorname{Argmin}\{\varphi_p(y)+\langle d^2,y\rangle:A^3y=b,\ y\geq0\}\Longrightarrow y^*\text{ is a pessimistic bilevel optimal solution}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Stability Directional Necessary Condition for a Bilevel Local Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directional first-order necessary condition derived from strong stability of a convex parametric lower-level problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(x^0,y^0)$ be a local solution of the bilevel problem, and suppose its convex parametric lower-level problem satisfies MFCQ, SSOC, and CRCQ at $(x^0,y^0)$. Then the optimal value of
\[
\min_{\alpha,r}\ \alpha
\]
subject to
\[
\nabla_xF(x^0,y^0)^\top x'(y^0;r)+\nabla_yF(x^0,y^0)^\top r\leq\alpha,
\]
\[
\nabla G_i(y^0)^\top r\leq\alpha\quad\forall i\text{ with }G_i(y^0)=0,
\qquad \|r\|\leq1,
\]
is nonnegative. If ULR also holds, this condition is equivalently expressed by nonnegativity of the optimal value of
\[
\min_{\|r\|\leq1}\ \nabla_xF(x^0,y^0)^\top x'(y^0;r)+\nabla_yF(x^0,y^0)^\top r
\]
subject to $\nabla G_i(y^0)^\top r\leq0$ for every active upper-level inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a bilevel local minimum, strong stability assumptions on the convex lower-level problem imply that the stated normalized directional optimization problem cannot have a negative optimal value. Under upper-level regularity, the epigraph form may be replaced by minimization over the upper-level linearized feasible directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal value function, argminimum mapping, and inner semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a parameterized lower-level optimization problem underlying bilevel value-function models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be lower semicontinuous and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) have closed graph. Define \(\vartheta(x):=\inf\{\varphi(x,y)\mid y\in F(x)\}\) and \(M(x):=\{y\in F(x)\mid\varphi(x,y)=\vartheta(x)\}\). The mapping \(M\) is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}M\) if, for every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) with \(x_k\in\operatorname{dom}M\), there exist \(y_k\in M(x_k)\) such that \(y_k\to\bar y\). The Lipschitz-like property of \(M\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) implies this inner semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal value is the infimum of the parameterized objective over the feasible-response mapping, and the argminimum mapping collects attaining responses. Inner semicontinuity at a graph point means that every convergent sequence of parameters in the argminimum mapping's domain admits minimizing responses converging to the specified minimizer. Lipschitz-like behavior of the argminimum mapping implies this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \vartheta(x)=\inf_{y\in F(x)}\varphi(x,y),\quad M(x)=\{y\in F(x)\mid\varphi(x,y)=\vartheta(x)\},\quad M\text{ Lipschitz-like at }(\bar x,\bar y)\Rightarrow M\text{ inner semicontinuous there}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Region of stability of an optimal basic matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric linear-programming basis stability used in linear bilevel analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a basic matrix $\mathbf B$, its region of stability is

\mathcal R(\mathbf B)=\left\{y:\mathbf B^{-1}(a-A^2y^2)\ge0,\ (y_B^1)^\top\mathbf B^{-1}A^1-(y^1)^\top\le0\right\}.

It is the set of parameters $y$ for which $\mathbf B$ remains an optimal basic matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear bilevel program with coupling constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the general two-level linear formulation and identifies removable and coupling terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear bilevel program has upper-level variables $x\in\mathbb R^{n_1}$ and lower-level variables $y\in\mathbb R^{n_2}$ and is formulated as
\[
\min_{x,y}\;c_1x+d_1y
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad A_1x+B_1y\le b_1,\;x\ge0,
\]
where $y$ solves
\[
\min_y\;c_2x+d_2y
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad A_2x+B_2y\le b_2,\;y\ge0.
\]
Here $c_i\in\mathbb R^{1\times n_1}$, $d_i\in\mathbb R^{1\times n_2}$, $b_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}$, $A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n_1}$, and $B_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n_2}$ for $i=1,2$. For fixed $x$, $c_2x$ is constant and may be omitted from the lower-level objective. Upper-level constraints involving both $x$ and $y$ are coupling (joint) constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear bilevel program minimizes a linear upper-level objective subject to linear upper-level constraints, while the lower-level variable must solve a parameterized linear program. The lower-level term depending only on the fixed upper-level decision is constant and can be removed. Upper-level constraints involving variables from both levels are coupling or joint constraints.
assumptions_latex: c_i\in\mathbb R^{1\times n_1},\quad d_i\in\mathbb R^{1\times n_2},\quad b_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}
A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n_1},\quad B_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n_2},\quad i\in\{1,2\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{c_1x+d_1y:A_1x+B_1y\le b_1,\ x\ge0,\ y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\ge0}\{d_2z:A_2x+B_2z\le b_2\}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-gradient method with backtracking and decreasing parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic iteration for the source-defined smooth function family \(w_\sigma\) over the set \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\bar\alpha>0\), \(\theta,\eta\in(0,1)\), \(x^0\in P\), and \(\sigma_0>0\). Given \(x^k\), define \[z^k(\alpha)=\Pi_P\bigl(x^k-\alpha\nabla w_{\sigma_k}(x^k)\bigr).\] Let \(m_k\) be the smallest integer \(m\ge0\) for which \[w_{\sigma_k}\bigl(z^k(\eta^m\bar\alpha)\bigr)\le w_{\sigma_k}(x^k)+\theta\nabla w_{\sigma_k}(x^k)^{\top}\bigl(z^k(\eta^m\bar\alpha)-x^k\bigr).\] Set \(\alpha_k=\eta^{m_k}\bar\alpha\), \(x^{k+1}=z^k(\alpha_k)\), choose \(0<\sigma_{k+1}\le\sigma_k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a point in P, take a projected-gradient step for the current function w indexed by sigma. Backtrack geometrically until the stated Armijo inequality holds, accept the step, choose a positive nonincreasing next sigma, and iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{k+1}=\Pi_P\bigl(x^k-\alpha_k\nabla w_{\sigma_k}(x^k)\bigr),\quad \alpha_k=\eta^{m_k}\bar\alpha,\text{ where }m_k\text{ is the smallest index satisfying the Armijo inequality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pessimistic Semivectorial Bilevel Programming Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The follower solves a multiobjective problem, and pessimism ranges over its efficient solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability of Epsilon-Solutions and Values under Continuous Data Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability for each fixed positive regularization tolerance under continuous convergence of problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact and \(Y\) convex and compact. Suppose \(F_n\to F\) and \(g_{i,n}\to g_i\) continuously on \(X\times Y\), \(L\) is lower semicontinuous there, and \((C_1)-(C_4)\) hold. For every \(n\in\mathbb N\), assume: (i) each \(g_{i,n}(x,\cdot)\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(Y\); (ii) for every \(x\in X\), some \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(\max_{1\le i\le k}g_{i,n}(x,y)<0\); and (iii), whenever \((x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)\), \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}L_n(x_n,y_n)\le L(x,y)\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the \(\varepsilon\)-solution sets satisfy the stability inclusion (4.4.3), and \(\lim_{n\to\infty}w_n^{\varepsilon}=w^{\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the compactness, continuous-data convergence, semicontinuity, strict quasiconvexity, strict feasibility, and limsup assumptions stated above hold, then for every positive epsilon the epsilon-solution sets satisfy the specified stability inclusion and the epsilon-values converge.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is compact, and }Y\text{ is convex and compact.}
F_n\to F\text{ and }g_{i,n}\to g_i\text{ continuously on }X\times Y.
L\text{ is lower semicontinuous on }X\times Y.
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ \forall x\in X,\quad g_{i,n}(x,\cdot)\text{ is strictly quasiconvex on }Y.
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \forall x\in X,\ \exists y\in Y:\ \max_{1\le i\le k}g_{i,n}(x,y)<0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0,\quad \text{the stability inclusion (4.4.3) holds and }\lim_{n\to\infty}w_n^{\varepsilon}=w^{\varepsilon}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar y\in Y(\bar x):=\{y:g(\bar x,y)\le0\}\), with every \(g_i\) Lipschitz continuous. The pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is lower-level regular if, for every selection \((u_i,v_i)\in\partial^{Cl}g_i(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)\), \[\sum_{i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)}\lambda_i v_i=0,\quad \lambda_i\ge0\ \forall i\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_i=0\ \forall i\in I(\bar x,\bar y).\] The analogous condition for active upper-level constraints is called upper-level regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bilevel pair is lower-level regular when every choice of Clarke subgradients of the active lower-level constraints has positively linearly independent components in the lower variable. The analogous upper-constraint condition defines upper-level regularity.
assumptions_latex: g_i\text{ is Lipschitz continuous for every lower-level constraint}
(u_i,v_i)\in\partial^{Cl}g_i(\bar x,\bar y)\quad\forall i\in I(\bar x,\bar y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient basis-region tests for pessimistic local nonoptimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two sufficient failure certificates under the source's stated genericity assumption; the result does not claim necessity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\bar x,\bar y)$ be feasible for the pessimistic linear bilevel problem, with $A^3\bar y=b$, $\bar y\ge0$, $\bar x\in\Psi_L(\bar y)$, and $\langle d^1,\bar x\rangle=\varphi_p(\bar y)$. Assume the stated genericity assumption. Then $\bar y$ is not a pessimistic local optimum in either of the following cases:

(i) There exist $\mathbf B\in\mathcal M(\bar y)$ and $\widehat y$ such that
\[
\widehat y\in\mathcal R^0(\mathbf B),\quad A^3\widehat y=b,\quad \widehat y\ge0,
\quad \langle d^1,x^{\mathbf B}(\bar y)\rangle<\varphi_p(\bar y).
\]

(ii) $\varphi_p(\bar y)=\varphi_o(\bar y)$ and there exist $\mathbf B\in\mathcal M(\bar y)$ and $\widehat y$ such that
\[
\bar y\in\mathcal R(\mathbf B),\quad \widehat y\in\mathcal R^0(\mathbf B),
\quad A^3\widehat y=b,\quad \widehat y\ge0,
\]
and
\[
\left\langle d_B^1,\mathbf B^{-1}A^2(\widehat y^2-\bar y^2)\right\rangle
<\left\langle d^2,\bar y-\widehat y\right\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated genericity assumption, either of two basis-region certificates rules out pessimistic local optimality: a basis whose induced follower solution is strictly better than the pessimistic value, or—when optimistic and pessimistic values coincide—a feasible strict stability-region perturbation satisfying the strict improvement inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Either displayed case implies that }\bar y\text{ is not a pessimistic local optimum}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract denotes the functional by \(\mathcal Q_{EP_n}\) and the minimized risk measure by \(EP_\eta\); both notations are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\) and fix \(\eta\in\mathbb R\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w)\), \(R_1\) is the ℓp regularizer from the model, and \(\bar\lambda\) denotes the remaining hyperparameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded global convergence guarantee for the sequence generated by the preceding bilevel algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex. Let \(F,f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable with locally Lipschitz-continuous gradients, and suppose that \(F\) and \(f\) are bounded below on \(P\) by \(\bar F\) and \(\bar f\), respectively. Let the solution set \(S\) of (4.2) be nonempty and bounded. If \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\sigma_k=0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sigma_k=\infty,\] then the sequence \(\{x^k\}\) generated by the preceding algorithm satisfies \[\lim_{k\to\infty}d(x^k,S)=0,\qquad d(x,S):=\inf_{z\in S}\|x-z\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the feasible set is closed and convex, the two convex smooth functions are bounded below on it, the solution set of (4.2) is nonempty and bounded, and the algorithmic parameters tend to zero while having divergent sum, then the generated iterates approach the solution set in distance.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex.}
F,f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ are convex and differentiable with locally Lipschitz-continuous gradients.}
F(x)\ge\bar F\text{ and }f(x)\ge\bar f\quad\forall x\in P.
S\text{ is the nonempty and bounded solution set of (4.2).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pessimistic Linear Bilevel Multi-Follower Problem with a Partially Shared Variable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a common follower variable together with follower-specific variables; the extract's final nonnegativity notation is internally inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,M\), let
\[
\Psi_i(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y_i,v}\{w_i^\top y_i+z_i^\top v:A_ix+B_iy_i+C_iv\le b_i,\ y_i,z\ge0\}.
\]
A pessimistic linear bilevel multi-follower problem with partially shared variable \(v\) is represented by
\[
\min_{x\in X}\max_{(y_i,v)\in\Psi_i(x),\ i=1,\ldots,M}
\left[c^\top x+\sum_{i=1}^M d_i^\top y_i+s^\top v\right].
\]
The stated additional dimensions are \(s,v,z_i\in\mathbb R^l\) and \(C_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times l}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The followers have individual variables y_i and a partially shared variable v. Each follower solves a linear problem involving both, while the leader evaluates the worst follower-optimal joint response. The extracted nonnegativity condition uses z although v is the displayed decision variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\max_{(y_i,v)\in\Psi_i(x),\ i=1,\ldots,M}\left[c^\top x+\sum_{i=1}^M d_i^\top y_i+s^\top v\right].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and an exact multiplier representation of the lower-level value-function subdifferential under affine data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Special mixed-discrete bilevel model and its stability regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the structured discrete-follower model, optimistic and pessimistic solution functions, and stability regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Y_D=\{y\in\mathbb Z^n:Ay\le b\}, f(x,y)=h(y)-y^\top x, and \Psi_D(x)=\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y_D}f(x,y), where h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is differentiable and strongly convex with modulus \theta>0. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic and Pessimistic ε-Bilevel Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines follower value and response sets and the original optimistic and pessimistic leader problems when the follower feasible set is independent of the leader variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that, for every \(x\in X\), the follower problem \(\min_{v\in Y}f(x,v)\) is solvable. Define \(\varphi(x):=\min_{v\in Y}f(x,v)\), \(S(x):=\arg\min_{v\in Y}f(x,v)\), and, for \(\varepsilon>0\), \(S_\varepsilon(x):=\{y\in Y\mid f(x,y)\leq\varphi(x)+\varepsilon\}\). Then \(\psi_\varepsilon^o(x):=\min_{y\in S_\varepsilon(x)}F(x,y)\) and \(\psi_\varepsilon^p(x):=\max_{y\in S_\varepsilon(x)}F(x,y)\) are the optimistic and pessimistic leader value functions, and the corresponding original bilevel problems minimize these functions over \(X\). The exact models are obtained by setting \(\varepsilon=0\). Under the stated standard regime of continuous \(f,F\), nonempty compact \(X,Y\), and a convex follower problem, the perturbed problems are solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The follower value, exact solution set, and epsilon-optimal response set are obtained from the follower problem. The optimistic leader chooses its best epsilon-optimal follower response, whereas the pessimistic leader accounts for the worst such response. Epsilon zero gives the exact models. The source also states standard sufficient conditions for solvability.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the solvability statement: }f,F\text{ are continuous, }X,Y\text{ are nonempty and compact, and the follower problem is convex.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\psi_\varepsilon^o(x)=\min_{x\in X}\min_{y\in S_\varepsilon(x)}F(x,y),\qquad \min_{x\in X}\psi_\varepsilon^p(x)=\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in S_\varepsilon(x)}F(x,y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MPEC necessary condition under a unique lower-level multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplified directional stationarity system for a bilevel MPEC with a unique lower-level multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let (\bar x,\bar y) be a local minimizer of (MPEC), suppose MSCQ holds at (\bar x,\bar y), and suppose \bar\Lambda=\{\bar\lambda\}. Then there exist \bar v\in\bar K_\Gamma, an index set \mathcal I^+ satisfying \bar J^+(\bar\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal I^+\subseteq\bar I(\bar v), and w\in\mathbb R^m,\xi\in\mathbb R^q such that
\[
0=\nabla_xF(\bar x,\bar y)-\nabla^2_{xy}f(\bar x,\bar y)w,
\]
\[
0=\nabla_yF(\bar x,\bar y)-\nabla^2_{yy}f(\bar x,\bar y)w-\nabla^2(\bar\lambda^Tg)(\bar y)w+\nabla g(\bar y)^T\xi,
\]
\[
\xi_i=0\quad(i\notin\bar I(\bar v)),
\]
\[
\xi_i\ge0,\quad \nabla g_i(\bar y)^Tw\le0\quad(i\in\bar I(\bar v)\setminus\mathcal I^+),
\]
and
\[
\nabla g_i(\bar y)^Tw=0\quad(i\in\mathcal I^+).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an MSCQ local minimizer with a unique lower-level multiplier, there are a critical direction, an intermediate active-index set, and vectors w and xi satisfying a simplified second-order stationarity system together with support, sign, and complementarity-type conditions.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a local minimizer of (MPEC)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\bar v\in\bar K_\Gamma,\ \mathcal I^+,\ w\in\mathbb R^m,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^q\text{ satisfying the stated stationarity and indexwise conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value and outer solution convergence for regularized follower problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of follower optimal values and minimizers under simultaneous parameter convergence and vanishing quadratic regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose Y is compact and convex, F is continuous on X\times Y, and \lambda_n\to+\infty. Then, for every x\in X and every sequence x_n\to x, \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in Y}\left(F(x_n,y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda_n}\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}\right)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y),\] and, with M(x)=\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y), \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}\left(F(x_n,y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda_n}\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}\right)\subseteq M(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous follower objective on a compact convex feasible set, regularized optimal values converge to the unregularized value as both the leader parameter and regularization vary, and every outer limit of regularized minimizers is an unregularized follower minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in Y}\left(F(x_n,y)+\frac{\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}}{2\lambda_n}\right)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y),\quad \operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}\left(F(x_n,y)+\frac{\|y\|_{\mathbb Y}^{2}}{2\lambda_n}\right)\subseteq M(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard Value-Function Reformulations of Optimistic and Pessimistic Bilevel Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint leader-follower reformulations and the boundary between global correspondence and possible local nonequivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_\varepsilon(x)=\{y\in Y\mid f(x,y)\leq\varphi(x)+\varepsilon\}\). The standard optimistic formulation is \[\min_{x,y}F(x,y)\quad\text{s.t. }x\in X,\ y\in Y,\ f(x,y)\leq\varphi(x)+\varepsilon.\] The additional condition \(F(x,y)\leq\psi_\varepsilon^o(x)\), although present in principle to select an optimistic response, can be omitted from this minimization formulation as redundant for global optimization. The standard pessimistic formulation is \[\min_{x,y}F(x,y)\quad\text{s.t. }x\in X,\ y\in Y,\ f(x,y)\leq\varphi(x)+\varepsilon,\ F(x,y)\geq\psi_\varepsilon^p(x).\] Each standard formulation has complete correspondence with its original formulation at the level of global optimal points, whereas local optimal points of the standard formulations need not yield corresponding local optimal points of the original formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nested optimistic and pessimistic models can be expressed as joint programs using the follower value-function constraint. In the optimistic minimization model, the explicit best-response-value condition can be omitted for global optimization; the pessimistic model retains a worst-response-value constraint. Global optima correspond between original and standard formulations, but local optima may not.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The original and standard formulations correspond globally, but corresponding local optimality can fail.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothing Method for a Nonsmooth Bilevel Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer continuation scheme using approximate KKT solutions of smooth reformulations; SQP is given only as an example inner solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\mu_0\ne0\), \(\beta_1,\beta_2\in(0,1)\), and \(\widehat\varepsilon_0\ge0\), and set \(k=0\). Repeatedly find a \(\widehat\varepsilon_k\)-approximate KKT point \((w^{k+1},\lambda^{k+1},\zeta^{k+1},\eta^{k+1})\) of the smooth reformulation with \(\mu=\mu_k\), then update \[\mu_{k+1}=\beta_1\mu_k,\qquad \widehat\varepsilon_{k+1}=\beta_2\widehat\varepsilon_k,\] increment \(k\), and stop when \((w^k,\lambda^k,\zeta^k,\eta^k)\) converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each outer iteration, approximately solve the current smooth bilevel reformulation, then geometrically decrease both the smoothing parameter and the permitted KKT residual until the primal-multiplier sequence converges.
assumptions_latex: \text{An }\widehat\varepsilon_k\text{-approximate KKT point of each smooth subproblem can be found}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_k=\beta_1^k\mu_0,\qquad \widehat\varepsilon_k=\beta_2^k\widehat\varepsilon_0,\quad\text{with termination upon convergence of }(w^k,\lambda^k,\zeta^k,\eta^k).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Optimality Transfer from Weak Global Bilevel Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate optimistic and pessimistic transfer guarantees based on a response attaining the auxiliary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varepsilon>0. In the optimistic case, suppose x^0\in X is a weak global optimistic solution, y^0\in\widehat{\Psi}_o(x^0), and F(x^0,y^0)=\bar{\varphi}_o(x^0). Every x\in O(y^0) satisfying F(x,y^0)\leq F(x^0,y^0)+\varepsilon is then an \varepsilon\text{-optimal optimistic solution}. Respectively, if x^0\in X is a weak global pessimistic solution, y^0\in\widehat{\Psi}_p(x^0), and F(x^0,y^0)=\bar{\varphi}_p(x^0), then every x\in P(y^0) satisfying F(x,y^0)\leq F(x^0,y^0)+\varepsilon is an \varepsilon\text{-optimal pessimistic solution}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a weak global optimistic or pessimistic solution and a corresponding response that attains its auxiliary value, any point in the matching set O(y0) or P(y0) whose objective is no more than epsilon above the reference objective is epsilon-optimal for that same case.
assumptions_latex: \text{Optimistic case: }x^0\in X\text{ is a weak global optimistic solution},\ y^0\in\widehat{\Psi}_o(x^0),\ F(x^0,y^0)=\bar{\varphi}_o(x^0),\ x\in O(y^0),\ F(x,y^0)\leq F(x^0,y^0)+\varepsilon

\text{Pessimistic case, respectively: }x^0\in X\text{ is a weak global pessimistic solution},\ y^0\in\widehat{\Psi}_p(x^0),\ F(x^0,y^0)=\bar{\varphi}_p(x^0),\ x\in P(y^0),\ F(x,y^0)\leq F(x^0,y^0)+\varepsilon
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-optimal in the corresponding optimistic or pessimistic case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tikhonov regularization selects the minimum-norm minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and limiting selection for a convex regularized minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A be compact and convex, let J be lower semicontinuous and convex on A, let \lambda_n\to+\infty, and set V=\operatorname{Argmin}_{z\in A}J(z). For every n\in\mathbb N, the Tikhonov-regularized problem (P)_{\lambda_n}^{\mathcal T} has a unique solution \bar a_n^{\mathcal T}\in A. Moreover, \bar a_n^{\mathcal T} converges to the minimum-norm element of V, and \left\|\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar a_n^{\mathcal T}\right\|_{\mathbb A}=\inf_{a\in V}\|a\|_{\mathbb A}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact convex set, Tikhonov regularization of a lower-semicontinuous convex objective has a unique solution for each regularization parameter and, as the parameter tends to infinity, these solutions converge to the minimum-norm minimizer of the original objective.
assumptions_latex: J\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex on }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ (P)_{\lambda_n}^{\mathcal T}\text{ has the unique solution }\bar a_n^{\mathcal T}\in A,\quad \bar a_n^{\mathcal T}\to\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in V}\|a\|_{\mathbb A}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Sequential Compactness Framework for a Bilevel Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standing Banach-space assumptions used by subsequent bilevel existence results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Z\) be Banach spaces. The functionals \(F,f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) are weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous; \(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\subset\mathcal X\) is nonempty and weakly sequentially compact; \(\Gamma:\mathcal X\rightrightarrows\mathcal Z\) satisfies \(X_{\mathrm{ad}}\subset\operatorname{dom}\Gamma\); and \((X_{\mathrm{ad}}\times\mathcal Z)\cap\operatorname{gph}\Gamma\) is weakly sequentially compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility, reaction, and pessimistic value in bilevel optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the constraint region, leader projection, follower feasible and rational-reaction sets, inducible region, and worst-case upper-level value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:=\{(x,y):G(x)\le 0,\ g(x,y)\le 0\}\) and \(S(X):=\{x\in X:\exists y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in S\}\). For every \(x\in S(X)\), define \(Y(x):=\{y:g(x,y)\le 0\}\) and \(\Psi(x):=\{y:y\in\arg\min\{f(x,y):y\in Y(x)\}\}\). Then \(\mathrm{IR}:=\{(x,y):(x,y)\in S,\ y\in\Psi(x)\}\), and \(\varphi(x):=\sup_{y\in\Psi(x)}F(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The leader projection identifies leader decisions admitting a jointly feasible follower decision. Each such decision has a follower feasible set and optimal-reaction set. The inducible region consists of jointly feasible pairs with an optimal follower response, while the pessimistic value is the supremum of the leader objective over all such responses.
assumptions_latex: x\in S(X)\text{ for the definitions of }Y(x)\text{ and }\Psi(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{IR}=\{(x,y):(x,y)\in S,\ y\in\Psi(x)\},\qquad \varphi(x)=\sup_{y\in\Psi(x)}F(x,y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subsequential limit guarantee for regularized Stackelberg solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional characterization of limits of convergent subsequences, relative to the security value of the underlying problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that X is compact, Y is compact and convex, L and F are continuous on X\times Y, F(x,\cdot) is convex on Y for every x\in X, and \lambda_n\to+\infty. For every n\in\mathbb N, let \bar x_n^{\mathcal T} be a solution of (SP)_{\lambda_n}^{\mathcal T}. If a subsequence of \bigl(\bar x_n^{\mathcal T},\bar\varphi_n^{\mathcal T}(\bar x_n^{\mathcal T})\bigr) converges to (\bar x,\bar y), then L(\bar x,\bar y)\leq w and \bar y\in M(\bar x), where w is the security value of (PB).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness, continuity, follower convexity, and diverging regularization parameters, every convergent subsequence of regularized Stackelberg solution-response pairs has a follower-optimal limit whose leader value does not exceed the security value.
assumptions_latex: F(x,\cdot)\text{ is convex on }Y\quad\forall x\in X
\bar x_n^{\mathcal T}\text{ solves }(SP)_{\lambda_n}^{\mathcal T}\quad\forall n\in\mathbb N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\bar x_{n_j}^{\mathcal T},\bar\varphi_{n_j}^{\mathcal T}(\bar x_{n_j}^{\mathcal T})\bigr)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\Longrightarrow L(\bar x,\bar y)\leq w\ \text{ and }\ \bar y\in M(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Viscosity solution under an inner regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition using the regularized reaction sets \(\mathcal T^\varepsilon(x)\), follower solution map \(M(x)\), and pessimistic value \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak T=\{\mathcal T^\varepsilon:\varepsilon>0\}\) be an inner regularization for \(\{(P_x):x\in X\}\). A point \(\bar x\in X\) is a \(\mathfrak T\)-viscosity solution of \((PB)\) if, for every sequence \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), there exist \(x^{\varepsilon_n}\in X\) such that: (V1) some subsequence of \((x^{\varepsilon_n})_n\) converges to \(\bar x\); (V2) each \(x^{\varepsilon_n}\) attains the corresponding regularized pessimistic minimax value, namely \(\sup_{y\in\mathcal T^{\varepsilon_n}(x^{\varepsilon_n})}L(x^{\varepsilon_n},y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in\mathcal T^{\varepsilon_n}(x)}L(x,y)\); and (V3) \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{y\in\mathcal T^{\varepsilon_n}(x^{\varepsilon_n})}L(x^{\varepsilon_n},y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in M(x)}L(x,y)=w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is a viscosity solution if every sequence of regularization parameters tending to zero admits regularized minimizers with a subsequence converging to that point and with regularized pessimistic values converging to the original pessimistic value.
assumptions_latex: \mathfrak T=\{\mathcal T^\varepsilon:\varepsilon>0\}\text{ is an inner regularization of }\{(P_x):x\in X\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(x^{\varepsilon_n})_n\subset X\text{ satisfying (V1)--(V3)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner Regularization of a Family of Minimum Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a parameterized family of set-valued approximations to the minimum-solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathfrak T=\{\mathcal T^\varepsilon:\varepsilon>0\}\), with \(\mathcal T^\varepsilon:X\rightrightarrows Y\), is an inner regularization of \(\{(P_x):x\in X\}\), whose solution map is \(M\), if: (R1) \(M(x)\subseteq\mathcal T^\varepsilon(x)\subseteq\mathcal T^\eta(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(0<\varepsilon<\eta\); (R2) whenever \(x_n\to x\) and \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), \(\operatorname{Limsup}_n\mathcal T^{\varepsilon_n}(x_n)\subseteq M(x)\); and (R3) \(\mathcal T^\varepsilon\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of set-valued maps is an inner regularization when it contains the exact solution map, expands monotonically with epsilon, has no outer limit points outside the exact solution map as both parameters and epsilon converge, and is lower semicontinuous for every positive epsilon.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathfrak T\text{ is an inner regularization}\iff (R_1),(R_2),(R_3)\text{ hold as stated.}

knowledge_statements.title: MPEC Reformulation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT-based single-level reformulation of a convex lower-level problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the lower problem is \(\min_y f(x,y)\) subject to \(g(x,y)\le0\), where for fixed \(x\), the functions are differentiable and convex in \(y\), and Slater's condition holds. Then \(y\) solves the lower problem if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that
\[\nabla_y f(x,y)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla_y g_i(x,y)=0,\quad g(x,y)\le0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x,y)=0\ \text{for all }i.\]
Substituting these conditions into the upper-level model produces an MPEC whose complementarity equations are intrinsically nonsmooth and violate standard constraint qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and Slater regularity, lower-level optimality is equivalent to KKT conditions, yielding a single-level program with complementarity constraints.
assumptions_latex: For fixed \(x\), \(f(x,\cdot)\) and each \(g_i(x,\cdot)\) are differentiable and convex
Slater's condition holds for the lower-level inequalities
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\) is lower-level optimal if and only if the displayed KKT system holds for some \(\lambda\ge0\)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The KKT-based representation is appropriate for an MPEC reformulation, and convexity plus Slater regularity supports KKT sufficiency. However, complementarity products are not intrinsically nonsmooth when their defining functions are differentiable; it is the complementarity feasible geometry or nonsmooth reformulations that cause the difficulty. The blanket constraint-qualification statement also needs precise qualification and an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed nonlinear-complementarity representation of an MPEC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the VI-Lagrangian and slack-variable mapping used to express the KKT reformulation as a complementarity-constrained optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For (x,y,\lambda)\in Z\times\mathbb R_+^\ell, define L(x,y,\lambda)=F(x,y)+\sum_{i=1}^\ell\lambda_i\nabla_y g_i(x,y). Introduce u\in\mathbb R_+^\ell and define G(x,y,\lambda,u)=\begin{pmatrix}L(x,y,\lambda)\\u+g(x,y)\end{pmatrix}. Then the KKT formulation can be written as minimizing f(x,y) subject to (x,y)\in Z,\ G(x,y,\lambda,u)=0,\ (\lambda,u)\geq0, and \lambda\circ u=0, where (\lambda\circ u)_i=\lambda_i u_i. The same form with an arbitrary mapping G models an optimization problem constrained by a general complementarity system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI-Lagrangian combines the VI mapping with the constraint gradients and multipliers. A nonnegative slack converts the inequalities and complementary multipliers into a nonlinear equation, nonnegativity conditions, and componentwise complementarity. The same template represents optimization with general complementarity constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(x,y,\lambda,u)=0,\quad (\lambda,u)\geq0,\quad \lambda\circ u=0\quad\text{is the mixed nonlinear-complementarity form of the KKT-reformulated MPEC}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit-programming reduction of an MPEC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eliminates an unconstrained equilibrium variable through a single-valued generalized-equation solution map; Lipschitz directional differentiability is an additional regime supporting analysis and numerical methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the MPEC solution map $S$ is single-valued on $U_{\mathrm{ad}}$ and $Z=\mathbb R^k$. Then the equilibrium variable can be eliminated and the MPEC is reduced to
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in U_{\mathrm{ad}}}\Theta(x),\qquad \Theta(x):=f(x,S(x)),
\]
where $S$ is implicitly defined by the generalized equation. Techniques based on this reduction are called the implicit-programming approach. If, additionally, $S$ is Lipschitz and directionally differentiable, this formulation can be used to derive optimality conditions and as a basis for numerical methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the equilibrium solution map is single-valued and the equilibrium variable has no separate constraints, that variable can be eliminated, producing an optimization problem in x alone with objective f(x,S(x)). This is the implicit-programming approach. Lipschitz directional differentiability of S is an additional condition supporting optimality analysis and numerical methods.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is the solution map implicitly defined by the generalized equation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in U_{\mathrm{ad}}}\Theta(x),\qquad \Theta(x)=f(x,S(x));\quad S\text{ Lipschitz and directionally differentiable}\Rightarrow\text{ suitability for optimality analysis and numerical methods}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT reformulation of a convex lower-level problem as an MPEC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the KKT-based single-level representation, solution-correspondence directions, and the nonconvex and reverse-local failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that, for every feasible upper-level decision \(x\), the lower-level problem \(\min_y\{g(x,y):d(x,y)\ge 0\}\) is convex, has a nonempty compact feasible region, and satisfies an appropriate constraint qualification. Then its KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient, permitting replacement of the lower-level optimality condition by \(\nabla_y g(x,y)-\nabla_y d(x,y)\lambda=0\) and \(0\le\lambda\perp d(x,y)\ge0\). Under lower-level Slater qualification, each global or local bilevel solution corresponds to a global or local MPEC solution, respectively, and each global MPEC solution corresponds to a global bilevel solution. The reverse local correspondence can fail without stronger assumptions guaranteeing multiplier uniqueness. If the lower-level problem is nonconvex, an MPEC solution may be infeasible for the bilevel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex lower-level problem with a nonempty compact feasible region and a suitable constraint qualification, the follower problem can be replaced by its KKT system to obtain an MPEC. Slater qualification supports the stated global correspondences and the bilevel-to-MPEC local correspondence, but a local MPEC solution need not be locally bilevel-optimal without multiplier uniqueness. The reformulation can fail for a nonconvex lower level.
assumptions_latex: f,g,c,d\text{ are at least continuously differentiable in their arguments}
\forall x\text{ feasible at the upper level, the lower-level problem is convex}
\forall x\text{ feasible at the upper level, }\{y:d(x,y)\ge0\}\text{ is nonempty and compact}
\text{Lower-level Slater qualification holds for the stated solution correspondences}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla_y g(x,y)-\nabla_y d(x,y)\lambda=0,\quad 0\le\lambda\perp d(x,y)\ge0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global-minimizer equivalence of the MPEC KKT reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers global minimizers between a VI-constrained MPEC and its KKT complementarity formulation, with a bounded-multiplier formulation under compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the assumptions of the preceding KKT characterization theorem, the original MPEC is equivalent to minimizing f(x,y) over (x,y)\in Z and \lambda\in\mathbb R_+^\ell subject to F(x,y)+\sum_{i=1}^\ell\lambda_i\nabla_y g_i(x,y)=0,\ g(x,y)\leq0, and \lambda^Tg(x,y)=0. If (x^*,y^*) is a global minimizer of the original problem, then (x^*,y^*,\lambda^*) is a global minimizer of the KKT formulation for every \lambda^*\in M(x^*,y^*). Conversely, any globally minimizing triple with \lambda^*\in M(x^*,y^*) projects to a global minimizer (x^*,y^*) of the original problem. If Z is additionally compact, there exists c>0 such that an equivalent formulation is obtained by imposing \lambda\in\mathbb B(0,c)\cap\mathbb R_+^\ell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding theorem's assumptions, replacing the VI constraint by its KKT stationarity, feasibility, nonnegativity, and complementarity conditions preserves global minimizers. Every multiplier at an original global minimizer produces a globally minimizing lifted triple, and every globally minimizing lifted triple projects to an original global minimizer. If the side-constraint set is compact, one fixed bound on the multiplier can be imposed without losing equivalence.
assumptions_latex: g_i(x,\cdot)\text{ is convex for every }x\in X
\nabla_y g_i\text{ exists and is continuous on an open set containing }\mathcal F
Z\text{ is compact for the bounded-multiplier formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}(\mathrm{MPEC})\Rightarrow\forall\lambda^*\in M(x^*,y^*),\ (x^*,y^*,\lambda^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}(\mathrm{KKT});\quad (x^*,y^*,\lambda^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}(\mathrm{KKT})\Rightarrow(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname*{argmin}(\mathrm{MPEC});\quad Z\text{ compact}\Rightarrow\exists c>0\text{ permitting }\|\lambda\|\leq c.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mathematical programs with affine equilibrium constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The affine-equilibrium subclass of MPECs and its mixed linear complementarity reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F(x,y)=q+Nx+My$ and $g(x,y)=b+Ax+By$. The corresponding KKT-form MPEC is
$\min f(x,y)$ subject to $(x,y)\in Z$, $q+Nx+My+B^T\lambda=0$, $\lambda\ge0$, $b+Ax+By\le0$, and $\lambda^T(b+Ax+By)=0$. Apart from $(x,y)\in Z$, these constraints form a mixed linear complementarity system. An MPEC whose equilibrium constraint is an AVI is called a mathematical program with affine equilibrium constraints (MPAEC). If $Z$ is polyhedral, its feasible set is a finite union of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An MPAEC is a mathematical program whose equilibrium constraint is an affine variational inequality. Its KKT formulation consists of affine stationarity, primal and dual inequalities, and complementary slackness; except for a possible joint constraint in Z, it has mixed linear complementarity form. With polyhedral Z, the feasible set is a finite union of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ has the displayed mixed linear complementarity representation, and if }Z\text{ is polyhedral then }\mathcal F\text{ is a finite union of polyhedra.}

knowledge_statements.title: Strategic-Game Gap Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nikaido–Isoda-type gap certificate for a finite cost-minimization game.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider players \(i=1,\ldots,p\) with nonempty strategy sets \(X_i\), product set \(X:=\prod_iX_i\), and costs \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\). Define
\[G(x):=\sup_{y\in X}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(y_i,x_{-i})\bigr).\]
Because \(y=x\) is admissible, \(G(x)\ge0\). A profile \(x^*\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(G(x^*)=0\): the zero value certifies that no player can decrease its cost by a unilateral feasible deviation. The supremum structure generally makes \(G\) nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The game gap is the largest aggregate gain from unilateral deviations; it is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at Nash equilibria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is a Nash equilibrium if and only if \(G(x^*)=0\)

notation.meaning: strategies of all players except i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind exactly fits the strategic-game gap leaf, and for the product strategy set the displayed aggregate unilateral-deviation gap is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at Nash equilibria. The exact Nikaido-Isoida-type sign and aggregation convention is source-sensitive, however, and the record provides no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Gap Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nikaido–Isoda gap for finite-player games with independent feasible strategy sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let player \(i\) maximize \(u_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) over a nonempty set \(X_i\), and let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\). Assuming each unilateral optimal value is finite, define the equilibrium gap by \[G(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N\left(\sup_{y_i\in X_i}u_i(y_i,x_{-i})-u_i(x_i,x_{-i})\right),\qquad x\in X.\] Then \(G(x)\ge 0\), and \(G(x)=0\) exactly when every \(x_i\) is a best response to \(x_{-i}\), equivalently when \(x\) is a Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gap sums all players’ maximal unilateral gains. It is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at Nash equilibria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x)\ge 0\), and \(G(x)=0\iff x\) is a Nash equilibrium.

knowledge_statements.title: Disequilibrium Merit Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-best-response merit model for games with possibly set-valued response maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\), define the best-response correspondence \(B(x)=\prod_{i=1}^N B_i(x_{-i})\), where \[B_i(x_{-i})=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y_i\in X_i}u_i(y_i,x_{-i}).\] If every \(B_i(x_{-i})\) is nonempty, the disequilibrium merit function \[D(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,B(x))=\inf_{y\in B(x)}\lVert x-y\rVert\] is nonnegative. When \(B(x)\) is closed, \(D(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in B(x)\), hence precisely when \(x\) is a Nash equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disequilibrium is measured by distance from the current strategy profile to its joint best-response set; zero merit characterizes equilibrium when that set is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\neq\varnothing\) and \(B_i(x_{-i})\neq\varnothing\) for every player and profile.
\(B(x)\) is closed in the chosen finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(x)\ge 0\), and \(D(x)=0\iff x\in B(x)\iff x\) is a Nash equilibrium.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear complementarity problems whose coefficient matrix is symmetric, without assuming positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the linear complementarity problem \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) seeks \(z,w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[w=Mz+q,\qquad z\ge 0,\qquad w\ge 0,\qquad z^{\mathsf T}w=0.\] It is a symmetric LCP model when \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\). Symmetry alone imposes no sign condition on \(z^{\mathsf T}Mz\) and therefore does not by itself make the associated quadratic objective convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric LCP has a symmetric coefficient matrix. Symmetry alone does not imply monotonicity or convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is symmetric; positive semidefiniteness is not implied.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP monotonicity expressed through the positive-semidefinite quadratic form of the coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine mapping \(F(z)=Mz+q\) and its linear complementarity problem are monotone when \[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle=(x-y)^{\mathsf T}M(x-y)\ge 0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently, \(v^{\mathsf T}Mv\ge 0\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or the symmetric part \((M+M^{\mathsf T})/2\) is positive semidefinite. The matrix \(M\) need not itself be symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP is monotone when its affine map is monotone, equivalently when the symmetric part of its matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is monotone \(\iff v^{\mathsf T}Mv\ge0\) for all \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\iff (M+M^{\mathsf T})/2\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Monotone LCP Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic-program representation of an LCP with a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\) and \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A vector \(z\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) if and only if it solves the convex quadratic program \[\min_{x\ge0}\left\{\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Mx+q^{\mathsf T}x\right\}.\] Indeed, the optimality system is \(z\ge0\), \(w=Mz+q\ge0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}w=0\). Thus the LCP solution set equals the minimizer set, including the possibility that both are empty when the objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric monotone LCP is exactly the optimality system of a convex quadratic program over the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\ge0}\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Mx+q^{\mathsf T}x\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be positive semidefinite, let $(B,C)$ be a splitting of $M$ such that $B-M$ is symmetric positive definite, and let $q\in K(M)$. For every initial vector $z^0\ge 0$, the iteration specified by the splitting algorithm produces a uniquely defined sequence $\{z^\nu\}$ that converges to a solution of $\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If M is positive semidefinite and its splitting (B,C) satisfies that B−M is symmetric positive definite, then for every q in K(M) and every nonnegative starting vector, the referenced splitting iteration is uniquely defined and converges to a solution of LCP(q,M).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{z^\nu\}\text{ is uniquely defined and converges to some }z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M).

children.title: P-Matrix LCP Models
children.top_down_role: Linear complementarity models governed by P-matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: P-Matrix LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP class characterized by strict positivity of every principal minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a P-matrix when every principal minor of \(M\) is strictly positive. An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is a P-matrix LCP when its coefficient matrix has this property. Equivalently, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there exists an index \(i\) such that \(x_i(Mx)_i>0\). For a P-matrix, \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) has a unique solution for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A P-matrix has all principal minors positive; its LCP has exactly one solution for every right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a P-matrix \(\Longrightarrow |\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)|=1\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

children.title: P0-Matrix LCP Models

knowledge_statements.title: P0-Matrix LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure-type relaxation of the P-matrix class using nonnegative principal minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a P0-matrix when every principal minor of \(M\) is nonnegative. An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is a P0-matrix LCP when its coefficient matrix satisfies this condition. Equivalently, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there exists an index \(i\) with \(x_i\ne0\) and \(x_i(Mx)_i\ge0\). This class contains all P-matrices but does not retain their universal uniqueness conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A P0-matrix has all principal minors nonnegative. This includes P-matrices but does not guarantee unique LCP solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in P_0\iff \det(M_{II})\ge0\) for every principal index set \(I\).

children.title: Sufficient-Matrix LCP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient-Matrix LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP class based on simultaneous row- and column-sufficiency of the coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is column sufficient when \[x_i(Mx)_i\le0\ \text{for every }i\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_i(Mx)_i=0\ \text{for every }i.\] It is row sufficient when \(M^{\mathsf T}\) is column sufficient, and sufficient when it is both row and column sufficient. An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is a sufficient-matrix LCP when \(M\) is sufficient. This class supports strong structural and algorithmic properties without requiring symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficient matrix is both row and column sufficient, as defined by a componentwise sign implication involving x and Mx.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is sufficient \(\iff M\) and \(M^{\mathsf T}\) are column sufficient.

children.title: Q-Matrix LCP Models
children.top_down_role: Linear complementarity models organized by Q-matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Q-Matrix LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP class defined by solvability for every offset vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a Q-matrix when, for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\), there exist \(z,w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[w=Mz+q,\qquad z\ge0,\qquad w\ge0,\qquad z^{\mathsf T}w=0.\] Thus an LCP with a Q-matrix coefficient belongs to a class having universal existence over right-hand sides. The Q-property does not, by itself, assert uniqueness of the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Q-matrix produces at least one LCP solution for every right-hand side, but it need not produce a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in Q\iff\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

children.title: Copositive LCP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Copositive LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP class whose coefficient matrix has a nonnegative quadratic form on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is copositive when \[x^{\mathsf T}Mx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n.\] An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is copositive when its coefficient matrix has this property. Unlike positive semidefiniteness, copositivity tests the quadratic form only on the nonnegative orthant; it therefore does not imply monotonicity of the affine mapping on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A copositive LCP matrix has a nonnegative quadratic form on nonnegative vectors, a weaker domain requirement than positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is copositive \(\iff x^{\mathsf T}Mx\ge0\) for every \(x\ge0\).

children.title: Semimonotone LCP Models
children.top_down_role: Linear complementarity models organized by semimonotone matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Semimonotone LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semimonotone matrix class, also commonly denoted by the class E0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is semimonotone when, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\), there exists an index \(i\) satisfying \[x_i>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad (Mx)_i\ge0.\] An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is semimonotone when its coefficient matrix satisfies this condition. Equivalently, there is no nonzero \(x\ge0\) for which \((Mx)_i<0\) at every index in the positive support of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semimonotone matrix maps every nonzero nonnegative vector to a vector having a nonnegative component on that vector’s positive support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in E_0\iff (\forall x\ge0,\ x\ne0)(\exists i)\ x_i>0\ \text{and}\ (Mx)_i\ge0\).

notation.meaning: indices i for which x_i is positive

knowledge_statements.title: Z-Matrix LCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LCP class with nonpositive off-diagonal matrix entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a Z-matrix when \[m_{ij}\le0\qquad\text{for all distinct }i,j.\] Equivalently, \(M=sI-B\) for some scalar \(s\in\mathbb{R}\) and some entrywise nonnegative matrix \(B\). An LCP model \(\operatorname{LCP}(q,M)\) is a Z-matrix LCP when its coefficient matrix is a Z-matrix. No restriction on the diagonal entries, solvability, or uniqueness follows from the Z-property alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Z-matrix has nonpositive off-diagonal entries. This sign pattern alone does not ensure LCP existence or uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is a Z-matrix \(\iff m_{ij}\le0\) whenever \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: entry of M in row i and column j

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone NCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional NCP with a monotone mapping on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The monotone nonlinear complementarity problem is to find \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[
x\ge 0,\qquad F(x)\ge 0,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0,
\]
where inequalities are componentwise and \(F\) is monotone on \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\), meaning
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n.
\]
Equivalently, every component satisfies \(x_iF_i(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone NCP seeks complementary nonnegative vectors x and F(x), with F satisfying the monotonicity inequality on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone NCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional NCP whose defining mapping fails monotonicity on the orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A nonmonotone nonlinear complementarity model seeks \(x\) satisfying
\[
x\ge0,\qquad F(x)\ge0,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0,
\]
but \(F\) is not monotone on \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\). Thus there exist \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\) for which
\[
\langle F(u)-F(v),u-v\rangle<0.
\]
Nonmonotonicity classifies the mapping; it does not alter the complementarity conditions defining a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmonotone NCP retains the usual complementarity conditions but has a mapping that violates the monotonicity inequality somewhere on the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\), while \(F\) is nonmonotone.

children.title: Bounded NCP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded NCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard NCP supplemented by finite a priori upper bounds on its variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(F:[0,u]\to\mathbb{R}^n\), a bounded NCP model seeks \(x\in[0,u]\) satisfying the ordinary NCP conditions
\[
x	hickspace\ge	hickspace0,\qquad F(x)	hickspace\ge	hickspace0,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle	hickspace=	hickspace0.
\]
Hence \(x_i>0\) implies \(F_i(x)=0\), including when \(x_i=u_i\). The upper bound restricts the admissible domain but does not introduce the upper-bound sign condition used by a box-constrained complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded NCP imposes finite upper caps on variables while retaining ordinary nonnegative complementarity, including at an attained upper cap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in[0,u]\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\).

children.title: Box-Constrained NCP Models
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear complementarity models whose feasible region has box geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained NCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity model with finite lower and upper bounds and bound-dependent signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(\ell_i<u_i\), and let \(F:B\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A box-constrained NCP solution is a point \(x\in B\) satisfying, for every \(i\),
\[
x_i=\ell_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\ge0,\qquad
\ell_i<x_i<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)=0,\qquad
x_i=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\le0.
\]
Equivalently, it solves the generalized equation \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\), with \(N_B\) the convex-analytic normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component is either at its lower bound with nonnegative residual, interior with zero residual, or at its upper bound with nonpositive residual.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the box at x

children.title: Active-Bound NCP Regimes
children.top_down_role: Residual behavior associated with solutions on active lower or upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Bound NCP Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index partition and residual signs induced by a box-complementarity solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a solution \(x\) of the box-constrained complementarity problem on \(B=[\ell,u]\), define
\[
L(x)=\{i:x_i=\ell_i\},\quad I(x)=\{i:\ell_i<x_i<u_i\},\quad U(x)=\{i:x_i=u_i\}.
\]
These sets form a disjoint partition of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and complementarity imposes
\[
F_i(x)\ge0\ \text{on }L(x),\qquad F_i(x)=0\ \text{on }I(x),\qquad F_i(x)\le0\ \text{on }U(x).
\]
A bound is strongly active when the corresponding displayed inequality is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-active, interior, and upper-active indices partition all variables and determine the allowable residual sign in each regime.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) solves the box-constrained complementarity problem on \([\ell,u]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x)\), \(I(x)\), and \(U(x)\) partition the indices and impose the stated residual signs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed P0 and Mixed P Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a partitioned matrix with two m-column blocks and one ell-column block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q=[A\ B\ C], where A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+\ell)\times m} and C\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+\ell)\times\ell}. It has the mixed P_0 property if C has full column rank and, for every r,s\in\mathbb{R}^m and t\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}, Ar+Bs+Ct=0 and (r,s)\ne0 imply that r_i s_i\ge0 for some i satisfying |r_i|+|s_i|>0. It has the mixed P property if C has full column rank and the same hypotheses imply r_i s_i>0 for some i. When \ell=0, C is vacuous and the qualifier \text{mixed} is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitioned matrix [A B C] has the mixed P0 property when C has full column rank and every nonzero pair (r,s) satisfying Ar+Bs+Ct=0 has an index with a nonzero pair of components and nonnegative product. It has the mixed P property when some component product must be strictly positive. If C is absent, these are called the P0 and P properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ satisfies the stated mixed }P_0\text{ or mixed }P\text{ definition; when }\ell=0\text{, the qualifier mixed is omitted.}

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Bound MCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed complementarity problem with two finite bounds on every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\ell_i<u_i\), and let \(F:[\ell,u]\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The finite-bound mixed complementarity problem seeks \(x\in[\ell,u]\) such that, for each \(i\),
\[
F_i(x)\ge0\ \text{if }x_i=\ell_i,\qquad
F_i(x)=0\ \text{if }\ell_i<x_i<u_i,\qquad
F_i(x)\le0\ \text{if }x_i=u_i.
\]
This componentwise system is equivalent to \(0\in F(x)+N_{[\ell,u]}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-bound MCP gives every variable finite lower and upper bounds, with the residual sign determined by whether the variable is lower-active, interior, or upper-active.

notation.meaning: normal cone to the finite box

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided-Bound MCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MCP allowing components with only a finite lower bound or only a finite upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), where endpoints may be infinite but \(\ell_i<u_i\), and let \(F:B\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A one-sided-bound MCP seeks \(x\in B\) satisfying
\[
\ell_i<x_i<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)=0,
\]
together with \(x_i=\ell_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\ge0\) when \(\ell_i\) is finite, and \(x_i=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\le0\) when \(u_i\) is finite. At least one component has exactly one finite endpoint. Equivalently, \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided-bound MCP permits infinite endpoints and applies a residual inequality only at each finite active endpoint; interior components have zero residual.
assumptions_latex: At least one interval has exactly one finite endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\) with the stated one-sided component conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit MCP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone inclusion representation of mixed complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) be a nonempty closed box, allowing infinite endpoints, and let \(F:B\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The implicit mixed complementarity model is the generalized equation
\[
0\in F(x)+N_B(x).
\]
It is equivalent to the componentwise conditions
\[
x_i=\ell_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\ge0,\quad
\ell_i<x_i<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)=0,\quad
x_i=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\le0,
\]
with a bound implication omitted when its endpoint is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An MCP can be written implicitly as a zero of the sum of its residual mapping and the normal-cone mapping of the bound box.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed Cartesian box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\) is equivalent to the MCP component conditions.

children.title: Conic Complementarity Problems
children.top_down_role: Complementarity systems posed relative to cone geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Complementarity Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity over a closed convex cone and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let
\[
K^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,z\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }z\in K\},
\]
and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The conic complementarity problem is to find \(x\in K\) such that
\[
F(x)\in K^*,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0.
\]
For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^n\), these conditions reduce to the ordinary nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic complementarity solution lies in a cone, its image lies in the dual cone, and the two vectors are orthogonal.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in K\), \(F(x)\in K^*\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\).

children.title: Generalized Complementarity Problems
children.top_down_role: Complementarity systems extending the standard orthant-based problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Complementarity Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-map complementarity model over a cone-dual-cone pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(G,H:D\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The generalized complementarity problem is to find \(z\in D\) satisfying
\[
G(z)\in K,\qquad H(z)\in K^*,\qquad \langle G(z),H(z)\rangle=0.
\]
The conic complementarity problem is recovered by taking \(D=K\), \(G(z)=z\), and \(H(z)=F(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized complementarity problem requires two mapped vectors to belong to dual cones and be orthogonal, with conic complementarity as a specialization.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(z)\in K\), \(H(z)\in K^*\), and \(\langle G(z),H(z)\rangle=0\).

children.title: Cone-Induced Residual Models
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth residual representations arising from cone-based complementarity structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Induced Residual Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural projection residual for finite-dimensional conic complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\Pi_K\) denote Euclidean projection onto \(K\). Define the natural cone residual by
\[
R_K(x)=x-\Pi_K\bigl(x-F(x)\bigr),\qquad x\in K.
\]
Then
\[
R_K(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in K,\quad F(x)\in K^*,\quad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0.
\]
Thus conic complementarity is represented as the generally nonsmooth equation \(R_K(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the cone yields a natural residual whose zeros are exactly the conic complementarity solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_K(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) solves the conic complementarity problem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard natural-map residual for cone complementarity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The natural projection residual and its zero-set characterization are mathematically standard, and representation is the correct content kind, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Affine Variational Inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional variational inequality with an affine operator on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and let \(q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The affine variational inequality \(\operatorname{AVI}(C,M,q)\) is to find \(x\in C\) such that
\[
\langle Mx+q,y-x\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
0\in Mx+q+N_C(x).
\]
No conic, polyhedral, or monotonicity assumption is part of the definition; monotonicity holds when the symmetric part of \(M\) is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine VI seeks a point in a closed convex set whose affine image has nonnegative pairing with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Mx+q,y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous linear operator on a finite-dimensional closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). The linear variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,M)\) is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
\langle Mx^\star,y-x^\star\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, \(x^\star\) solves the normal-cone inclusion \(0\in Mx^\star+N_C(x^\star)\), where \(N_C(x):=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le 0\text{ for all }y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear VI seeks a feasible point whose image under a linear map has a nonnegative inner product with every feasible direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in C\) and \(\langle Mx^\star,y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for all \(y\in C\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to C at x
linear variational inequality determined by C and M

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-to-Linear Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous linear VI obtained by setting the affine offset to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and consider the affine variational inequality with \(F(x)=Mx+q\). Its solution set is
\[
\operatorname{SOL}(C,M,q):=\{x\in C:\langle Mx+q,y-x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
\]
When \(q=0\), this problem specializes exactly to the linear variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,M)\), and \(\operatorname{SOL}(C,M,0)=\{x\in C:0\in Mx+N_C(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Setting the constant term of an affine VI to zero yields the corresponding homogeneous linear VI without changing the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q=0\Longrightarrow \operatorname{SOL}(C,M,q)=\{x\in C:0\in Mx+N_C(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: solution set of the affine variational inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional VI with an unrestricted nonlinear single-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a single-valued map, not assumed affine. The nonlinear variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) asks for \(x^\star\in C\) satisfying
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
With the convex normal cone convention, this is equivalent to the generalized equation \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear VI finds a feasible point where the nonlinear operator forms a nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in C\) and \(\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Characterization of a Product-Set VI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposes the global variational inequality into blockwise inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a product feasible set \(X=\prod_i X_i\) and a correspondingly partitioned mapping \(f=(f_i)_i\), a vector \(x^*\in X\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(X,f)\) if and only if
\[
(x_i-x_i^*)^{\prime}f_i(x^*)\ge0\qquad\forall x_i\in X_i,\ \forall i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian-product feasible set, a point solves the global variational inequality exactly when it satisfies the variational inequality separately in every block while the other blocks remain fixed at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(X,f)\iff (x_i-x_i^*)^{\prime}f_i(x^*)\ge0\quad\forall x_i\in X_i,\ \forall i.
