knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Convergence under Block Pseudo-Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers well-defined nonlinear Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel iterations induced by a linearized VI map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to X\) be the one-iteration map of a linearized algorithm determined by block-diagonal positive-definite scaling matrices \(\{A(x):x\in X\}\). Suppose \(T\) is a pseudo-contraction with respect to a block-maximum norm, and let \(x^*\) be its fixed point. If the nonlinear Jacobi iteration
\[
x(t+1)=Q(x(t))
\]
is well defined, meaning that its defining variational inequality always has a solution, then \(x(t)\to x^*\) geometrically. The corresponding nonlinear Gauss\text{-}Seidel algorithm also converges geometrically to \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linearized VI map built from positive-definite block-diagonal scalings, block pseudo-contraction implies geometric convergence of the nonlinear Jacobi and nonlinear Gauss–Seidel algorithms, provided the nonlinear Jacobi subproblem is solvable at every iteration.

T\text{ is a pseudo-contraction in a block-maximum norm}.
Q(x)\text{ is well defined for every iterate, equivalently its defining VI always has a solution}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x(t)\to x^*\text{ geometrically for both the nonlinear Jacobi and nonlinear Gauss\text{-}Seidel algorithms}.

children.title: Box Variational Inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Box Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate characterization for a finite box, including infinite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=[\ell,u]:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ell_i\le x_i\le u_i\}\), where \(\ell_i<u_i\) and endpoints may be infinite, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x^\star\in C\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) if and only if, for every coordinate \(i\),
\[
\ell_i<x_i^\star<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x^\star)=0,
\quad x_i^\star=\ell_i\Rightarrow F_i(x^\star)\ge0,
\quad x_i^\star=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x^\star)\le0,
\]
with conditions involving an infinite endpoint omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a box, the VI is equivalent to coordinatewise zero, nonnegative, or nonpositive operator values according to which bounds are active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) exactly when the displayed coordinate conditions hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercivity and exact minimization of the box-Q merit function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global merit-function result for a variational inequality on a compact rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact rectangle and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous. Then \(\theta_{\mathrm Q}^{\mathrm{box}}\) is coercive: \(\lim_{\lVert x\rVert\to\infty}\theta_{\mathrm Q}^{\mathrm{box}}(x)=+\infty\). Consequently, \(\theta_{\mathrm Q}^{\mathrm{box}}\) attains an unconstrained minimum, and each minimizing point solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: VI over a convex polyhedron represented through KKT-type multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\,Ex=d\}\) be nonempty and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x^\star\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) if and only if there exist multipliers \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(\nu\) such that
\[
F(x^\star)+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda+E^{\mathsf T}\nu=0,
\quad Ax^\star\le b,
\quad Ex^\star=d,
\quad \lambda_i(Ax^\star-b)_i=0\ \text{for every }i.
\]
Thus the polyhedral VI is represented by feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI over a polyhedron is equivalent to a multiplier system comprising primal feasibility, stationarity, dual nonnegativity, and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\) if and only if the displayed multiplier system is feasible.

children.title: Conic Variational Inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: VI on a closed convex cone expressed through dual-cone complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(K^*:=\{z:\langle z,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for all }x\in K\}\), and let \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x^\star\in K\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\) if and only if
\[
x^\star\in K,
\qquad F(x^\star)\in K^*,
\qquad \langle F(x^\star),x^\star\rangle=0.
\]
Hence a conic VI is equivalently a nonlinear complementarity problem over the primal-dual cone pair \((K,K^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed convex cone, the VI is equivalent to primal membership, dual membership of the operator value, and orthogonality.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff x^\star\in K,\ F(x^\star)\in K^*,\ \langle F(x^\star),x^\star\rangle=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard complementarity representation of a variational inequality on a cone

children.title: Monotone VI Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone VI Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity condition and convexity of the resulting VI solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A map \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) defines a monotone VI regime when
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
If \(F\) is also continuous, then the Stampacchia solution set equals
\[
\{x\in C:\langle F(y),y-x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C\},
\]
and is therefore convex; it may nevertheless be empty or contain multiple points without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI is monotone when operator differences have nonnegative pairing with point differences; under continuity its solution set is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotonicity implies the displayed Minty representation and convexity of the VI solution set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard monotonicity predicate and finite-dimensional Minty characterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly requires both monotonicity and continuity for the Minty equivalence, but conclusion_latex incorrectly attributes that equivalence to monotonicity alone. A supporting source and a conclusion explicitly retaining continuity are required.

children.title: Nonmonotone VI Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone VI Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the monotonicity inequality on the feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The associated VI is in a nonmonotone regime when there exist \(x,y\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle<0.
\]
For example, on \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), the linear map \(F(x)=Mx\) is nonmonotone exactly when the symmetric part \((M+M^{\mathsf T})/2\) is not positive semidefinite. In this regime, monotonicity-based convexity and Minty-equivalence conclusions are not generally available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI is nonmonotone when some pair violates the monotonicity inequality; an indefinite symmetric part produces this failure for linear maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x,y\in C:\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle<0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: logical negation of monotonicity with the standard linear-operator characterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure_boundary fits the leaf, and the negation of monotonicity is correct. The plain statement’s “indefinite symmetric part” is narrower than the displayed exact condition “not positive semidefinite,” and no source is supplied.

children.title: Weak-Monotonicity Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate operator regimes near the boundary of monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Monotonicity Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypomonotonicity parameterizes controlled departure from monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A map \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(\rho\)-weakly monotone, for \(\rho\ge0\), when
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge-\rho\|x-y\|^2
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, \(x\mapsto F(x)+\rho x\) is monotone on \(C\). The boundary value \(\rho=0\) recovers monotonicity, while \(\rho>0\) permits a quantitatively bounded monotonicity violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak monotonicity bounds negative curvature by a quadratic term; zero parameter is exactly the boundary of the monotone regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is \(\rho\)-weakly monotone if and only if \(F+\rho I\) is monotone on \(C\).

notation.meaning: identity mapping on the ambient space

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Generalized Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a convex-set VI and a normal-cone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The normal-cone generalized equation seeks \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).
\]
Using \(N_C(x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\), this inclusion holds if and only if
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C,
\]
so it represents precisely the variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the convex normal cone to the operator converts a variational inequality exactly into a generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star)\iff x^\star\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\).

notation.meaning: set-valued sum defining the generalized equation

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal-Monotone Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-finding inclusion governed by a maximal monotone set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\). The operator \(T\) is monotone when
\[
\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge0
\quad\text{whenever }u\in T(x),\ v\in T(y),
\]
and maximal monotone when its graph has no proper monotone extension in \(H\times H\). A maximal-monotone inclusion is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in H\) such that \(0\in T(x^\star)\). Its solution set is the zero set \(T^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal-monotone inclusion seeks a zero of a monotone set-valued operator whose graph cannot be enlarged while retaining monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Find \(x^\star\in T^{-1}(0)=\{x\in H:0\in T(x)\}\) with \(T\) maximal monotone.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Set-Valued Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued zero inclusion whose operator violates graph monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\). The inclusion \(0\in T(x)\) is governed by a nonmonotone operator when there exist \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}T\) satisfying
\[
\langle u-v,x-y\rangle<0.
\]
Thus \(T\) fails the monotonicity predicate, and it cannot be maximal monotone. The solution set remains \(T^{-1}(0):=\{x\in H:0\in T(x)\}\), but conclusions and algorithms requiring operator monotonicity do not apply without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued inclusion is nonmonotone when two graph points have a negative monotonicity pairing, although its zero set remains well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gra}T:\langle u-v,x-y\rangle<0\).

notation.meaning: set of pairs (x,u) with u in T(x)

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the canonical displacement residual for a single-valued fixed-point equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-point problem of finding \(x\in D\) such that \(x=T(x)\), define the displacement residual by \[R_T(x):=x-T(x).\] Its zero set is exactly the fixed-point set: \[R_T^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{Fix}(T):=\{x\in D:x=T(x)\}.\] Thus the norm merit function \(m(x):=\lVert R_T(x)\rVert\) is nonnegative and satisfies \(m(x)=0\) exactly at fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting a mapping value from its argument produces a residual whose zeros are precisely the mapping's fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(T:D\to X\) is defined on a nonempty set \(D\subseteq X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Function Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise equation reformulation of the nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the scalar minimum function and its componentwise residual by \[\phi_{\min}(a,b):=\min\{a,b\},\qquad (r_{\min}(x))_i:=\phi_{\min}(x_i,F_i(x)).\] For scalars, \(\phi_{\min}(a,b)=0\) holds exactly when \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(ab=0\). Consequently, \[r_{\min}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge0,\quad F(x)\ge0,\quad x_iF_i(x)=0\ \text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The componentwise minimum of a variable and its mapping value vanishes exactly at nonlinear complementarity solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\min}(x)=0\iff 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative C-Function Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic complementarity-function construction, covering residuals other than minimum and Fischer-Burmeister.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar complementarity function is any function \(\psi:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) whose zero set is exactly \[\{(a,b):a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0\}.\] Its induced nonlinear-complementarity residual is defined componentwise by \[(r_\psi(x))_i:=\psi(x_i,F_i(x)),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Therefore \[r_\psi(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge0,\quad F(x)\ge0,\quad x_iF_i(x)=0\ \text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any scalar function whose zeros encode complementary nonnegative pairs yields an equivalent componentwise complementarity residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\psi(x)=0\iff 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box Complementarity B-Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar residual functions whose zeros encode lower-bound, interior, and upper-bound complementarity conditions, allowing infinite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \tau\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} and \tau'\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} satisfy \tau<\tau'. A function \phi(\tau,\tau';\cdot,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R} is a B-function if, for every (r,s)\in\mathbb{R}^2, \phi(\tau,\tau';r,s)=0\iff \tau\le r\le\tau'\text{ and }\bigl(r=\tau\Rightarrow s\ge0\bigr),\ \bigl(\tau<r<\tau'\Rightarrow s=0\bigr),\ \bigl(r=\tau'\Rightarrow s\le0\bigr).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A B-function is a scalar residual whose zeros exactly encode box complementarity: s is nonnegative at the lower bound, zero in the interior, and nonpositive at the upper bound. Either endpoint may be infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(\tau,\tau';r,s)=0\iff \tau\le r\le\tau'\ \land\ (r=\tau\Rightarrow s\ge0)\ \land\ (\tau<r<\tau'\Rightarrow s=0)\ \land\ (r=\tau'\Rightarrow s\le0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar residual functions whose zero set exactly represents scalar complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\psi:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) is a complementarity function (C-function) if, for every \((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \[\psi(a,b)=0\iff a\ge 0,\ b\ge 0,\ \text{and }ab=0.\] Equivalently, its zero set is the union of the two nonnegative coordinate semiaxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A C-function is a scalar function of two real variables whose zeros are exactly the complementary nonnegative pairs: both components are nonnegative and their product is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2,\quad \psi(a,b)=0\iff (a\ge0\land b\ge0\land ab=0).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(x:=\Pi_K(z)\) and define the normal-map residual by \[F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z):=F(x)+z-x=F(\Pi_K z)+z-\Pi_K z.\] Then \[F_K^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\Pi_K(z),\ z=x-F(x),\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -F(x)\in N_K(x).\] Hence zeros of the normal map correspond to solutions of the variational inequality \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K\), with the recovery rule \(x=\Pi_K(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal-map zero in the unconstrained variable projects to a variational-inequality solution, and every solution supplies such a zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\), define the natural residual by \[R_\alpha^{\mathrm{nat}}(x):=x-\Pi_K(x-\alpha F(x)).\] The projection characterization gives \[R_\alpha^{\mathrm{nat}}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\Pi_K(x-\alpha F(x))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -F(x)\in N_K(x).\] Therefore its zero set equals the solution set of the variational inequality \[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in K.\] This equivalence holds for every \(\alpha>0\), without monotonicity of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance between a feasible point and its projected forward step vanishes exactly at variational-inequality solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Residual Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic projected fixed-point equation; the natural VI residual is obtained by a forward-step choice of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projected equation associated with \(G\) is \[x=\Pi_K(G(x)),\qquad x\in K.\] Its residual may be written as \[R_G^{\mathrm{proj}}(x):=x-\Pi_K(G(x)),\] so \(R_G^{\mathrm{proj}}(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) solves the projected fixed-point equation. For a variational inequality with mapping \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n\), choosing \(G(x):=x-\alpha F(x)\) with \(\alpha>0\) yields \[R_G^{\mathrm{proj}}(x)=x-\Pi_K(x-\alpha F(x)),\] whose zeros are precisely the variational-inequality solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting a projected mapping value from the current point converts a projected fixed-point condition into a residual equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_G^{\mathrm{proj}}(x)=0\iff x=\Pi_K(G(x))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Residual Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard positive-parameter smoothing of the Fischer-Burmeister residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), define \[\phi_\mu(a,b):=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2\mu^2}-a-b,\qquad (r_\mu(x))_i:=\phi_\mu(x_i,F_i(x)).\] The scalar function \(\phi_\mu\) is continuously differentiable, and \(\phi_\mu(a,b)\to\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Moreover, \[\phi_\mu(a,b)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a>0,\quad b>0,\quad ab=\mu^2.\] Thus solving \(r_\mu(x)=0\) enforces a perturbed-complementarity system whose limiting equation is the Fischer–Burmeister complementarity residual. Smoothness of \(r_\mu\) additionally depends on the regularity of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scalar smoothing replaces complementarity by a perturbed equation converging to the Fischer–Burmeister residual; regularity of the composed residual also depends on the mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\mu(x)=0\iff x_i>0,\ F_i(x)>0,\ x_iF_i(x)=\mu^2\ \text{for every }i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically regularized gap certificate for a finite-dimensional variational inequality.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.1 The regularized gap function p. 913
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\), define \[g_c(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac{c}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2\right\}.\] The supremum is attained uniquely at \(y_c(x)=\Pi_K(x-c^{-1}F(x))\). Because \(y=x\) is admissible, \(g_c(x)\ge0\). Furthermore, \[g_c(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }y\in K.\] Hence the regularized gap is an exact nonnegative merit certificate for the variational inequality, without requiring \(K\) to be bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic regularization makes the gap finite and uniquely attained; its nonnegative value is zero exactly at variational-inequality solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Gap Functions

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_0(x)\ge0\) for \(x\in K\), and \(g_0(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical primal gap obtained by maximizing the linearized variational-inequality violation.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.2 The linearized gap function p. 921
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\), define the linearized gap by \[g_0(x):=\max_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle.\] Compactness of \(K\) ensures that the maximum is attained. Since \(y=x\) is feasible, \(g_0(x)\ge0\). Moreover, \[g_0(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle F(x),x-y\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }y\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).\] Thus \(g_0\) measures the largest violation of the linearized variational-inequality condition and is an exact solution certificate on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest linearized variational-inequality violation over a compact feasible set is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Gap Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2.2 The linearized gap function p. 921

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{a,b}(x)\ge0\) for \(x\in K\), and \(G_{a,b}(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference of two regularized gaps with distinct positive regularization parameters.

source_refs.locator: 10.3 The D-Gap Merit Function p. 930
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[g_c(x):=\sup_{y\in K}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac{c}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2\right\}\] and define the D-gap function by \[G_{a,b}(x):=g_a(x)-g_b(x).\] Since \(0<a<b\), the defining objective for \(g_a\) dominates that for \(g_b\), so \(G_{a,b}(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in K\). In addition, \[G_{a,b}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\Pi_K(x-a^{-1}F(x))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).\] Thus the D-gap is an exact nonnegative merit certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The difference between two regularized gaps is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at variational-inequality solutions when the parameters are ordered.
knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 10.3 The D-Gap Merit Function p. 930

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_c(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the regularized VI envelope sense; the literature contains other implicit-Lagrangian conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in K\), define the regularized implicit Lagrangian bifunction and its envelope by \[L_c(x,y):=\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac{c}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2,\qquad M_c(x):=\sup_{y\in K}L_c(x,y).\] The implicit response is uniquely determined as \[y_c(x):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in K}L_c(x,y)=\Pi_K(x-c^{-1}F(x)).\] Consequently, \(M_c(x)=L_c(x,y_c(x))\ge0\), and \[M_c(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y_c(x)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -F(x)\in N_K(x).\] Thus minimizing the envelope supplies a merit model whose zero set is the variational-inequality solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing a regularized implicit Lagrangian over its auxiliary variable produces a nonnegative envelope whose zeros solve the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Lagrangian Merit Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the claimed implicit-Lagrangian convention. As written, the bifunction and envelope are exactly the regularized gap construction already assigned to another terminal node, and the exact-zero claim functions as a certificate rather than merely a representation. A precise source and locator are required to establish the intended distinct implicit-Lagrangian model and its correct content kind.

knowledge_statements.title: Merit-Model Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of residual-norm merit minimization when consistency or level-boundedness is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous and define \(\psi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert R(x)\rVert^2\). A global minimizer certifies a residual solution only when the minimum value is zero. If \(R^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\), minimizing \(\psi\) cannot produce a residual zero; moreover, without level-boundedness the infimum may be approached only by escaping sequences. For example, \(R(x)=e^{-x}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(R^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\), \(\inf_x\psi(x)=0\), and \(\psi(x_k)\to0\) for \(x_k\to+\infty\), although no certificate point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-norm minimization need not yield a solution: an inconsistent, non-level-bounded residual can have merit values tending to zero only along an escaping sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency and attainment at value \(0\) are necessary for merit minimization to certify \(R(x)=0\).

children.title: Degenerate Residual Systems
children.top_down_role: Residual systems exhibiting deficient local regularity or singular geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-generalized-Jacobian degeneracy for a square locally Lipschitz residual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and suppose \(R(\bar x)=0\). The residual system is Clarke-Jacobian degenerate at \(\bar x\) when its Clarke generalized Jacobian contains a singular matrix; equivalently,
\[\text{there exists }A\in\partial_C R(\bar x)\text{ such that }\det A=0.\]
It is Clarke-Jacobian nondegenerate at \(\bar x\) when every matrix in \(\partial_C R(\bar x)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square locally Lipschitz residual system is Clarke-Jacobian degenerate at a solution when some matrix in its Clarke generalized Jacobian is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is Clarke-Jacobian degenerate at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\partial_C R(\bar x)\) contains a singular matrix.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the residual mapping at the solution.

children.title: Nonisolated Residual Solutions
children.top_down_role: Residual systems whose solution points lack local isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Residual Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological nonisolation of a zero of a continuous residual mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(S=R^{-1}(0)\). A point \(\bar x\in S\) is a nonisolated residual solution if every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains another residual solution. Equivalently,
\[\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}\bigl(S\setminus\{\bar x\}\bigr),\]
or there exists a sequence \((x_k)\subset S\setminus\{\bar x\}\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual solution is nonisolated when distinct residual zeros occur arbitrarily close to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution \(\bar x\) is nonisolated exactly when \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}(S\setminus\{\bar x\})\).

notation.meaning: Zero set of the residual mapping.

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Solution Continua
children.top_down_role: Continuous solution families associated with degenerate residual geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Solution Continua
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-deficient affine residuals exhibit continua of solutions rather than isolated zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}A<n\), choose \(b\in\operatorname{range}A\), and define \(R(x)=Ax-b\). For any particular solution \(x_p\),
\[R^{-1}(0)=x_p+\ker A.\]
Because \(\dim(\ker A)=n-\operatorname{rank}A>0\), the zero set contains an affine continuum through every solution. Thus no residual zero is isolated, and the rank degeneracy supplies nonzero tangent directions along which the residual remains identically zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent rank-deficient affine residual has an affine continuum of zeros, so every solution is nonisolated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is \(x_p+\ker A\), an affine set of positive dimension.

notation.meaning: Any particular solution of the affine residual equation.
Null space of the residual matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inconsistency defined by emptiness of the residual zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A residual system generated by \(R:X\to Y\), where \(X\) is a nonempty set and \(Y\) is a normed space, is inconsistent when
\[R^{-1}(0)=\varnothing.\]
Equivalently, \(R(x)\neq0\) for every \(x\in X\). Inconsistency does not imply a positive residual gap: either \(\inf_{x\in X}\lVert R(x)\rVert>0\), or the infimum can equal zero without being attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual system is inconsistent when it has no zero; its smallest residual norm may nevertheless be either positive or zero but unattained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is inconsistent exactly when \(R^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Residual Level-Set Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition identifying failure of level-boundedness for a residual merit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\psi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert R(x)\rVert^2\). The residual merit model is in an unbounded level-set regime if there exists \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[L_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\psi(x)\leq\alpha\}\]
is nonempty and unbounded. Equivalently, some sequence \((x_k)\) satisfies \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\) while \(\sup_k\psi(x_k)\leq\alpha\). This condition precludes coercivity of \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual merit model has an unbounded level-set regime when bounded merit values occur along a sequence escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some nonempty sublevel set of \(\psi\) is unbounded, so \(\psi\) is not coercive.

notation.meaning: Merit-function sublevel set at level alpha.

children.title: Residual-Regularity Failures
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns of local regularity properties for residual mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Regularity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of metric regularity for a set-valued residual mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) have locally closed graph and let \((\bar x,0)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Metric regularity fails at \((\bar x,0)\) if, for every \(\kappa>0\) and all neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\), there exist \(x\in U\) and \(y\in V\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))>\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x)).\]
Thus no uniform local Lipschitz error estimate holds simultaneously for nearby residual right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual regularity fails when no uniform local distance estimate controls solutions for all nearby right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No neighborhoods and finite constant satisfy the metric-regularity inequality near \((\bar x,0)\).

notation.meaning: Solution set for residual right-hand side y.
Euclidean distance to a point or set.
Graph of the set-valued residual mapping.

children.title: Error-Bound Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where residual size does not reliably control distance to the solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic residual demonstrating failure of a local Lipschitz error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(R:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(R(x)=x^2\), with zero set \(S=\{0\}\). A local Lipschitz error bound at zero would require constants \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|x|\leq\kappa|R(x)|=\kappa x^2\qquad\text{whenever }|x|<\delta.\]
For every finite \(\kappa\), this inequality fails at nonzero \(x\) with \(|x|<\min\{\delta,1/\kappa\}\). Hence vanishing residual need not control solution distance linearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual R(x)=x² has an isolated zero but admits no local linear error bound because the residual vanishes faster than distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite \(\kappa\) and positive \(\delta\) give \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa|R(x)|\) for all \(|x|<\delta\).

children.title: Local-to-Global Error-Bound Gaps
children.top_down_role: Failures arising when local residual control does not extend across larger regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Error-Bound Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded residual exhibiting a local error bound but no global counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(R:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(R(x)=x/(1+|x|)\), so \(S=R^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\). For \(|x|\leq1\),
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|x|\leq2|R(x)|,\]
so a local error bound holds at zero. Globally, however, \(|x|/|R(x)|=1+|x|\) for \(x\neq0\), which is unbounded. Consequently, no finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa|R(x)|\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded residual can control distance near its zero while failing every global linear error bound as points escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A local error bound holds at \(0\), but no global error-bound constant exists.
